Abstract

Abstract. This Latin–English reading and reference edition presents Vitruvius’s
De  architectura with  translation,  notes, and  historical and  architectural
commentary. The English derives from Diego Kurilo’s authorial Spanish
translation;  the  Latin  is  checked  against Krohn  (1912). Documentary
testimony, editorial reconstruction, architectural explanation, and the author’s
hermeneutic proposals are distinguished. The editorial principles define the
scope of the selective apparatus. References follow the Chicago Manual of Style,
18th edition (2024), with American English spelling.
Keywords. Vitruvius; De architectura; Roman architecture; architectural
theory; bilingual  critical edition; Latin philology; history of architecture;
proportion; symmetria; Vitruvian Man.

PRELIMINARY STUDY

The Vitruvian Man





Figure 1. Modern line rendering after Leonardo da Vinci, Vitruvian Man,  c. 1490.
Historical original: Gallerie dell’Accademia, Venice, Gabinetto dei Disegni e delle Stampe,
inv. 228r. Vector source: Wikimedia Commons, Da Vinci Vitruve Luc Viatour 2.svg; public
domain.

Leonardo’s Vitruvian Man, c. 1490, is an individual drawing preserved in the
Gabinetto dei Disegni e delle Stampe of the Gallerie dell’Accademia, Venice,
inv. 228r. The modern line rendering reproduced here derives from that sheet
and  illustrates  the  relationship between  bodily measure and  geometric
construction.

The Geometric Dilemma
Leonardo's drawing is, in essence, an exercise in proportional reconciliation
rather than an attempt to solve the squaring of the circle. In Book III of De
architectura, Vitruvius had proposed that the human body could be inscribed

                            1

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

within both a square and a circle. Mathematically, however, this posed a
difficulty: the squaring of the circle is impossible by means of elementary
Euclidean geometry.
Through  his drawing, Leonardo proposed a graphical  interpretation of
Vitruvius’s description:
•     The square represents the earthly realm—stability and the human
measure derived from height, since the span of the outstretched arms equals the
height of the body. Its center lies at the groin.
•      Leonardo places the center of the circle at the navel and that of the
square at the groin. These distinct centers allow him to reconcile the figures
graphically. The construction does not provide a geometrical solution to
squaring the circle. In the interpretation proposed here, the body mediates
between the stability of the square and the cosmic associations of the circle.

2. Anatomical and Technical Characteristics
Leonardo did not base this drawing on Vitruvius’s text alone; he enriched it with
his own anatomical research:

•      Proportion and modularity. The drawing reflects Leonardo's
preoccupation with the module. He divides the body into sections
governed by the head (approximately one-eighth of the total height) and
the  hand  (approximately  one-tenth),  confirming  the  Vitruvian
measurements through dissection and the study of proportion in living
men.
•     Canon and mechanism. The superimposition of two poses—arms
outstretched horizontally and raised in a V-shape—presents the body at
once as a static canon and as a dynamic mechanism. The lines serve not
as decoration but as axes of symmetry and proportional guides.

3. Philosophical and Symbolic Interpretations
Leonardo’s drawing may be read as a link between earthly and cosmic orders.
The square, centered at the groin, suggests material stability and human
measure. The circle, centered at the navel, suggests perfection and the celestial
realm. These symbolic associations belong to the interpretation proposed here.
•       This reading aligns with the Neoplatonic and Pythagorean tradition,
widely diffused in Renaissance  intellectual  circles, according to which a


                            2

PRELIMINARY STUDY

correspondence was held to obtain between the microcosm (man) and the
macrocosm (the universe).
•      Such  symbolic  interpretations,  however  culturally  significant,
represent a later interpretive layer rather than a direct reconstruction of
Vitruvius’s own intentions, which were proportional and technical.
•       In the author's own interpretive proposal, Leonardo's graphic solution
— the shifting of the two centers — constitutes not merely an anatomical study
but a visual meditation on the tension between ideal geometry and embodied
reality.

4. A Critical Reading: Art or Science?
In scholarly terms, the drawing must be classified as a document of technical
research. Through the precision of his line, Leonardo transforms an ancient
theoretical text into a manual of practical application. Where Vitruvius had
proposed the body as a norm—a rule to be followed—Leonardo presents it as
evidence: something that can be measured, tested, and observed.
The Vitruvian Man should be read as a visual exegesis of the classical canon, in
which the anatomical figure functions as a system of coordinates. Leonardo does
not merely illustrate Vitruvian theory; he submits it to empirical verification,
employing geometry as the language through which the human subject is
integrated into the cosmic order. The superimposition of the two figures, far
from being a mere aesthetic device, constitutes a study of the body’s operation
in space, and  it reaffirms the architect’s role as the agent charged with
harmonizing the laws of nature with the construction of the human habitat.





                            3

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

Preliminary Note: Scope and Methodology

Purpose and audience. The central aim of this edition is to offer English-
speaking readers—and architects, architecture students, and art historians in
particular—a complete bilingual Latin–English edition of Vitruvius's Ten
Books, accompanied by  a study  that  gathers and  orders  the  treatise's
architectural doctrine together with the anecdotes that illustrate it. It is not
conceived as a new recension of the Latin text—which is drawn from the
established critical editions (Krohn 1912, checked against Rose 1899 and the
Budé edition)—but rather as a means of presenting the English translation
derived from the author’s original Spanish version, checked against the Latin
where necessary and annotated, within reach of the professional and the scholar,
for whom, to the best of our knowledge, a complete and accessible bilingual
version of this kind has not hitherto existed. Alongside this philological and
pedagogical purpose, a separate and clearly distinguished section sets out a
personal interpretive proposal.
On the place of this edition within the publishing tradition:  it  is
important to situate this edition honestly within the tradition of Vitruvian
editions, so as to make clear what it contributes and what it does not claim to
be. The definitive critical edition remains that of the Collection des Universités
de France (the “Budé,” Les Belles Lettres, 1969–2009), directed by Pierre Gros
and prepared by Louis Callebat, Jean Soubiran, Philippe Fleury, and other
specialists: it establishes the Latin text from the manuscripts, book by book,
with a critical apparatus and a monographic commentary. Anyone seeking a
definitive textual constitution of Vitruvius should turn to it.

Kr. abbreviation of Krohn in the apparatus.
Bud. abbreviation of the Budé edition in the apparatus.
Gr. abbreviation of Granger in the apparatus.
edd. recent. editiones recentiores: the later (Renaissance and modern) editions,
as opposed to the manuscripts.
In the bilingual sphere, Frank Granger’s Loeb edition (Harvard University
Press, 1931–1934) presents the Latin and English on facing pages, based on the
Harleianus 2767; its usefulness is undeniable, even if its translation and notes
have aged. In English, the version by Ingrid D. Rowland and Thomas Noble


                            4

PRELIMINARY STUDY

Howe (Cambridge University Press, 1999) is today the standard, with a sound
commentary and Howe’s technical reconstructions, although  it does not
reproduce the Latin on facing pages. In Italian, the edition by Antonio Corso
and Elisa Romano, under the direction of Gros (Einaudi, 1997), is notable for
the breadth of its commentary.
Complete bilingual editions — presenting the Latin alongside a fluent modern
translation for reading and reference — remain comparatively few. In Spanish,
for instance, the available versions are translations rather than complete
bilingual editions. The most widely circulated—that of José Luis Oliver
Domingo, with an introduction by Delfín Rodríguez Ruiz (Alianza, 1995)—is
a Castilian version without the Latin text; Francisco Manzanero’s translation
for Gredos covers only the first five books; and the historic translation by José
Ortiz y Sanz (1787), of  great  value,  is  likewise monolingual and now
linguistically remote. To the best of our knowledge, no complete Latin–English
bilingual edition of all ten books, designed specifically for the architect-reader
and uniting critical apparatus with architectural analysis, yet exists.
It is precisely this gap that the present edition aspires to  fill. It is offered,
therefore, not as a new critical edition—a domain in which the Budé remains
unsurpassed—but as a bilingual edition for reading and reference: it reproduces
the Latin text already established by philology (Krohn 1912, checked against
Rose 1899 and the Budé edition), accompanies it with an English translation
derived from the author’s original Spanish version and an apparatus of notes,
analytical indexes, and indexes of Greek words, places, and names, and places it
at the service of the English-speaking architect, student, and historian. Its
ambition is not to rival French textual criticism, but to place at the service of the
English-speaking reader—as a contribution from the Hispanic  scholarly
tradition—a bilingual reference edition that unites an up-to-date philological
apparatus with the architect's technical and symbolic analysis.
This work seeks to explore the intersection between the architectural practice of
classical antiquity and the systems of meaning that shaped its symbolic world.
To  that end,  it  is  essential  to  set out  the methodological framework
underpinning the study, so that the reader may clearly grasp the nature of the
materials presented. The method operates on two distinct levels.



                            5

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

This work therefore proceeds on two distinct but complementary levels, which
are kept apart throughout: historically verifiable data and technical analysis on
the one hand, and interpretive proposals of a more speculative nature on the
other.
The first level adheres to the canons of architectural historiography and classical
philology, drawing on material evidence, epigraphy, and textual sources—such
as Vitruvius’s De architectura or the writings of Pliny the Elder—to reconstruct
the techniques of layout and setting-out and the  roles of the building
professions in the Greco-Roman world. Here documentary rigor governs
throughout, subordinating the analysis to archaeological verification and
established scholarly consensus.
The second  level  is hermeneutical, addressing the symbolic and cultural
dimensions of architectural form. The readings it proposes — of sacred space
and of numerical iconography —  are offered  expressly  as the author’s
interpretive contribution, clearly signalled as such, and are not presented as a
substitute for the philological and archaeological consensus.
The author is fully aware that such approaches, in proposing semantic links
beyond archaeological literalism, belong to the realm of scholarly speculation.
Every effort has therefore been made to separate historical data precisely from
symbolic inference, leaving the reader to judge the validity of these correlations.
Ultimately, the work aspires not to a single, definitive truth but to the opening
of an interdisciplinary dialogue between the precision of constructional data
and the depth of symbolic thought in antiquity.

PRELIMINARY STUDY

Introduction

This book centers on the figure of Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the most influential
surviving architectural theorist of antiquity.
De architectura is by no means confined to technical matters. Clearly inspired
by Hellenism, and with explicit references to inventors such as Ctesibius, the
treatise  treats, in encyclopedic fashion, the architectural orders, building
materials, decorative techniques, building types, hydraulics, the use of color,
gnomonics (Book IX), and both  civil and military machinery (Book X).
Vitruvius describes, for instance, the workings of the water-wheel and of various
lifting and siege engines, displaying an exceptional command of the engineering
of his day.
      The influence of De architectura has endured across the centuries. First
printed in Rome in 1486 by the humanist Giovanni Sulpicio da Veroli, the
treatise became one of the foundational texts of the Renaissance. Petrarch was a
major force behind its rediscovery, and its influence reached figures such as Leon
Battista Alberti, Andrea Palladio, and Leonardo da Vinci, who based his
celebrated Vitruvian Man on the human proportions described in the treatise.
For Vitruvius, the ideal architect had to command a broad range of knowledge:
writing, drawing, geometry, arithmetic, history, philosophy, music, medicine,
law, and astronomy. Only through this comprehensive formation—which he
called  encyclios  disciplina  [encyclopedic  education;  cf.  Vitruvius, De
architectura 1.1.12]—could one attain the summum templum architecturae
[the summit of the art of architecture; cf. Vitruvius, De architectura 1.1.11], the
                                                                                  .highest peak of the discipline
This book seeks to present both the historical and technical dimensions of
Vitruvius and the rich symbolic readings his work has prompted over time. The
historical and philological sections rest on primary sources and specialized
critical literature; the hermeneutic and interpretive sections, clearly identified as
such, set out the author’s proposals on Pythagorean symbolism and the
architectural traditions of antiquity. The aim, ultimately, is a comprehensive
approach to one of the most influential thinkers in Western culture.




                            9

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

The Six Fundamental Principles of Architecture
In Book I of his treatise (De architectura 1.2.1), Vitruvius holds that architecture
is composed of six essential principles (principia), which form the theoretical
foundation of the entire discipline. These six concepts are not isolated elements;
they operate in an interdependent, organic way, articulating the technical,
aesthetic, and ethical dimensions of building.

1. The Vitruvian triad: firmitas, utilitas, and venustas
Before setting out the six principles, Vitruvius affirms that every building must
satisfy three fundamental conditions (De architectura 1.3.2):

   •    Firmitas (solidity): structural stability and the durability of
        materials.
   •    Utilitas (utility): functionality and fitness for the intended use.
   •    Venustas (beauty): aesthetic grace and visual harmony.
These three requirements form the basic triad of architecture and must be met
simultaneously for a work to be deemed accomplished.

The Six Operative Principles (principia)
On this basis, Vitruvius defines six technical and aesthetic concepts by which
the three foregoing requirements are achieved:

Table 1. The six operative principles of architecture

Note. The Greek equivalents follow the Budé edition (Pierre Gros et al.). The
term decor corresponds to τὸ πρέπον (that which is fitting), a concept central to
Vitruvian aesthetics and ethics. The Greek word θεματισμός that appears at 1.2.5
properly renders statio —ritual or institutional rule—, one of the three modes
by which decor is achieved (together with custom and nature), and not decor
itself.

2.1. Ordinatio (τάξις) – Ordering
It is the correct disposition of the members of the work according to a common
unit of measure (modulus or rata pars). It constitutes the quantitative, modular
aspect of architecture.

2.2. Dispositio (διάθεσις) – Disposition
It consists in the intellectual conception of the building and  its graphic
representation, expressed through three modes of representation:

   •    Ichnographia (the plan)
   •    Orthographia (the elevation)
   •    Scaenographia (the perspective view)
It is the creative, design moment par excellence.
2.3. Eurythmia (εὐρυθμία) – Eurythmy
It  is the  pleasing, harmonious appearance  that  arises from the  correct
application of proportion. It is not mere mathematical proportion, but the
agreeable visual effect that proportion produces.

2.4. Symmetria (συμμετρία) – Symmetria / Commensurability
It does not denote modern  bilateral symmetry, but  the proportional
correspondence between the parts and the whole, established from a common
measure (rata pars). It is the mathematical, rational principle par excellence.

2.5. Decor (decor) – Decorum / Propriety
The aesthetic, functional, and cultural appropriateness of the work. Vitruvius
distinguishes three kinds:

   •    by convention (statio);
   •    by custom (consuetudo);

   •    by nature (natura).
It governs, among other things, the choice of architectural order according to
the divinity or the function of the building.

2.6. Distributio (οἰκονομία) – Distribution / Economy
It is the sound management of material, financial, and spatial resources. It
comprises the rational distribution of spaces according to use and social
standing, as well as the prudent control of costs.

Scholarly Note
These six principles form a coherent, hierarchical system. While ordinatio,
symmetria, and eurythmia concern quantitative and aesthetic relationships,
dispositio and decor address the qualitative and intellectual dimension, and
distributio introduces the practical and ethical dimension of architecture. Their
formulation has exerted an extraordinary influence, from the Renaissance
(Alberti, Palladio) to contemporary architectural theory.
“Theories that attribute a sacred or esoteric meaning to the number 216 should

proportions, such speculative interpretations exceed the strictly technical and
geometric framework of his text. Scholarly analysis ought to be confined to the

Vitruvius: Life and Work

The name of Vitruvius

The name by which tradition knows the author —Marcus Vitruvius Pollio—
follows the tripartite structure of the Roman name: praenomen, nomen, and
cognomen. Of the three elements, only the nomen Vitruvius is securely attested
by the treatise itself; the praenomen Marcus and the cognomen Pollio derive from
later sources and are accepted with reservations.
The praenomen Marcus, one of the commonest at Rome, is usually connected
with the god Mars; its attribution to Vitruvius rests on the medieval manuscript
tradition rather than on any direct ancient testimony. The nomen Vitruvius
denotes the gens or family line and is of uncertain Italic origin: it has been linked
to vitrum (glass, or the dyer’s plant woad), which would suggest a remote
occupational origin, but the etymology is not secure. It is, in any case, the only
component of the name the author himself confirms.
The cognomen Pollio —from pollere, “to be strong or influential”— is first
associated with Vitruvius in the epitome of Marcus Cetius Faventinus (s. III–
IV AD). Hence some scholars have read the phrase “Vitruvius Pollio” not as a
single name but as the juxtaposition of two authors —Vitruvius and (Asinius)
Pollio—; the hypothesis, however, lacks firm proof. The coincidence with Gaius
Asinius Pollio (76 BCE – AD 4), orator, historian, and founder of the first
public library at Rome, has fed speculation; yet nothing in the ancient sources
indicates that the architect took the cognomen through any connection with
him. It is safest to understand Pollio as an ordinary Latin family name, without
honorific connotation.
It should be remembered, finally, that “Vitruvius” is not a surname in the
modern sense but the nomen of the gens Vitruvia: the inscriptions bearing
Vitruvius or Vitruvia (collected in the CIL and in epigraphic databases such as
the EDR) belong to other members of the line, not to the architect, whose tomb
and personal circumstances remain unknown.
       According to tradition, Vitruvius served as a military engineer under
Julius Caesar, most likely during the Gallic Wars (c. 58–51 BCE). After retiring
from military service, he dedicated himself to civil architecture and engineering.
During this period, he built the only building he explicitly claims as his own

        Vitruvius includes ten areas of knowledge that an architect should be
familiar with for the benefit of their architectural work: 1. Writing, 2. Drawing,
3. Geometry, 4. Arithmetic, 5. History, 6. Philosophy, 7. Music, 8. Medicine, 9.

       "The Ten Books on Architecture" represents the most copied and
translated classical treatise on architecture in history. One of the seminal texts of
the Italian Renaissance, it has come down to us as a compendium of ancient
knowledge and, according to Vitruvius, is also the first Latin treatise that aimed
to provide a comprehensive exposition of architecture and the  state of
knowledge in civil engineering at the time. These books are dedicated to the
Emperor Augustus as a token of gratitude for his support. Although they have
a textbook approach, they also possess literary elements, placing them more in
the genre of non-fiction than purely specialized works. The oldest known copy
of  this work dates from the 9th century. Currently, more than ninety
manuscripts of The Ten Books on Architecture have been preserved. No other
writings attributed to Vitruvius are recorded. The only clues for dating the
literary work are also provided by the work itself: based on information about
individual Roman buildings, the beginning of the composition and final text of
the book " The Ten Books on Architecture " can be dated to 27–23 BCE.5

Vitruvius lays down three cardinal requirements for any building — firmitas,
utilitas, and venustas, that is, that it should stand firm, serve its purpose, and
please the eye — and he treats the three as equal in weight (De architectura
1.3.2). Beyond them he sets out six governing concepts of architectural theory:
ordinatio, the orderly and modular arrangement of the parts according to a
chosen unit; dispositio, the conception and layout of the work; eurythmia
(εὐρυθμία), the visual harmony that follows from the right application of
symmetria (De architectura 1.2.3); symmetria; decor; and distributio — which
between them treat the building’s proportions, its design and disposition, its
stylistic propriety, and the distribution of materials and costs.
        Vitruvius also linked the different architectural orders (Doric, Ionic,
and Corinthian) with specific construction tasks, assigning each a distinctive
expression. The principle of the Orient, which states that the temple idol should
face west, is another of Vitruvius's construction concepts that influenced the
orientation of temples and altars.
        Vitruvius is known for his detailed description of the architectural
orders — the Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian —, as well as their proportions and
decorative elements.
These architectural principles influenced the development of the system of
column orders in the Renaissance, a canonical system of forms and proportions
for columns. Columns and architectural orders continued to be a fundamental
component of Renaissance and later architecture.

        Despite this, in the Renaissance, there was a renewed interest in the

      The credit for making Vitruvius's work widely known belongs to
Leon Battista Alberti (1404–1472), who incorporated it into his fundamental
treatise on architecture, "De Re Aedificatoria" (circa 1450). The first known
edition of Vitruvius's "De architectura" was published in Rome by Fra Giovanni
Sulpicius in 1486. Subsequently, translations were made into Italian, French,
English, German, Spanish, and other languages. The original illustrations had
been lost, and the first illustrated edition was published in Venice in 1511, with
woodcuts based on the descriptions in the text, probably by Fra Giovanni
Giocondo. Later, in the 16th century, Andrea Palladio provided illustrations for
Daniele Barbaro's commentaries on Vitruvius in the Italian and Latin versions.
However, the most famous illustration remains Leonardo da Vinci 's "Vitruvian
Man."

        Vitruvius is often loosely described as the first architect, but it is more
accurate to describe him as the earliest architect whose complete theoretical
treatise has survived to this day. Although he mentions earlier works, these are
less comprehensive. Vitruvius proved to be at least an original thinker and
possessed the creative intellect to systematize existing architectural practice. It is
important to note that Vitruvius had a much broader scope in his field than
modern architects. Roman architects were involved in a wide variety of
disciplines; in modern terms, they might be considered a combination of
engineers, architects, landscape designers, artists, and craftspeople. The word
"architect" originates from Greek words meaning "master" and "builder." The
first of Vitruvius' ten books addresses many topics that today would be
considered part of what we now call urban planning and landscape architecture.

construction of cities and dwellings in the first book.

       "De architectura" (also known as "Ten Books on Architecture, " De
architectura libri decem)  is a treatise written by the Roman architect and
military engineer Marcus Vitruvius Pollio; c. 80–70 BCE – d. after 15 BCE.
This work is dedicated to his patron, Emperor Caesar Augustus, and his sister
Octavia Minor, to whose commendation Vitruvius attributes his introduction
to the emperor. The treatise serves as a guide for building projects. Notably the
only  architectural  treatise to have survived from antiquity,  it has been
considered, since the Renaissance, as the first known book on architectural
theory. Furthermore, it has been recognized as a fundamental source on the
canon of classical architecture.11

that allows me to live without hardship until the end of my life, I began to write
these books for you, for I realized that you had erected many buildings, that you
were currently erecting others, and that in the future you would put your effort
into building public and private buildings in accordance with the magnitude of
your deeds, so that your memory may endure in posterity. "

raises the intriguing question of whether Vitruvius was present during the work
and, if so, in what capacity he participated? Did he perhaps play an advisory or
consultative role in the realization of this architectural project?

Octavian's wife, around 15 BCE on the Esquiline Hill. The shared choice of this
type of building, which served functions related to health, culture, and memory,
does not appear to have been accidental. Both women, Octavia and Livia,
demonstrated a shared appreciation for a multifunctional architectural space
that addressed diverse needs of Roman society.

entrance propylaeum of the church of Sant'Angelo in Pescheria, evidencing its

        Vitruvius and  his  principles.  It  is worth  clarifying  a common
misconception: although Vitruvius does explicitly state the triad of firmness
(firmitas), utility (utilitas), and beauty (venustas) in De architectura 1.3.2, he
does not present it as a universal and abstract axiom upon which all architecture
"depends," but rather as the three qualities that a well-made work must possess,
within the specific context of building construction. The interpretation of the
triad as a canonical and autonomous formula was consolidated later. However,
after the publication of a summary of the work by Claude Perrault in 1673,
which showed little respect for the original, the so-called Vitruvian triad became
established and became a  veritable "legend" repeated by generations of
architects.
        In fact, when Vitruvius dares to attempt an analysis of the art he
writes about, he proposes to understand architecture as composed of four
elements:  architectural  order  (relationship  of  each  part  with  its  use),
arrangement (" The kinds of arrangement [...] are the layout in plan, in elevation
and in perspective "), proportion (" Uniform concordance between the whole
work and its parts ") and distribution (in Greek oikonomía, it consists " in the
proper and best possible use of materials and land, and in ensuring the lowest
cost of the work achieved in a rational and balanced way ").
          It must be realized that his doubts on this matter are quite intense,
since four pages later he divides architecture into three parts: construction,
gnomonics, and mechanics (Vitruvian Royal Framework [Artus Vitruviani
regii: expression of the author's interpretation; in classical Latin, artus means "
joints, " not " conceptual framework " ]). However interesting and suggestive
this may be, it should not be forgotten that this treatise is the only classical
treatise that has come down to us, and the probability that it is the best of its
time is small.
      The history of the various versions of Vitruvius's  treatise aptly
summarizes the conflict surrounding the definition of architecture. In 1673,
Claude Perrault, a physician and physiologist specializing in cadaver dissection
and a skilled draftsman, published his abridged translation of Vitruvius's
treatise, which was completely reorganized. However, it was through Perrault 's

theories of subsequent centuries. And it is in this summary that the Vitruvian
triad emerged: firmitas, the concepts of firmitas (firmness), utilitas (utility), and
venustas (beauty).
Public buildings must satisfy three conditions: firmitas (structural soundness
and durability), utilitas (functional convenience and proper distribution of
space), and venustas (elegance and beauty of appearance). Critical note: The
translation of " firmitas " as " strength " is inaccurate; the Latin term designates
the stability achieved through the correct selection of materials and the solidity
of the foundations. " Venustas " is not simply " beauty " but the visual grace that
results from correct proportions; cf. Vitruvius, De architectura 1.3.2, and the
discussion in Rowland and Howe, 1999, 66.

•       Regarding utility, a more abstract concept, consideration is given to
both the minimum requirements to guarantee comfort and functionality in the
use of an independent space and the efficient relationship and communication
between the different spaces that make up the architectural program, which
shapes a typology (i.e., the function - space relationship).
•    On the other hand, beauty, an aspect that can be considered subjective
and inherent, is linked to the aesthetic value that arises from the interaction
between various design elements. These elements encompass the proportions
used to dimension the building's components, the architect's characteristic
style, the building's personality, the materials used in its finishes, and the
design  of  the  architectural  elements, whether  functional,  structural, or
decorative.

and scholarly work, being known and used in the 1st century BC by Pliny the

the same century, Frontinus mentions him in his treatise on the aqueducts of
Rome.

and Gargilius Martialis, in a compendium on architecture whose  title  is

         Vitruvius's work, "De architectura," was published in printed editions
after its manuscript. Among the printed editions, the following stand out:
       Incunabula edition (editio princeps): The first printed edition of "De
architectura" was published by Fra Giovanni Sulpitius in 1486. This edition was
the original version, without illustrations. A second edition was published in
1495 or 1496.
         Illustrated  edition  by  Fra  Giovanni  Giocondo:  Fra  Giovanni
Giocondo, a Dominican  friar, produced the  first illustrated edition with
woodcuts in Venice in 1511. This edition featured magnificent illustrations and
a meticulous philosophical approach.
         Italian translations: Italian translations began to circulate in the 1520s.
The first printed edition of an Italian translation, with new illustrations, was
produced by Cesare Cesariano in Como in 1521. Cesariano was a friend of the
architect Bramante.
        Translations into other European languages: Vitruvius's work was
quickly translated into other European languages. The first French version was
published in 1547, and the first German version followed in 1548. The first
Spanish translation was published in 1582 by Miguel de Urrea and Juan
Gracián. The most authoritative and influential edition was published in French
in 1673 by Claude Perrault, commissioned by Jean-Baptiste Colbert in 1664.
        English adaptations and translations: John Shute based his book "The
First and Chief Grounds of Architecture" on Vitruvius's text in 1563. Sir Henry
Wotton published " The Elements of Architecture" in 1624, an adaptation
heavily influenced by Vitruvius. The first complete English translation of the
first five volumes was completed in 1771, and the entire work was published in
1791.
        Later editions: Over the years, many later editions of "De architectura"
were published, with detailed and interpretive illustrations. Vitruvius's work
became a popular subject of hermeneutics thanks to printing and widespread
dissemination.

         Vitruvius’s De architectura comprises ten books, each introduced by a
preface. Their subjects are outlined below.

•      Book  I: In  this book, Vitruvius  addresses urban planning and
architecture in general. He also focuses on the training and skills necessary to be
an architect.
•      Book II: Construction techniques and materials are discussed here, as
well as the origin of architecture. Vitruvius explores the foundations of
construction.
•      Books III and IV: These books focus on temples and architectural
orders. Vitruvius describes in detail the different architectural styles and how
they are applied in temple construction.
•      Book V: Vitruvius focuses on public buildings, with special emphasis
on the forum, the basilica, and the theaters. He explains how these important
public spaces are designed and constructed.
•      Book VI: This book is dedicated to private constructions, including
location, building typologies and aspects such as plasters and paving.
•      Book VII: Vitruvius delves into the topic of coverings and decoration
in this book. He describes how to decorate and embellish buildings, paying
attention to decorative details.

•      Book VIII: In this book, the author addresses hydraulics, including
water supply systems and water-related technology.
•      Book IX: Vitruvius makes an astronomical and astrological digression

•      X: The last book is dedicated to mechanics, including the construction
of cranes, hydraulic machines and war machines. Vitruvius explores mechanical

       There is a story and a certain mythology associated with Archimedes
48that Vitruvius mentions in his book about the discovery of the principle that
bears his name. Legend has it that the genius from Syracuse uttered the word
Eureka 49(today synonymous with achievements of all kinds) when he entered
his bathtub and realized that the volume of water displaced fell over the circular
edge of the tub. This displacement was equal to the volume of his body. In this
way, he created the theoretical basis for what later became known as Archimedes
Principle.This principle describes:

A body wholly or partly immersed in a fluid at rest experiences
an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it
displaces. Vitruvius’s anecdote concerns displaced volume and
the composition of a crown; it does not formulate the modern
law of buoyancy in these terms.

Vitruvius recounts how King Hiero of Syracuse suspected that
silver had been substituted for some of the gold supplied for a
votive crown. He  asked Archimedes  to  investigate  the
suspected fraud. While entering a bath, Archimedes noticed
that the water displaced corresponded to the volume of his
submerged body. The account then describes comparative
tests with equal weights of gold, silver and the crown. The
details about sleepless nights and advice from his wife do not
occur in Vitruvius’s narrative and should not be treated as part
of his testimony.

The tetraktys (τετρακτύς) is, in the Pythagorean tradition, the triangular figure
of the number ten (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10), a symbol central to the school’s theory
of number. Vitruvius does not name it; it is recalled here only to situate the
Pythagorean background against which his occasional references to number and
proportion may be read.

The presence of Pythagoras in Vitruvius: Vitruvius does acknowledge the
Pythagorean influence on the theory of music and proportion. When Vitruvius
speaks of harmony and mathematical ratios (such as the proportions that
temples or the human body should maintain), he is operating under the same
theoretical framework as the Pythagoreans. However, he does so through
technical terms from architecture and geometry (such as module,  ratio,
proportion), not through the numerical mysticism  characteristic  of the
Pythagorean sect.

Although Vitruvius does not cite the tetraktys, modern commentators
on De architectura sometimes invoke it to describe the logic of his
proportional ratios. Such readings belong to the interpretive literature
rather than to Vitruvius’s own statements, and are reported here as that.
Difference in approach: Vitruvius is a technician and engineer who writes
from a practical and pragmatic perspective for a Roman professional audience.
The tetractys belongs to a more esoteric and metaphysical realm of Greek
philosophy, a field that Vitruvius prefers to set aside in favor of the constructive
applications of geometry.52

Elsewhere, at VII.praef.14, Vitruvius explains that he gathered useful material
from earlier technical writings into a single corpus. That statement can be

The analogy is with a cube’s stability: whichever face it rests on, it remains in
place until disturbed. Vitruvius uses that image to explain how a defined group
of verses may remain stable in memory.
This passage links 216-verse units, cubic stability and memory. It provides
material for later symbolic interpretations, but those interpretations should
remain distinct from what Vitruvius explicitly says. His other references to
Pythagoras need not be assumed to prescribe the same compositional rule.

When we speak of the “divine proportion,” 56we are referring to a numerical

line into two unequal parts, such that the larger segment is to the whole line as
the smaller is to the larger. In this way, a relationship of sizes is established, with
the same proportionality between the whole divided into larger and smaller
parts.

The extent to which the architecture of antiquity was actually composed
according to the golden ratio is much debated and far from settled. Vitruvius
himself nowhere invokes  it:  his system of proportion  is modular and
commensurable (symmetria), founded on whole-number ratios derived from a
common unit rather than on the irrational ratio Φ.
The golden ratio (Φ ≈ 1.618) is a mathematical relationship that expresses the
division of a segment into two unequal parts such that the ratio of the whole
segment to the larger part is equal to the ratio of the larger part to the smaller.
Its geometric expression in logarithmic spirals — known as " golden spirals " —
appears in numerous natural forms.
Vitruvius does talk extensively about proportions, symmetry (symmetria) and
harmony in architecture, especially in Book III (proportions of the temple and
the human body), but he uses rational proportions (simple fractions such as 1:2,
1:3, 2:3, 3:5, etc.), not the irrational proportion φ.

•      The Ionic volute of the capital, which has a spiral shape. However,
Vitruvius describes how to construct it using geometric methods of compass
and straightedge, not using the golden ratio.

For Vitruvius, architecture may be defined as the equilibrium of three governing
demands — durability (firmitas), serviceability (utilitas), and grace (venustas)
— no one of which should override the others, each rather sustaining and
completing the rest. To weigh any building without holding all three in view at
once would be to judge it only in part.
The canon established by Marcus Vitruvius in De architectura constitutes the
most influential formulation of this triad in Antiquity. Its principles served as
the basis for classical architectural composition, visually and conceptually
organizing buildings through modular proportions, symmetry, and eurhythmy.
Although Vitruvius does not mention the golden ratio (φ), his system of
anthropomorphic proportions exerted a profound subsequent influence on
architectural theory.

Symbolic and philosophical meaning
The figure of the man inscribed simultaneously in a circle and a square
represents several levels of meaning:
1.    Harmony between the Microcosm and the Macrocosm: Man is
seen as a perfect reflection of the universe. The circle symbolizes the divine, the
celestial, and the perfect (the cosmos), while the square represents the earthly,
the material, and the human.
2.     Squaring the Circle. The image alludes to the ancient geometric
problem of squaring the circle: constructing a square with the same area as a
given circle. This problem, considered unsolvable with classical tools, acquired
a profound symbolic meaning: the reconciliation between the finite (square)
and the infinite (circle), between matter and spirit.
3.     Proportion and Beauty: It represents the classical ideal that beauty
arises from harmonious proportion (symmetry). The human body becomes the
measure of all things.

Why was the Renaissance so obsessed with this image?
The Renaissance saw in the Vitruvian Man the perfect embodiment of Homo
Universalis (Universal Man), a central ideal of Renaissance humanism. The
main reasons were:

•      Anthropocentrism: Man was no longer just a creature of God, but
the  measure  of   all  things  (as  Protagoras  stated).  Leonardo  and  his
contemporaries saw in this figure the dignity and unlimited potential of
humankind.
•       Reconciliation between  Science and Art: The image united
geometry, anatomy, architecture and philosophy, fields that the Renaissance
sought to integrate.
•      Revival of Classicism: It represented the recovery of ancient wisdom
(Vitruvius) adapted to the new humanist spirit.

•       Spiritual symbolism: Man's ability to be inscribed both in the circle
(divine perfection) and in the square (material reality) symbolized the human
being's aspiration to unite the earthly and the celestial.

Definition of Homo Universalis
The expression Homo Universalis (Universal Man) refers to the Renaissance
ideal of an individual who develops all their faculties to the fullest: intellectual,
artistic, scientific, and physical. Leonardo da Vinci is the paradigmatic example:
painter, anatomist, engineer, architect, inventor, and theorist.
Thus the Vitruvian Man became the visual symbol of Homo Universalis: a
harmonious, proportional being capable of encompassing both the material and
spiritual worlds.62

This concept reached its full maturity during the Italian Renaissance, finding
one of its most prominent theorists in Leon Battista Alberti (1404–1472).
Alberti, an architect, humanist, and writer, argued that the artist should not be

aedificatoria (1452), Alberti asserted that the architect should possess a
comprehensive education encompassing the arts, sciences, and humanities, far
surpassing mere technical skill.
This  vision encapsulates one of the  essential  principles of Renaissance
Humanism: the dignification of humankind as beings capable of harmoniously
cultivating all their faculties. For Alberti and his contemporaries, architecture
was not only a practical  art, but the supreme discipline where scientific
knowledge, artistic creativity, and humanistic wisdom converged.
In this light, it can be said that the Renaissance was, to a large extent, a
product of architectural thought. Architecture became the quintessential
all-encompassing art, in which the ideal of Homo Universalis was materialized:
the harmonious man, capable of measuring, understanding, and beautifying the
world.
" The Renaissance was defined by a renewed anthropological conception that
placed humankind at the center of the cosmos, endowing it with an unlimited
capacity for understanding and transforming reality. This humanist imprint
urged the individual to cultivate encyclopedic knowledge, promoting the
flourishing of the arts and sciences as a manifestation of human potential."
Within this framework, the interest in "squaring the circle" transcended mere
mathematical curiosity to become a symbol of intellectual apotheosis: the
attempt to reconcile earthly finitude (the square) with divine infinity (the circle).
In this quest, the figure of the Vitruvian Man, embedded in the ad quadratum
paradigm, was consolidated as the archetype of the Uomo Universale, becoming
the ethical and aesthetic guiding principle of the era.
The reevaluation of Vitruvian thought was fundamental in this process,
materializing in critical translations and commentaries on De architectura that
allowed the integration of ancient theory into modern practice. Particularly

modular system.

Reception and exegesis of the Vitruvian canon: From Homo bene figuratus to
sacred geometry
The  "Vitruvian Man"  constitutes  a  paradigmatic  synthesis  of human
proportions, originally articulated under an architectural and geometric logic in
the treatises of the Roman theorist Vitruvius. While contemporary iconography
has been dominated by Leonardo da Vinci's celebrated illustration (c. 1490), it
is imperative to recognize that this figure represents only one of the many
interpretations that emerged during the Renaissance. Among these, Cesare
Cesariano's  version  (1521)  stands  out, whose  technical  precision and
compositional rigor position it as one of the most comprehensive treatises on
the representation of the human canon.
The nature of Da Vinci's sketch — originating from his personal notes —
transcends mere anatomical observation by superimposing two geometric
configurations: quadrature (homo ad quadratum) and circularity (homo ad
circulum). This duality underlies the Vitruvian principle of homo bene figuratus,
which postulates a harmonious correlation between anatomy and the laws of
cosmic order. As Vitruvius explains in De architectura (Book III, 1, 3):

circumference. Similarly, when the shape of the square is applied to the body, it

equal to the wingspan of the outstretched arms. ”
Historically, the absence of illustrations in Vitruvius's original manuscripts
acted as a creative catalyst, encouraging scholars and artists, such as Albrecht
Dürer and Villard de Honnecourt, to develop systems of visual representation.
In architecture, the construction method known as ad quadratum transcended
the artistic realm to become the governing system of spatial composition. This
paradigm, based on Euclidean geometry, was decisive in the construction of
Roman temples and Gothic cathedrals, where the square functioned as the
generating module for the arrangement of columns, the span of arches, and the
height of vaults.
The persistence of this model in the history of art and architecture underscores
the convergence between mathematical metrics and humanist aesthetics. Da
Vinci's representation, beyond being an anatomical study or a possible self-
portrait, embodies the Renaissance aspiration to grasp the order of the universe
through bodily measurement. Thus, what began as a note in a technical treatise
has transformed into a universal canon of Western culture, symbolizing the
moment when geometry ceased to be an abstraction and became the foundation
of human existence.

2.     The mathematical legacy (Alberti and Pacioli): Dürer not only
drew upon Alberti's theory of perspective, but also incorporated Luca Pacioli's
research on the Divine Proportion. The application of the golden section and
regular polygons in the representation of female anatomy allowed Dürer to
"rationalize" the body, moving it away from a casual, organic representation and
placing it within a system of precise measurements.

The Female Figure as a metric canon
In  his  treatise The Four Books on Human Proportion (Vier Bücher von
menschlicher Proportion, 1528), Dürer establishes a system where the female
figure is articulated through a complex network of geometric proportions. This
study stands out for two fundamental contributions:
•       Variability of the canon: Unlike Vitruvius's static and universal
canon, Dürer proposes a "variability of proportions." He classifies different
types of bodies according to their constitution, anticipating a more scientific
and empirical view of the subject.

•     The geometry of the female body: For Dürer, the female figure
corresponds to a geometry of curves that, nevertheless, are derived from perfect
rectangles and circles. The integration of these forms reflects his interest in the
quadratum and the circulum, where the female body becomes the "container"
of these mathematical laws.

Mariano di Jacopo, known as il Taccola (1382–1453), is an essential figure for

Taccola: The « Archimedes of Siena » and technique as Logos
Taccola was not just a compiler of machines; he was one of the  first to
conceptualize technology as a graphic language. His treatises, De ingeneis
and De machinis, represent a qualitative leap in the history of architecture and
engineering.
1.      Illustration as a means of transmitting knowledge: Unlike the
manuals of his time, Taccola used drawing not as decorative illustration, but as
a  tool  for  technical  communication.  His  diagrams  of  pulleys,  lifting
mechanisms, and hydraulic systems allowed engineering knowledge to be
standardized.
2.      Engineering as the basis of architecture: For Taccola, there was no
rigid distinction between architecture and mechanics. The construction of a
building required a deep understanding of forces, which directly links him to
Vitruvian firmitas. His studies on motion (gears and transmissions) are, in
essence, a practical application of geometric reason to the material world.
3.     The background of Francesco di Giorgio: It is essential to note that
Francesco di Giorgio Martini was an indirect disciple and heir to Taccola's
legacy. Many of the technological principles that Francesco integrated into his
fortification projects were taken directly from Taccola's notebooks.

The geometric synthesis: Homo ad quadratum and
Homo ad circulum

The intellectual value of this piece lies in the superposition of two geometric
systems  that, for the 15th-century mindset, represented the relationship
between the finite and the infinite:
1.    Homo ad quadratum. In Leonardo’s drawing, the square has its center
near the groin; the navel is the center of the circle. The association of the square
with terrestrial stability and firmitas is the author’s symbolic interpretation.
Within the proposed reading of the cubic ratio and 216, it may be understood
as a planar base for a volume; that association is not an explicit doctrine of
Vitruvius.
2.    Homo ad circulum. Leonardo places the center of the circle at the
navel. The association of the circle with the celestial realm, divinity and
perfection belongs to the symbolic reading proposed here.  It should be
distinguished from  the  anatomical and  geometric  instructions  of De
architectura 3.1.3.

His De occulta philosophia (1533) is the compendium where geometry ceases to

3.      Translation as a tool for modernization: His French translation,
profusely illustrated and commented upon, was the one that finally "cleaned"
Vitruvius's text of the Neoplatonic interpretations of previous centuries,

The classical orders of architecture
The  classical orders of architecture are distinguished by their ornamental
characteristics, their treatment of the module, and the organic nature of their
composition. Classical antiquity bequeathed three main orders: the Doric, the
Ionic, and the Corinthian. Later, the Romans incorporated two additional
orders: the Tuscan and the Composite.
The Tuscan order, more austere and simple than the Doric, represents a Roman
reinterpretation of the Etruscan column. Each order is defined by its own
system of proportions, characteristic capitals, and entablatures. The column
shafts often featured vertical flutes along their surface. In the case of the Doric
order, the number of flutes was usually 20, a figure with clear symbolic
significance within the Pythagorean and Vitruvian traditions.
One of the characteristics common to the three Greek orders is entasis: the
columns are slightly wider at the base and gradually narrow imperceptibly





                           107

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

towards the capital, giving the column an organic elegance and vitality, avoiding
the visual rigidity of a perfect cylindrical shape.68

The gradual narrowing of the column shaft as it rises is called entasis. This
technical and aesthetic feature has the main purpose of correcting an optical
illusion: without this correction, the straight column would appear slightly
concave to the observer.
According to Heron of Alexandria, entasis precisely compensates for this visual
distortion, making the column appear perfectly straight and structurally sound.
For his part, historian Vincent Scully has emphasized that this subtle bulging of
the shaft produces the visual effect that the column, aware of the weight it bears,
seems to yield slightly under its own load, generating an impression of organic
tension and vitality.69

This interpretation coincides with the etymology of the term: the Greek word
ἔντασις (éntasis) derives from the verb ἐντείνω (enteínō), which means " to stretch
firmly ", " to tighten" or " to put under tension ".
      The height of columns in the classical orders was determined and
visually organized in relation to their lower diameter, used as the basic module
of proportion.
Doric column has a height-to-diameter ratio of between 6 and 7 meters, giving
it a robust and compact character. The Ionic column reaches a ratio of 8 meters,
while the Corinthian, the most slender of all, rises to 10 meters. In this last case,
the diameter of the base is repeated ten times in the total height of the column.
These modular  relationships were not mere  technical conventions, but
possessed a profound symbolic meaning, closely linked to the character and
aesthetic expression of each order.

De architectura, Vitruvius explicitly associates the architectural orders with

Doric order, due to its shorter height and its appearance of robustness and
solidity, was the most suitable for male deities. In contrast, the Ionic order, more
slender and elegant, was primarily reserved for goddesses.
The number 6, characteristic of the Doric column, occupied a prominent place
in Pythagorean symbolism, associated with cosmic fire and deities such as
Poseidon (Neptune), to whose temples this order was usually dedicated.
The number 8, characteristic of the Ionic column, was linked in Indo-European
antiquity to the movement of the planet Venus. This order was frequently used
in temples dedicated to maternal goddesses, such as Hera or Athena Nike

Ionic order
The Ionic order emerged in the 6th century BC in the region of Ionia, located
on the coastal and island strip of Southeast Asia Minor. It achieved great
popularity during the Archaic period (c. 750–480 BCE).
Vitruvius, in his treatise De architectura, establishes a symbolic distinction
between the orders, stating that the Doric is inspired by the robust proportions
of the male body, while the Ionic is based on the more elegant and slender forms
of the female body (De arch. IV, 1, 6-7). Although the Roman author does not
cite his direct sources, this interpretation is probably rooted in the Hellenistic
theoretical tradition, particularly in the ideas of architects such as Hermogenes
of Priene, author of the famous Temple of Artemis at Magnesia on the
Meander (present-day Turkey).
The Ionic order spread from the east to the Greek mainland. It is closely related
to the Aeolic order, which fell out of use at the end of the Archaic period. Its
most distinctive features are the slender shaft with finer and more numerous
flutes, a wider and more elaborate base, and above all, the capital with two

capital, six times greater than the width of its base.” This is how the Doric

Ionic order embodies the symbolism of the spiral and the numbers 8 and 5,

The Corinthian order is the last of the three classical Greek orders and developed
during the 4th century BC. It takes its name from the city of Corinth. The oldest
known example is found in the Temple of Apollo Epicurius at Bassae (Arcadia),
dating from between 450 and 420 BCE. It is not the main order of the temple
— which features an exterior Doric colonnade and an interior Ionic one — but
appears exceptionally within the cella.72

     On the Corinthian order
Vitruvius describes the Corinthian order as one that imitates the slenderness of
a maiden, for its form evokes the most delicate and graceful adornments of a
young woman in the bloom of her youth:
“The third style, called Corinthian, imitates virginal slenderness, because its
form recalls the most beautiful adornments of a maiden, depicted with the most
slender limbs due to her tender age. It is said that the discovery of this capital
occurred thus: a maiden of Corinth, already of marriageable age, fell ill and died.
Her nurse gathered the toys with which the girl used to play in life, placed them
in a small basket, and, taking it to her tomb, placed it upon her. To protect these
objects from the open air, she covered the basket with a tile. By chance, this
basket fell upon an acanthus root. When spring arrived, the acanthus root,
pressed by the weight, sprouted leaves and stems which, as they grew along the
sides of the basket and met the edges of the tile, bent outwards, forming volutes.
”

On the Corinthian order and its possible symbolic meaning
The author proposes a symbolic association between the Corinthian order and
the cultic spheres of Apollo and Asclepius, deities connected with healing and
renewal. The early Corinthian column inside the Temple of Apollo Epicurius
at Bassae provides a relevant comparison. Its presence does not, by itself,
establish the order’s origin in an Apollonian healing cult.
According to the account transmitted by Vitruvius (De architectura 4.1.8-9),
the Corinthian capital was invented by the sculptor and architect Callimachus.
The anecdote relates that, beside the tomb of a young Corinthian woman, a
nurse placed a basket containing the deceased's toys and covered it with a square
tile for protection. An acanthus root, growing beneath the basket, sent its leaves
sprouting through the mesh, curving gracefully under the weight of the tile and
giving rise to the characteristic shape of the Corinthian capital. This narrative,
which survives only in Vitruvius's treatise, constitutes the best-known legendary
explanation for the origin of the architectural order.
In the symbolic reading proposed here, the Corinthian column is compared
with arboreal imagery associated with Apollo. The acanthus basket, ascending
stems, and curling foliage invite an interpretation in terms of growth, renewal,

1.     The Nymphs and the Trees (Hamadryads): The original text refers
specifically to the Hamadryads (nymphs whose  fate  is  biologically and
temporally linked to a  specific  tree). The Greek term usually used by
Callimachus is drys, which strictly designates the holm oak or oak, not the generic

4.     The palm tree of Delos: A fundamental element of Apollonian
iconography. Leto gives birth while clinging to the sacred palm tree (phoenix) of
the island of Delos (formerly called Asteria, the floating island).
5.     The meter  of the swans and the  lyre:  This  passage from
Callimachus is a mythical etymology of the heptatonic scale. The Greek text
emphasizes the exact synchronicity between the seven turns of the swans
(kyknoi) and the subsequent structure of Apollo's lyre.

Critical Notes for the Exegetical Apparatus
1.     The invocation and the pain (Apollon, Apollon): The original text
is not a lyrical apologia to the "beautiful Sun" in a celebratory sense; it is a cry of
sacred terror. Cassandra invokes the god of light on the threshold of death. The
confusion with the "Sun" (Helios) stems from the late Hellenistic assimilation
(common in Euripides ' treatment of the god in tragedies such as Phaethon),
where sunlight is directly associated with Apollo's destructive rays.
The epithet Agyieus (Ἀγυιεύς): In the original Greek, the text alludes to
Apollo Agyieus, the protector of streets, entrances, and gates. In front of the
palace of Mycenae stood a conical pillar or baetylus representing the god. For
the prophetess, however, this pillar is no longer a symbol of architectural
protection; instead, it has become the boundary marker that delimits the space
where she will be sacrificed.
The philological core: the mythical etymology (Apóllymi): This passage
contains one of the most famous etymological puns in Greek tragedy. There is
a deliberate homophony between the name of the god Apollo (Ἀπόλλων) and
the verb ἀπόλλυμι (apóllymi), which means “to destroy,” “to annihilate,” “to
ruin,” or “to kill.” When the text declares that “mortals rightly call you Apollo,”
it enacts a linguistic revelation: the god of harmony and order is, for the one who
suffers his severity, “The Destroyer.”

Located directly adjacent to the forum, a proportional reconstruction from the

144 by 96 Roman feet (approximately 42.65 by 28.43 meters); this idealised
modular  figure  should  be  distinguished  from  the  provisional  on-site

also incorporates an internal peristyle of thirty-two tubular columns. However,
archaeological evidence and the  literary passage  itself reveal a substantial
divergence from the theoretical basilica model: the integration of an Aedes
Augusti, or temple dedicated to the imperial cult, into its rear flank. This
insertion altered the traditional axial symmetry of the Roman building by
displacing the classical tribunal, demonstrating that the material execution of
the cubus and the architectural order was flexibly adapted to the demands of the
terrain's topography and the pre-existing political and religious conditions of
the urban space.

        Latin word fanum properly designates the "sacred place" or the
"sanctuary" consecrated to a deity. From this root derives the adjective fanaticus,
a term that originally referred to a temple servant or one who manifested an
ecstatic enthusiasm provoked by the proximity of the deity; it was only with
historical development that the word acquired the pejorative connotation of
intransigence that it retains today. In contrast, everything that remained outside
the walls of the sacred precinct was called pro-fanum, the direct origin of the
modern concept of "profane," which delimits the realm of the secular from the
sacred.
Beyond the biographical outlines of Marcus Vitruvius Pollio —  scarce,
fragmentary, and difficult to verify historiographically — this study focuses on
his crucial theoretical and practical contributions to the field of architecture.
His  treatise  exerted  a  decisive  influence on  construction  practices and
architectural writing from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance, maintaining an
undeniable epistemological relevance. To understand the scope of his work, it is
essential to contextualize the author within the late Republic and the early
Principate of Rome, a chronological arc spanning the dictatorships of Julius
Caesar (49–44 BCE) and the reign of Octavian Augustus (27 BCE– 14 CE). It
should be noted that, within the catalog of Roman-era structures that survive
today, no epigraphic or archaeological documentation remains that would
allow any work to be formally attributed to him. The only exception to this
monumental void would be the Basilica of Fanum Fortunae (Fano), in northern
Italy; in Book V of his treatise De architectura, Vitruvius himself offers a detailed
description of a basilica of his own design built in that colony. Although
architectural historiography often establishes fruitful formal parallels between
this Vitruvian model and the Basilica of Ordona (in Apulia), it must be clarified
that in the current archaeological record of Fano, no substructural remains have

propaganda apparatus: upon entering, the first thing one encounters is the
statue or altar of the emperor.
       “Through the meticulous description of this Aedes Augusti, Vitruvius
holds the historiographical merit of having codified the semantic function of
the monumental apse in close symbiosis with the civil basilica, configuring a
space of strong ideological charge that projects the imperial auctoritas and
disseminates  a profoundly  innovative  typological program through  the
architecture of the State.”
As for his treatise De architectura, written and dedicated specifically to the
Emperor Augustus, its value transcends its immeasurable subsequent influence;
its exceptional status lies in being the only theoretical corpus of architectural
tradition from classical antiquity that has survived intact to this day. Rigorously
structured in ten books, the treatise addresses in its Book I the very ontology of
the discipline, postulating the celebrated triad upon which constructive practice
rests: firmitas (structural solidity), utilitas (spatial functionality), and venustas
(beauty and eurhythmy). While successive volumes are devoted to the science of
materials (Book II) or to the morphology and arrangement of the temples of the
immortal gods (Book III), the text is not limited to mere technical prescription,
but rises to a profound philosophical speculation on cosmic symmetry, musical
harmony, and anthropomorphic modulation. Vitruvius summarizes this theory
of the cosmic - human analogy with famous words:
" For no building can have a sense of composition without symmetry and
proportion, unless it has an exact proportion like that of the limbs of a well-
shaped man."¹
(“For no temple can possess an ordered compositional structure without
symmetry and proportion—that  is, unless  it maintains an exact modular
analogy with the members of a harmoniously configured human body”).»

Critical notes
1.      Clarification of the term Rationem (Analogy /Reason): In
Vitruvian Latin, ratio is not simply an abstract mathematical "reason "; it is the
method of calculation and the internal logic that unifies the parts with the
whole. When translated in the context of sacred geometry, the more precise
terms are modular analogy or geometric concordance.
2.     The Vitruvian triad: It is essential to maintain the Latin terms in
italics (firmitas, utilitas, venustas) to preserve the rigor of the theoretical
framework. Within the context of this edition, venustas  is not superficial
ornamentation, but rather the mathematical result of applying the symmetry of
the human body and musical consonances to the building plan.
3.     The human body as the matrix of space: The final quote is the
foundation of the Vitruvian Man theory; this demonstrates that the Roman
temple is not an isolated object, but a microcosm: Apollonian architecture takes
the perfect measurements fixed by nature in the human body and transfers them
to stone using the ruler and compass.
In Vitruvius’s metrological account, parts of the human body provide units
related by proportion. The finger, digitus, is the smallest of the units listed here.
Four fingers make a palm, palmus, and four palms make a foot, pes. The Roman
foot therefore contains sixteen fingers.
The reception of Vitruvius’s anthropometric canon raises questions about the
relation between textual ratios and observed anatomy. In 3.1.2, Vitruvius
distinguishes the distance from the upper chest to the hairline, one-sixth of the
total height, from the distance to the crown, one-quarter. These endpoints must
not be conflated. Leonardo’s accompanying notes give the foot as one-seventh
of the body’s height, rather than Vitruvius’s one-sixth; his drawing should
therefore be studied as an independent investigation as well as a response to the
ancient text.

Architecture and the column as a reflection of the human body
The fundamental postulate of  Vitruvius's  treatises  lies in the  fact that
architectural structures should be designed according to the same laws of
symmetry and proportion that govern the " body of a well-formed man " (De
architectura, III, 1, 1). This analogical correspondence finds its highest material
expression in the evolution of the classical orders, where the column is not
conceived as a mere tectonic support, but as a direct anthropomorphic
transposition: the Doric column embodies the robustness, proportion, and
strength of the male body, while the Ionic and Corinthian columns translate the
slenderness,  delicacy,  and  ornamentation  associated  with  the  female
physiognomy.

Critical Notes
1.    Roman metrology. In the Roman system of measurement, the palmus
was not equivalent to a finger (digitus). Rather, the standard relationship was:
one pes (Roman foot) equalled four palmi (palms) or sixteen digiti (fingers).
Consequently, one  palmus  corresponded  to  four  digiti.  Textual and
Metrological Note
2.     The precision of Ortiz y Sanz: The Spanish neoclassical academic
José Ortiz y Sanz (1787) made a rationalist critique of Vitruvius based on the
dissection and observation of real bodies, marking the Enlightenment's break
with the blind acceptance of ancient texts.
3.      Leonardo’s construction uses two centers: the navel for the circle and a
point near the groin for the square. Vitruvius explicitly identifies the navel as the
center of the circle and equates the span of the arms with bodily height. He does
not require the two figures to share a single center. Leonardo’s drawing is
therefore an interpretation of the transmitted instructions; the difference
between its centers does not by itself demonstrate that the Latin text was
geometrically mistaken.

16th century. Although he developed a preeminent ecclesiastical career after

Barbaro's most significant intellectual legacy lies in architectural treatises and
the science of vision. In 1556, he published his monumental I dieci libri
dell'architettura di M. Vitruvio, an annotated translation that established the
philological standard for Vitruvius's text thanks to his close collaboration with
the  architect  Andrea  Palladio.  Simultaneously,  Barbaro  expanded  the
boundaries of geometric representation in his celebrated treatise La pratica della
perspettiva (1568), where he rigorously analyzed the laws of conic projection and
anamorphosis. In this field, his empirical experiments with the camera obscura
proved pioneering for the history of science, introducing for the first time a
biconvex diaphragm to  correct chromatic aberrations and optimize the
sharpness of the projected image, prefiguring the  principles of modern
photographic optics.
These successive hermeneutical approaches — from Fra Giocondo's pioneering
schemes to Barbaro and Palladio's rigorous readings — demonstrate that the
reconstruction of the Basilica of Fano has not been a univocal process. On the
contrary, the building's restoration has operated as a  field of theoretical
experimentation throughout the history of architecture, where each designer
and  philologist has projected  their own  aesthetic,  scientific, and  spatial
assumptions onto the suggestive gaps in the original text.

Aurelius,  Publius  Numisius, and Gnaeus  Cornelius. The  scholar and

identified this circle of collaborators as citizens originally from Formia, a solid

This conjecture finds significant archaeological support in the figure of Publius
Numisius,  the  architect  whose  documented  authorship  includes  the
monumental  theater  of Herculaneum.  Architectural  historiography  has
revealed  remarkable  typological  and  structural  parallels  between  this
Herculaneum building and the Roman Theater of Formia, suggesting the
existence of a regional school or building tradition shared by Numisius and
Vitruvius.
Furthermore, Vitruvius's text reveals a profound geographical and technical
familiarity with the southern Latium  region, manifested  in  his  precise
descriptions of the Pontine Marshes and the physicochemical properties of the
thermal waters of Terracina (Neptune's spring). This topographical proximity
is further reinforced by his mention of prominent figures from the local
aristocracy and late Roman intellectual circles, such as Marcus Terentius Varro
and Licinius Murena, whose property holdings and influence in the Gulf of
Gaeta area strengthen Vitruvius's place within the social fabric of the Formia
elite.
Equally revealing is the episode linking the architect to the retinue of Gaius
Julius, son of Masinissa¹, the celebrated Numidian monarch. This international
contact not only  illustrates  Vitruvius's high technical  status within the
Caesarian administration, but also demonstrates the integration of Roman
engineers into the diplomacy and high  politics of the Neo- Hellenistic
Mediterranean. Although  the  debate surrounding  Vitruvius's  birthplace
remains open within the discipline, with historical candidates such as Verona,
Fano, or Fondi alternating, the density of epigraphic and geographical evidence
linked to Formia lends this hypothesis a high degree of scientific plausibility,
shaping the human backdrop from which the universal knowledge compiled in
De architectura would be projected.

testimonies and with securely identified inscriptions.
The proposed connection with Formiae offers one possible regional setting for
Vitruvius’s technical experience. The treatise itself demonstrates familiarity
with materials, construction and hydraulic problems, but it does not document
membership in a specifically identified Campanian guild. The association of
that practical knowledge with the cubic ratio and a cosmic order is the author’s
interpretive proposal. It should remain distinct from the biographical evidence.

Allegory of the duplication of the cube

Editorial note. — This allegory likewise forms part of the editor’s interpretive
perspective. The Delian problem of doubling the cube appears in Vitruvius (IX,
pref. 13–14) as a historical anecdote; the allegorical and symbolic reading
proposed here is the editor’s own and carries no philological authority.
“Following the devastating health  crisis that ravaged Athens during the
Peloponnesian War, and which claimed the life of the statesman Pericles, a
delegation of citizens went to the famous Oracle of Apollo on the island of
Delos¹ with the purpose of finding a divine remedy to alleviate the plague. The
deity's response dictated a condition of strict geometric precision: to appease
divine wrath, it was imperative to erect a new altar that exactly doubled the
volume of the pre-existing one, which had a perfect cubic configuration. The
Hellenic geometers, committing an error of linear proportionality, proceeded
to double the length of the edges of the original altar, which quadrupled its
surface area and exponentially increased its volume eightfold², thus failing to
solve the enigma.” Although the epidemic eventually subsided through natural
cycles, the mathematical challenge survived as a profound allegory about the
inadequacy of elementary arithmetic in the face of the complexity of three-
dimensional space.
This episode, recorded in the doxographical tradition by authors such as
Eratosthenes of Cyrene and Plutarch, transcends mere historical anecdote to
become the birth certificate of the "Delian problem."³ Apollo's demand was not
a mere ritual whim, but a subtle theoretical reproach to the Greeks for their
neglect of the geometry of solids, prompting mathematicians of the stature of
Hippocrates of Chios, Archytas of Tarentum, and Plato to explore the
properties of proportional lines and lay the foundations of the sacred geometry
of perfect volumes.95

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

the trisection of the angle, this challenge forms the triad of classical problems in
Greek  geometry.  While  modern  mathematics  has  demonstrated  the
impossibility of solving them using only the ideal ruler and compass³, for
ancient thought these dilemmas were not mere axiomatic puzzles, but rather
true instruments of theoretical transmutation. They represented states of
consciousness and the faculty of deciphering, within allegory, an ontological
reality that transcended the written word. To solve them, the geometer needed
to undergo a metanoia: to "turn the plane" and approach the archetype from a
higher dimension.
The first mathematician to formulate an analytical solution to this problem was
Hippocrates of Chios (c. 470 – c. 410 BCE). The pre-Socratic geometer
discovered that the problem of doubling the cube reduced geometrically to a
problem of interpolation: the insertion of two continuous mean proportionals
between a given segment and its double.

Mathematical and Philological Formalisation

In classical notation, and according to the theory of proportions set out in Book
VIII of Euclid’s Elements, if an initial segment a and its double 2a are given, and
two mean proportionals r and  s are inserted between them, the following
continued proportion is established:

                     a : r = r : s = s : 2a

In modern algebraic notation, this may be expressed as

                         a/r = r/s = s/2a.

From these equalities it follows that

                                     r² = as

and

                                          s² = 2ar.

Squaring the first equation and substituting the value of s² obtained from the
second yields

                           142

PRELIMINARY STUDY

                                    r⁴ = a²s²,

                                  r⁴ = a²(2ar),

                                    r⁴ = 2a³r.

Since r ≠ 0, division by r gives

                                     r³ = 2a³.

Thus the cube constructed on the first mean proportional r has exactly twice
the volume of the cube constructed on the original segment a. The celebrated
Delian problem — the duplication of the cube — therefore ceased to be a matter
of physical conjecture and became a rigorous problem in the theory of mean
proportionals. The search for the dimensions of the new Apollonian altar was
transformed into a precise mathematical investigation grounded in geometric
proportion.
Philologically, the designation “Delian altar” is preferable to “Apollonian
altar.” Although the tradition associates the episode with an altar of Apollo on
the island of Delos, classical and modern scholarship alike have generally
referred to the challenge as the Delian Problem (Problema Delium) or *the
Duplication  of the Cube. The use of “Delian  altar” therefore aligns the
terminology with the established historiographical and mathematical tradition.
