discovery of Hippocrates of Chios is a methodological stroke of genius. He
understood that a solid cannot be duplicated using simple proportions of (two-
dimensional) surfaces. By requiring two proportional means instead of one
(since a single mean, the geometric mean a: r :: r: 2a, serves to duplicate the
square, that is, r² = 2a²), Hippocrates forces the elevation from the plane to
volume, opening the door to rational three-dimensional geometry.

3.     Modern mathematical perspective. Wantzel’s result of 1837 establishes
that a cube cannot be doubled using straightedge and compass alone, because
the cube root of two is not constructible by successive quadratic extensions.
This modern proof must not be attributed to ancient geometers. The
constructions associated with Archytas and Menaechmus belong to the ancient
investigation of the problem by other means. Their association here with light
and the material plane is the author’s symbolic interpretation.
The first is of a historical - mathematical nature: the solutions of Archytas,
Menaechmus, and Eratosthenes were not approximate, but geometrically
exact. The misconception lies in the fact that they did not use only a ruler and
compass (which is impossible, as modern mathematics has demonstrated), but
rather developed advanced mechanical curves and conic sections of absolute
precision. The second point of clarification is philological -etymological: the
original name of the region was not Pyto, but Pito (from the Greek Pythó,
Πυθώ), derived from the verb pythein (to rot), alluding to the body of the
serpent defeated by Apollo.
“Building on the theoretical framework established by Hippocrates of Chios,
other preeminent geometers of antiquity took up the challenge of geometric
duplication. Far from proposing empirical approximations or estimated
calculations, scientists of the stature of Archytas of Tarentum, Menaechmus,
and Eratosthenes of Cyrene formulated solutions of strict geometric accuracy.
To overcome the operational limitations of the plane ruler and compass, these
authors needed to expand the horizons of the discipline: Archytas integrated the
third dimension through a bold constructive model of the intersection of three-
dimensional solids (a cylinder, a cone, and a torus); Menaechmus discovered
conic sections (the parabola and the hyperbola) as spatial cutting tools; and
Eratosthenes mechanized the process through a kinematic instrument known as
the mesolabe.”
Alongside this scientific development, the nerve center of the Apollonian cult,
the Oracle of Delphi, stood majestically on the slopes of Mount Parnassus in
Phocis. The sanctuary, dedicated to Apollo, was inextricably linked to a sacred
landscape where water acted as an agent of purification and prophecy. Among
the various springs that dotted the site, the Castalian Spring stood out, its waters
flowing flanked by a dense laurel forest, the plant attribute sacred to the god.

Mythical tradition celebrated this numinous setting as the meeting place of the
Muses, where Apollo's lyre orchestrated the song of the inspired deities. In the
context of Archaic and Classical Greece, this sacred site was originally called
Pytho, a theonym that evoked the chthonic decomposition of the defeated
monster. Over the centuries, linguistic usage assimilated both traditions, and the
original toponym of Pito yielded its preeminence to the definitive designation
of Delphi.

Critical Notes

science, it is vital to clarify that the solutions of the Academy and the
school of Tarentum were exact. Archytas of Tarentum (c. 428–347
BCE), a friend of Plato, solved the duplication of the cube using a double-
curvature  curve  that  foreshadows  modern  analytic  geometry.
Menaechmus (c. 380–320 BCE) demonstrated that the two continuous
mean  proportionals  corresponded  to  the  coordinates where two
parabolas, or a parabola and a hyperbola, intersect. To  call these
solutions "approximate" would weaken the thesis on the regularity of
Apollonian geometry.
2.     The etymology of Pytho (Pythó): The phonetic change to Pyto
should be corrected by its academic spelling: Pito. Philologically, the name
connects the physical space with the myth of the serpent's death: Apollo lets the
midday sun rot (pythein) the monster's corpse. From this "putrefaction" springs
the purification of the earth. The later transition to the name Delphi (Delphoi)
is etymologically associated with delphys (womb or matrix), signifying that the
sanctuary went from being the place of the dragon's death to becoming the
spiritual matrix and the Omphalos (navel) of the Greek world.96

“From  this toponym derives the  title of Pythia (pythōnissa), the  official
designation of the priestess who channeled prophecies in the sacred precinct of
Delphi. The term Pythō (Pythō) is inextricably linked to Python, the mythical
serpentine creature that guarded the buttresses of Mount Parnassus and which
Apollo slew to establish his oracular hegemony. According to mythographic
tradition, after defeating the monster, the god deposited  its ashes in an
underground receptacle located immediately beneath the omphalos; it was from
this 'navel of the world' that the priestesses assimilated the prophetic vapors
emanating from the chthonic entrails to deliver their oracular responses.” In the
sacred topography of Hellas, the temple consecrated to this deity was called
Pythion (in classical Greek, Πύθιον), and the god himself received the cultic
epithet of Apollo Pythius.
During the Archaic period, the veneration of Apollo took on a markedly
geometric character, being worshipped in the form of a plinth (πλινθός), a term
that in classical sources designates both the mud brick and the cubic pedestal.
This aniconic form of worship — the sacralization of a pure geometric volume
in  place  of anthropomorphic or  figurative  representation —  is  solidly
documented in ancient literature and the archaeology of Latium and Greece. In
the grammar of the classical architectural orders, the plinth constitutes the
smooth, quadrangular element that serves as the base and interface between the
column shaft and the stereobate, symbolizing the cubic fixity upon which the
verticality of the Doric and Tuscan orders unfolds.

Critical Notes
1.      Architectural Clarification (Plinth vs. Abacus): It is vital for
technical rigor not to confuse the plinth with the abacus. The plinth is at the
base of the column (earth, cubic stability). The abacus is at the top, crowning
the capital. The plinth, as a "cubic pedestal," acquires perfect coherence with the
concept of the cubic altar of Delos: the god of geometry manifests himself at the
very base of the structure, in the cubic rooting with matter.
2.     The Aniconic Cult and the Cube: The mention of the plinth as a
primitive form of Apollo. Authors such as Pausanias document that in Megara
and Amyclae, Apollo was worshipped as a bronze column or a quadrangular

3.     The Omphalos as a transmuter: The presence of the serpent's ashes

Vitruvius's journey
      The biographical details of Marcus Vitruvius Pollio remain shrouded
in a dense historiographical obscurity; virtually all information about his life
comes from passages in his own treatise, De architectura. The determination of
his three names is the subject of long-standing philological debates. While the
late manuscript tradition consolidated the cognomen "Pollio, " the epigraphic
record has opened alternative avenues of research: an inscription found in
Verona documents a Lucius Vitruvius Cordo, while another epigraphic evidence
in Thibilis (Numidia, North Africa) records the name Marcus Vitruvius
Mamurra. This latter coincidence has fueled the intriguing hypothesis of a
family relationship, or even a shared identity, between the treatise writer and
Mamurra, the celebrated and influential chief engineer (praefectus fabrum) of
Julius Caesar. However, none of these attributions finds explicit endorsement
in the text of De architectura, a work that the author formally dedicated to
Octavian Augustus.
On an institutional and professional level, Vitruvius served as a military engineer
within the legionary establishment, performing functions similar to those of a
praefectus fabrum or an architectus assigned to the armamentarium (the state
artillery arsenal). His technical relevance was confirmed in later literature: Pliny
the Elder includes him by name in the index auctorum of his Naturalis Historia
as an authority on the science of materials and mosaic paving techniques, while
Sextus Julius Frontinus, at the end of the 1st century AD, explicitly refers to
"Vitruvius the architect" in his treatise De aquaeductu when addressing the
standardization of lead pipe modules (fistulae).

PRELIMINARY STUDY

According to the autobiographical statements in his prefaces, Vitruvius was
born into a family of free Roman citizens and pursued his career in the
campaigns of the late Republican civil wars. He served in Julius Caesar's artillery
forces alongside a select corps of technical officers including Marcus Aurelius,
Publius Numisius, and Gnaeus Cornelius. During these campaigns,  his
geographical postings encompassed various fronts of the Roman Empire: North
Africa, Hispania, Pontus, and  Gallia Comata (including the regions of
Aquitania and Gallia Narbonensis).

The nature of the military Apparatio in the Roman army
To accurately gauge the operational scope of Vitruvius's rank as a military
engineer, historiography frequently turns to the later testimony of Flavius
Vegetius Renatus in his Epitoma  rei militaris. Vegetius  details the vast
responsibilities of the praefectus castrorum (camp prefect), a high-ranking officer
in charge of the army's construction and logistics: the fortification of the
perimeter, the digging of trenches, the organization of tent accommodations, as
well as the maintenance and provisioning of siege machinery and transport
vehicles.
Within  this  technical framework, Vitruvius  specialized in the apparatio
tormentorum, that  is, the construction and calibration of torsion artillery
pieces, primarily ballistae and scorpions, crucial ballistic weapons for siege
warfare. Various indications suggest that this training took place under the
direct orders of Lucius Cornelius Balbus, the influential praefectus fabrum of
Julius Caesar's Gallic campaigns. The precise passages in Vitruvius's treatise
analyzing siege mechanics reflect firsthand experience in the major theaters of
operations of 52 BCE, such as the fierce siege of Avaricum, the tactical
operations before the walls of Gergovia, and finally, the monumental work of
circumventing and besieging the stronghold of Alesia.

Critical Notes
1.      Clarifying the Mamurra Case: The connection between Vitruvius
and Mamurra is fascinating. Mamurra was Caesar 's praefectus fabrum in Gaul,
famous for his immense wealth and for having introduced the first Carrara
marble (marmor lunense) paneling into his palace on the Caelian Hill. If
Vitruvius was not Mamurra himself, he undoubtedly belonged to the same
technical management. This gives Vitruvius a status far higher than that of a

2.     The technical precision of the weapons: Ballistae and scorpions
were not calibrated empirically or randomly. In Book X, Vitruvius details how
Roman engineers used a mathematical formula based on the weight of the
projectile to calculate the diameter of the bore in the bundles of torsion tendons.
Roman artillery, therefore, was pure geometry applied to military ballistics.
3.     The  parallel with Vegetius: Although Vegetius wrote  several
centuries later (at the end of the Empire), his description of the legions' technical
environment confirms that Roman architects were not trained in academies of
fine arts, but in the mud of the trenches, surveying the terrain, building
palisades, and ensuring the water supply. This is the origin of Vitruvian firmitas:
the solidity that must withstand both the ravages of time and the enemy's
catapults.97

enduring legacy lies in his role as a theorist and systematizer of architecture. In
the context of ancient Rome, architectura was a discipline of a vastly broader
scope than its contemporary counterpart;  it encompassed urban planning,
construction management and  physics,  civil and  materials  engineering,
metallurgy, hydrodynamic mechanics, military ballistics, and the science of
mechanical devices. This cross-disciplinary nature has led the historiography of
technology to recognize Vitruvius as the seminal pioneer of architectural
engineering and technical building.”

Technical Standardization: Hydraulics and Theatrical Acoustics
Vitruvius's expertise in the development of public infrastructure was confirmed
by Sextus  Julius Frontinus, who acknowledged  his contribution to the
metrological standardization of the diameter of lead pipes (fistulae), a critical
advance  for the  distribution of imperial water  resources.  Similarly, the
historiography of science hails him as the founder of architectural acoustics
thanks to his meticulous description of bronze resonating vessels or echeia
(ἠχεῖα). These devices, arranged in symmetrical niches beneath the seating tiers
of theaters according to strict laws of Pythagorean musical harmony, served to
amplify the actors' voices through physical resonance.
Although the catalog of his material works remains undocumented, the author
left evidence of his direct involvement in the construction of the Basilica of
Fanum Fortunae (modern-day Fano), whose erection dates to the first decades
of Augustus's reign (c. 27–15 BCE). The material remains of this structure have
disappeared from the surface, opening a complex archaeological debate about
its exact topographical location. One of the most plausible historiographical
hypotheses suggests  that, given the recurring  early Christian practice of
Christianizing civil forum spaces, the substructures and colonnade of the
Vitruvian basilica may have been absorbed and integrated into the medieval
fabric of the current Romanesque cathedral of Fano.

1.     Miasmatic Theory as the Ordering of Chaos: The section on
miasmas is vital. Vitruvius demonstrates that the architect not only arranges the
stones, but also regulates the invisible elements (air, water, heat). The corrupt
air of the swamps represents the chaos of untouched nature; architecture, by
choosing the elevated site and laying out the walls, acts as a filter that purifies the
environment and allows the Apollonian light and clean air to sustain the life of
the citizen.

echeia described in Book V (V, 5) are  definitive proof that Vitruvian

intervals of a fourth,  fifth, and octave. This connects directly with the
proportional means of doubling the cube: the Roman theater is not just a
building for leisure, but a mathematical instrument designed to attune the
vibrations of the human voice to the mathematical harmonies of the cosmos.

Vitruvius' basilica underlies the cathedral of Fano closes the evolutionary cycle
of the building: the civil structure built by Augustus' architect to house the
Aedes Augusti (the cult of the emperor) ended up becoming the formal matrix
of the Christian temple, demonstrating the perenniality of its geometric axes.

Critical Notes
1.     The value of the Preface to Book VII: This text is the first Western
"history of architecture." Vitruvius constructs his intellectual family tree here. It
is significant that he  relates the physics of Thales to the machinery of
Archimedes, and the symmetry of Hermogenes demonstrates that all ancient
knowledge forms a unified matrix.
2.     The Interpolation of Optics (Agatarchus, Democritus, Anaxagoras):
The mention of these authors in the section "On Divergence"  is crucial.
Vitruvius explains that Agatharchus painted a stage set for Aeschylus and left a
treatise on how straight lines must curve or diverge to suit the human eye. This
demonstrates that Roman sacred geometry was not rigid; architects knew that
for a building to appear perfectly cubic or symmetrical to the human eye, they
had to apply invisible optical corrections to the actual lines.
3.     The legitimization of Cossutius and Mucius: By including Roman
architects (Cossutius, Mucius) on the same level as the Greek geniuses Ictinus or
Chersiphron, Vitruvius  is performing an act of cultural nationalism: he
demonstrates that Augustan Rome has reached the technical and artistic
maturity necessary to inherit and perfect the geometric canon of the Hellenistic
world. Roman space is now the definitive container of Sophia.

To consolidate this crucial chapter on the historiographical fortune of the
Vitruvian treatise, it is necessary to specify the technical transition between the
Roman world and its humanist rediscovery.
From the perspective of the archaeology of construction, the relative silence of
Antiquity was not solely due to obscure language, but also to a technological
shift: Vitruvius wrote at the dawn of the Principate (still within an architectural
tradition rooted in Hellenistic stonework and lintels), just before the great
revolution of opus caementicium (Roman concrete) and the monumental
vaulted  structures  that  characterized  the  1st  and 2nd  centuries AD
(amphitheaters, large baths, and aqueducts supported by arcades). Furthermore,
the discovery at Poggio Bracciolini in 1416 was not the only manuscript found,
but rather the catalyst for the humanist philology that led to Sulpicius da
Veroli's editio princeps and Alberti's creative reinterpretation.
" The reception of De architectura in the literature of classical antiquity presents
a historiographical paradox: despite being the only theoretical corpus of the
discipline preserved in its entirety, its immediate impact on imperial texts was
remarkably restricted, limited to the technical mentions of Pliny the Elder,
Sextus Julius Frontinus, and the late antique epitome of Cetius Faventinus. This
hermeneutical asymmetry is due to stylistic and technical-structural reasons. On
the one hand, Vitruvius's prose — characterized by archaic Latin and neological
terminology of Hellenistic origin — was difficult to assimilate outside the guilds
of the state apparatus. " On the other hand, the treatise was written during the
transition from the Republic to the  first Empire, a tectonic horizon  still
anchored in the trabeated orders of Greek origin; because of this, Vitruvius did
not systematize the imminent Roman building revolution that would define the
following centuries, characterized by the monumental exploitation of opus
caementicium, the  large  tiers of amphitheaters, the development of the
engineering of pillars and arches, and the physics of concrete vaults.
Despite this retreat in the visual culture of the High Empire, the treatise survived
the fragmentation of the West through a robust network of manuscript
transmission during the Early and Late Middle Ages. Contemporary philology
documents the survival of approximately eighty codices of medieval tradition,

among which stand out copies from the Anglo-Saxon and Carolingian eras
produced around 800 CE. The preservation of these testimonies in the
scriptoria of abbeys and basilica monasteries — such as St. Gallen, Cluny,
Canterbury, and Oxford — demonstrates that the Vitruvian text functioned as
a repository of Latinity and encyclopedic knowledge, preserving the conceptual
framework that would link classical theory with the Renaissance.
The advent of Quattrocento humanism radically transformed this scholarly
status, elevating Vitruvius to the position of canonical authority for the
refounding  of  constructive  practice. The ad  fontes movement  spurred
intellectuals  like  Poggio  Bracciolini  to  undertake  philological  research
campaigns in monastic libraries; in 1416, Bracciolini unearthed a critical copy
of De architectura in the Monastery of St. Gallen, an event that catalyzed the
constructive exegesis of the Quattrocento. This process of literary restitution
reached its apotheosis with the publication of the editio princeps of the treatise,
printed in Rome around 1486 by the humanist Giovanni Sulpicio da Veroli
(Sulpicius of Aquila), an event that inaugurated the era of architectural printing
and the standardization of European theoretical debate.

Hermeneutics and the Genesis of the Modern Treatise
Given that medieval manuscripts lacked Vitruvius's original graphic apparatus
(the figures mentioned in the text had been lost in the copying process),
Renaissance architects were compelled to adopt a methodologically dual
approach. The practical application of the ten books demanded a constant
dialectical confrontation between the abstract text and the direct examination
of the surviving archaeological ruins on Italian soil. Far from being an obstacle,
the frequent discrepancies between Vitruvian prescriptions and the materiality of
imperial monuments — such as the Colosseum or the Pantheon — opened up
a fertile space for interpretive freedom. This hermeneutical gap allowed modern
masters to deploy a high degree of creativity and geometric rigor in their spatial
design.
The Vitruvian influence shaped the foundations of Western architectural
theory well into the 19th century. As early as 1452, Leon Battista Alberti
completed his De re aedificatoria, a seminal work that adopted the decemviral
structure and tripartite conceptual framework of his Roman predecessor, albeit
reconfigured through the lens of Platonic philosophy. The expansion of the

Critical Notes
1.     The Fracture of Opus Caementicium: Regarding sacred space and
the cube, this point is crucial. Vitruvius defends the use of dressed stone and the
traditional Greek  static  structure  because he  sees  in  it an immutable
mathematical order. However, later emperors (from Nero with the Domus
Aurea to Hadrian with the Pantheon) preferred concrete, a malleable material
that allowed them to curve space and create colossal domes. By not addressing
these developments, Vitruvius preserved the purity of the straight line and the
elemental cubic volume, which is precisely what Alberti and the Renaissance
architects inherited to purify sacred space in contrast to the Gothic style.
2.     The paradox of the missing figures: It is crucial to emphasize the
significance of the absence of illustrations in the text discovered by Poggio
Bracciolini. Without drawings, the Renaissance had to imagine proportions
through the pure abstract geometry described in the words. Architects like
Bramante, Raphael, and Palladio had to rediscover the modular law by
reconstructing plans using only  ruler and compass, which transformed
architecture into a superior mental and mathematical science, detached from
the mere medieval craftsmanship of stonemasons.
3.     The transition from Vitruvius to Alberti: Leon Battista Alberti did
not simply copy Vitruvius; he effected a subtle theoretical transmutation. While
the Roman presented an eminently practical vision linked to state engineers,
Alberti elevated venustas to the category of Concinnitas  (the universal
harmony of all parts regulated by absolute mathematical laws, where nothing
can be altered without destroying the whole). This is the direct bridge to the
hypothesis put forward here: Renaissance architecture takes Vitruvius's military
and pragmatic heritage and transforms  it into a three-dimensional spatial
theology.99

      “A key pillar of Vitruvian sacred anthropometry is the theoretical
formulation of homo bene figuratus (De architectura, III, 1, 1), a concept that
prescribes the intrinsic geometric correspondences of the human body and its
precise inscription within the perfect forms of the circle and the square. This
microcosmic analogy acted as a powerful catalyst for Renaissance artists and
humanists, finding its most celebrated iconic embodiment in Leonardo da Vinci
’s Vitruvian Man (c. 1490). Centuries later, on the horizon of 20th-century
modernity, the Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier revived Vitruvian modular
methodology through the development of the Modulor (1948).” This system of
spatial regulation constituted a harmonic scale that combined the proportions
of human physiognomy with the golden section and the mathematical series of
Fibonacci, with the purpose of standardizing architectural and industrial
production to the measure of man.
Regarding the material transmission of the text, contemporary historiography
has debunked the myth of the sudden "rediscovery" of Vitruvius by Poggio
Bracciolini in 1416 at the Abbey of St. Gall (and not, as a later tradition now
discarded claimed, at Montecassino in 1414). Philological research clarifies that
Bracciolini unearthed a critical codex of De architectura in the library of the
Monastery of St. Gallen in 1416; however, this event did not represent a complete
break with the medieval past, but rather the culmination of a latent process of
assimilation. Preeminent humanists of the Trecento, such as Francesco Petrarch
and Giovanni Boccaccio, had already frequented and annotated Vitruvian
manuscripts during the 14th century, demonstrating that the knowledge of
Augustus's architect never completely died out in the cultural substratum of
pre-Quattrocento Italian intellectuals.

“Francesco Petrarch’s intervention in the Vitruvian tradition did not result in a
linguistic transposition into Italian, but rather in a work of rescue, collation, and
philological exegesis in Latin during the 14th century. Petrarch, considered the
herald of Renaissance humanism, located and preserved in his private library
manuscript copies of De architectura — at a time when the treatise was
considered an extremely opaque text — marking its margins with valuable
critical annotations (scholia) that clarified the careless syntax of Imperial
technical Latin. His approach to the architect of Augustus was literary and
archaeological in nature, motivated by his desire to reconstruct the topography
and monumental glories of classical Rome, thus establishing the method that
the humanists of the Quattrocento would inherit.”
The history of vernacular reception includes manuscript translations as well as
print. Cesariano’s Como edition of 1521 was the first printed Italian translation,
distinguished by its extensive commentary and woodcuts. Daniele Barbaro’s
Venetian edition of 1556, with contributions by Palladio, belongs to a later stage
of that reception. Petrarch’s engagement with Vitruvius was Latin and
scholarly; it should not be confused with these printed vernacular translations.

1.     The myth of Petrarch's translation: It is a common mistake to
confuse Petrarch's love for the vernacular (expressed in his Canzoniere) with his
scholarly work. For Petrarch, the works of Roman science, philosophy, and
architecture had to be treated in the language of the Empire: Latin. His work
with Vitruvius consisted of cleaning the text of the errors that medieval copyists
had introduced over centuries.

2.      Cesare Cesariano (1521). His first printed Italian translation is a
milestone in the visual and vernacular reception of Vitruvius.  Its
commentary and  illustrations make  technical  questions  accessible
through the architectural culture of the Italian Renaissance, rather than
simply reproducing a lost ancient illustrative program.
3.     In the author’s interpretation, the passage from learned Latin
reception to vernacular architectural writing marks a widening of the
treatise’s readership. That symbolic reading should be distinguished from
evidence for the actual circulation, ownership, and use of particular

Vitruvius and his Work
John Ruskin's quotation, while methodologically brilliant in contrasting the
19th-century view with the classical one, introduces a dichotomy (architect vs.
builder) that did not exist in that form in the Roman world: for Vitruvius, the
architect  is the ultimate builder because he masters both fabrica (manual
practice) and ratiocinatio (mathematical theory). Furthermore, in the last
paragraph, it is crucial to clarify that for Vitruvius, architecture does not imitate
nature in  its formal or ornamental aspects, but rather in  its operational
principles and rational laws (tectonic mimesis).
“In the programmatic design of De architectura, Vitruvius (c. 80–15 BCE)
configures the building discipline not as an empirical or sectoral craft, but as an
encyclopedic and unifying episteme. By assigning it a primordial epistemic
character,  the  treatise  writer maintains  that  architecture subsumes and
structures practically all areas of human knowledge. For Vitruvius, excellence in
architectura demands a bidirectional training founded on the symbiosis of
fabrica (executive practice) and ratiocinatio (the theoretical and mathematical
demonstration of proportions). This universal propaedeutic requires of the
architect a rigorous mastery of a broad spectrum of disciplines:
•      Geometry (Geometria): An indispensable instrumental axiom for the
delineation of plans (ichnographia), elevations (orthographia) and perspectives
(scaenographia), guaranteeing the exact translation of abstract diagrams into
physical space.
•      Mathematics (Arithmetic): Foundation of modular metrology and
cost  calculation,  essential  for  the  computation  of  symmetries  and
proportionality relationships that ensure tectonic stability against material
loads.
•     Anatomy and Medicine (Medicine): An analytical prescription that
governs sacred anthropometry — synthesized in the canon of homo bene
figuratus — and urban health. It includes the study of climatic vectors, water
quality, and the sanitation of residential districts.
•      Optics and Acoustics (Optice et Musica): Physical knowledge
applied to the correction of optical illusions in the entablatures and tonal

•     Law  (Iura): Knowledge  of Roman  civil and urban  planning
jurisprudence,  regulating  easements  of  light,  drainage,  party  walls and
construction contracts to avoid tax disputes.
•      Theology and Astrology (Theologia et Astrologia): Doctrines that
determine the correct observance of decorum  (decor), ensuring that the
typologies of the temples correspond to the ontological attributes of each deity,
as well as for the layout of the solar quadrants (gnomonica) and the cosmic
orientation of the oracular cellas.
•      Meteorology  (Caeli  Ratio):  Microclimatic  analysis  of  the
geographical environment that determines the orientation of openings, the
thickness of walls and ventilation systems according to the prevailing winds.

The Historical Dialectic of Design and Tectonic Mimesis
This holistic vision of the architect as a universal sage contrasts with the
aestheticist derivations of modernity. Centuries later, the 19th-century critic
John Ruskin would condense the Romantic turn by stating that “no one who is
not a great sculptor or painter can be an architect; if he is not, he can only be a
builder.” For Vitruvian pragmatism, however, beauty (venustas) is not a plastic
ornament superimposed by the fine arts, but a mathematical property emerging
from correct structural arrangement.
In Vitruvian cosmology, architecture operates under the principle of mimicking
nature, not through the slavish copying of its biomorphic forms, but through
the emulation of its laws of efficiency and protection. Just as birds and bees
configure their nests in response to instinctive needs for preservation, primitive
humanity erected the primitive hut as a primary refuge against the harshness of
the elements. The transition from this primitive organic functionalism to the
refinement of the art of building was completed when Hellenic civilization
translated the tectonics of wood into the laws of stone, canonizing this process
through the invention of the architectural orders: the structural vigor of the
Doric, the golden elegance of the Ionic, and the vegetal exuberance of the
Corinthian.

Critical Notes
1.     The Vitruvian-Ruskin Tension: It is excellent to introduce Ruskin.
Ruskin writes from the perspective of Romanticism and the Gothic Revival,
where the architect is an individual artist and the builder is a mere industrial
worker. For Vitruvius, this separation is an aberration: the fabric (knowing how
to lay the bricks) and the ratiocinatio (knowing why they are laid) form an
indissoluble unity. By recovering this Roman sense, this edition advocates a
return to the unity of thought and matter.
2.     The Primitive Hut as Archetype: Vitruvius's account of the origins
of architecture (Book II) is the foundation of all Western architectural theory
(later revisited by Laugier in the 18th century). The hut of logs and leaves is the
"womb" of architecture. The Greeks did not invent the orders from nothing;
they petrified the wooden structure of the hut (the triglyphs of the Doric order
are the stony memory of the original beam ends). Architecture is, therefore, an
alchemical transmutation: converting the ephemeral wood of nature into the
eternal order of geometric stone.
3.     The concept of Decorum: In the theology section, it is essential to use
the Vitruvian technical term Decorum. Decorum is the mystical suitability of
the building to its function. Vitruvius explains that a temple to Minerva, Mars,
or Hercules should be Doric (robust, austere, masculine), while a temple to
Venus,  Flora,  or  Proserpina  should  be  Corinthian  (delicate,  slender,
ornamental). The architectural order is not chosen for aesthetic taste, but for a
cosmic correspondence with the energy of the divinity that will inhabit the
space.
          " Vitruvian epistemology finds its operative core in the indissoluble
symbiosis between fabrica and ratiocinatio. Vitruvius rigorously warns that
those practitioners who devoted themselves exclusively to manual skill (fabrica)
without the aid of letters failed to achieve an authority commensurate with their
efforts; conversely, theorists who took refuge solely in abstract reasoning
(ratiocinatio) pursued a shadow instead of material reality. Consequently, the
architect of excellence is defined as that scholar capable of transmuting theory
into practice, governing their activity by an encyclopedic knowledge that unifies
the exact sciences, the liberal arts, and the humanistic culture of the imperium.
"

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

This systematic approach unfolds with architectural rigor in the internal
structure of De architectura, a corpus divided into ten books or volumes
(volumina). Each section opens with a proemium  (preface)  of profound
philosophical and historical depth that legitimizes the subsequent topic in light
of the figure of Emperor Augustus. It is in Book I that the author establishes the
three ontological and immutable vectors that must govern all construction,
universally known as the Vitruvian triad:

•      Firmitas  (Solidity):  Guaranteed by  the  scientific  selection  of
materials, the firmness of the foundations  (substructio) and the  correct
distribution of structural loads without blindly relying on empirical resistance.
•       Utilitas  (Utility  or  Functionality):  Achieved  through  the
functional and obstacle-free arrangement of the plants, ensuring that the
distribution of spaces accurately reflects the public or private use for which they
are intended.
•      Venustas (Beauty or  Grace): An  aesthetic emergence  that  is
consolidated when the appearance of the plane is pleasing and harmonious,
based on the laws of proportion (proportio) and the modular correspondence of
the homo bene  figuratus, whose geometric  translation would  inspire the
Renaissance canon of Leonardo da Vinci.

Critical Notes
1.     The Interdependence of the Triad: It is crucial to emphasize that
firmitas, utilitas, and venustas are neither optional nor divisible. In the Roman
mindset, beauty (venustas) is not a superficial aesthetic added at the end; it is the
direct result of the building being solid (firmitas) and perfectly fulfilling its
function (utilitas). The proportion that makes a temple beautiful is the same
mathematical proportion that prevents its dome or entablature from collapsing.
2.     The Descending Order of Knowledge: The geometric beauty of the
treatise's structure. Vitruvius begins in Book I by examining the entire territory

(the macrocosm of the city) and ends in Book X by analyzing the tooth of a gear
or the rope of a catapult (the microcosm of the machine). There is a conscious
descent from the divine laws of heaven and temples (Books III and IV) to the
humble matter of the earth and military technology (Books VII and X).
3.     The Link of Book II to the Origin: The transition from Book I to
Book II is pivotal to the treatise's argument concerning development. Vitruvius
introduces the materials (sand, stone, wood) immediately after explaining what
a city is, because the raw material must be consecrated by the architect's logos
before becoming a wall or temple. The clay of the earth is elevated to the
category of classical order through the geometric intervention of the sage.
•     Book V (De  publicis  locis): Volume devoted to  institutional
architecture and  the  organization  of  civic meeting  spaces. The author
systematizes the proportions of the forum, the typology of the forum basilica
(inserting his own construction experience in Fano) and, most importantly, the
physics of theaters, where he introduces the science of harmonic acoustics and
the optical optimization of the seating areas.
•     Book VI (De privatis aedificiis): Treatise dedicated to domestic
architecture and the organization of private space. Vitruvius analyses the
climatic orientation of rooms, the typologies of the atrium of the Roman
domus, and the configuration of suburban villas, establishing that the dwelling
should reflect the socioeconomic condition and the decorous status of its
owner.
•     Book VII (De expolitionibus): A technical monograph focused on
the arts of finishing and coating materials.  It describes with engineering
precision the preparation of mortar, the execution of high-strength pavements,
the plastering of stuccos, and the mineral and vegetable chemistry for obtaining
imperishable decorative pigments.
•     Book VIII (De aquis): Section dedicated to hydraulic engineering
(aquarum ductus). Vitruvius addresses the geological prospecting of springs, the
medicinal properties of waters, the methods of topographic leveling using the
chorobates, and the technologies of conduction through masonry channels, lead
pipes (fistulae), or clay (tubuli).
•     Book  IX  (On  Gnomonics): A  cosmological  and  physical
-mathematical digression that links architecture with the celestial order. The
author explains the foundations of geocentric astronomy, the movement of the

The Paradox of the Lost Figures and the Hermeneutics of Space
In terms of textual transmission, the definitive loss of the original graphic
apparatus that complemented Vitruvius's manuscript constitutes one of the
most influential phenomena in the history of Western architectural theory.
Throughout his ten books, the author  explicitly  refers to diagrams and
illustrations (figurae) —originally placed at the end of the papyrus scrolls —
intended to visually clarify the complex geometric formulas of the orders, the
eurhythmy of the facades, or the mechanisms of the lifting machines.
The disappearance of this visual atlas during the early medieval manuscript
copying process transformed De architectura into a purely abstract and
conceptual text. However, far from diminishing its relevance, this absence of
images became the main driving force behind European architectural thought.
Lacking a single, unambiguous graphic model, architects and humanists —
from Fra Giocondo and Cesare Cesariano to Andrea Palladio — were
compelled to reinvent, draw, and design the treatise, forcing a dialectical
confrontation  between   classical  text  and  archaeological  ruins.  This
hermeneutical gap transformed a rigid military manual from the Augustan era
into a living, inexhaustible, and foundational text for the history of Western
science and aesthetics.

Critical Notes
1.     The precision of Book VII: Maintaining pavements and plasterwork
in Book VII. Vitruvius explains that a good plaster requires up to six layers of
mortar made from lime and powdered marble. This is not merely decoration; it
is the pursuit of material perfection. The wall should reflect light like a mirror.
Venustas (beauty) is achieved when the craftsman's physical technique elevates
opaque matter to a state of pure luminosity.
2.     The Chorobates and the Leveling of the Land: In Book VIII, the
use of the chorobates (a twenty-foot-long wooden ruler with plumb lines and a
water channel for leveling) represents the imposition of the horizontal straight
line upon the irregularity of the land. For water to flow to the city, the engineer
must correct nature. Vitruvian hydraulics is, therefore, a branch of applied
geometry that purifies and orders the land.

3.     The Analemma of Book IX: The design of sundials using the
analemma is mathematical proof that Roman architecture is a cosmological
science. The architect projects onto the plane of the earth the shadows cast by
the sun on its annual journey through the zodiac. A well-oriented Vitruvian
building is not isolated from its surroundings; it is an astronomical instrument
that beats in unison with the time of the universe. The space of architecture and
the time of the stars are unified under the rule of the treatise writer.
Translation  (1847),  published  in  Paris by Panckoucke,  is one  of  the

strip Vitruvius's text of the overly romantic interpretations of his time, restoring
the technical rigor and military pragmatism of the Latin original. In line with
contemporary editorial standards, chapter titles are standardized by combining
Maufras's 19th-century rubric with modern technical-legal and archaeological

STUDY OF THE TEN BOOKS
Academic Restitution and Writing (Books I and II)
The structural breakdown of the first two books of De architectura reveals the
epistemic matrix upon which Vitruvius builds the entirety of his treatise. Far
from constituting a mere summary of trades, the index of these foundational
books traces the ontological transition that runs from the training of the scholar
and the geopolitical delimitation of territory (Book I) to the physico-chemical
analysis of raw materials and the anthropology of building (Book II).
The systematic organization of these chapters  is reconfigured under the
following academic standard:

BOOK I: De architectura et de urbis ordinatione
(From architectural science and the organization of urban space)
•       Chapter I: The epistemology of building and the propaedeutics of the
architect. Definition of the discipline through the coexistence of the fabric and
the ratiocinatio; breakdown of the encyclopedic training of the professional.
•       Chapter II: The constitutive axioms of architecture. Analysis of the six
theoretical principles that govern classical design: ordinatio (arrangement),
dispositio (arrangement), eurythmia (eurhythmy), symmetria (symmetry), decor
(decorum) and distributio (distribution or economy).

•       Chapter III: The parts of architectural science and the ontological
triad. Division of knowledge in the construction of buildings (aedificatio),
gnomonic (gnomonice) and mechanics (machinatio). Introduction of the three
universal requirements: firmitas, utilitas and venustas.
•       Chapter IV: Environmental Teratology and Selection of Urban Sites
(De electione locorum sanissimorum). Hygienist and Hippocratic Criteria for the
Founding of Cities; Analysis of Winds, Marsh Fogs, and the Salubrity of
Humours.
•       Chapter V: Poliorcetics and Fortification: The erection of walls and
towers. Deep foundation techniques (substructio) and defensive geometry to
repel enemy siege engines.
•       Chapter VI: Climatic urbanism and street orientation. Street layout
and interpolation of walls based on the wind rose (anemometry) to neutralize
harmful currents in public space.
•       Chapter VII: Sacred and civil zoning (Dispositio moeniorum). Spatial
distribution and allocation of plots for the temples of the immortal gods and the
common spaces of the citizens according to liturgical decorum.

BOOK II: De materiae facultatibus
(From the physical and chemical properties of materials and the origin of
tectonics)
•       Chapter  I: Cultural Anthropology and the Genesis of Building.
Account of the primitive hut; the domestication of fire as the origin of human
society and the transition from the cave to the geometric order.
•       Chapter II: Cosmology of the elements according to the philosophical
schools. Theory of matter based on the pre-Socratic principles (Thales' water,
Anaximenes'  air, Heraclitus   '  fire and Democritus' atoms) as the key to
understanding building materials.
•       Chapter III: The adobe brick (De lateribus). Modular typologies
(Lydian, pentador, tetrador), seasonal drying processes and quality control of
clay.
•       Chapter IV: Sand (From harena). Mineralogy classification of quarry
sands  (fossicia), river sands (flumina) and sea sands (marina), and their
suitability for mortar cohesion.

Critical Notes
1.    On the rendering of pulvere puteolanum: the Roman term pulvere
puteolanum corresponds directly to modern pozzolana. This chapter (II.6) is
among the most important in the history of Roman civil engineering: pozzolana
allowed the Romans to build ports, docks, and bridge foundations submerged
directly in water, breaking the limitation of Greek architecture, which always
relied on dry rock.
2.      Chapter VI of Book I as cosmic geometry: The layout of streets
according to the winds was not merely a matter of convenience. Vitruvius
describes the placement of a gnomon (a vertical pillar) in the center of the future
city to mark the line of the shadow in the morning and afternoon. By joining
these points, the East-West line was obtained, and from there the city was
divided into a perfect octagon corresponding to the eight principal winds. The
Roman city is, therefore, an inhabited sundial, a sacred space perfectly oriented
with the axes of the cosmos.
3.     From Atom to Brick: In the order of the chapters of Book II, Vitruvius
does not jump directly to explaining how to build a wall; he first dedicates an
entire chapter (Chapter II) to the philosophy of matter. He explains that to be
a good architect, one must understand the behavior of the four elements of
nature, because brick, lime, and wood expand, contract, and react according to
the  invisible  laws  of  pre-Socratic  physics. Knowledge  always  precedes
technique.100

Books III and IV of De architectura constitute the dogmatic core of the theory
of sacred design in Antiquity. Vitruvius articulates a system where beauty
(venustas) is not a subjective criterion, but an emergent mathematical property
based on the module (M). Book III takes the human microcosm as its starting

Critical Notes
1.     The Scamilli Impares as a Geometric Secret: In Book III, Chapter
IV, Maufras translates the technical term scamilli impares as "unequal bearings."
This is one of the most debated passages among Renaissance architects. It refers
to the subtle upward curve given to the stylobate (the temple platform). If the
platform were perfectly straight in the geometric plane, the human eye would
perceive it as sunken due to an optical distortion. By curving it slightly towards
the center, the temple appears perfectly stable and regular to the observer.
True symmetry requires curving the material straight line.

2.     The Doric Angular  Conflict  as a Mathematical Dilemma:
Chapter III of Book IV explains why Greek architects (such as Tarcesius)
abandoned the Doric order for the Ionic: due to the rigidity of the triglyph. By
law, a triglyph must be positioned exactly over the center of each column and
the center of each intercolumniation. However, at the corners of the temple, the
triglyph must be placed at the very edge of the frieze, which misaligns the last
metope. This dilemma forced the shift from a two-dimensional approach (the
façade) to a three-dimensional adjustment of the intercolumniation (corner
contraction). Classical geometry prefers to change the physical module rather
than disrupt the visual harmony of the whole.
3.     The Altar as a Cosmic Interface: The final chapter of Book IV
eloquently concludes the hypothesis concerning Delphi and the archetypes.
Vitruvius details that the altars of Jupiter and the celestial gods should be
elevated; those of Gaia and the underworld (chthonic) deities should be rustic
and at ground level; and those of the water nymphs should be intermediate. The
altar is the vanishing point where the geometry of the temple communicates
with the invisible forces of nature, the same principle that united the ashes of
the serpent Python beneath the oracular omphalos of Delphi.

1.     Opus Signinum and Roman  hydraulic  waterproofing:  In
Chapter VII of Book  VIII, Vitruvius  treats lime and cement  cisterns.

chemical reaction that renders the mortar absolutely impermeable. This detail is
technically significant: the channeled water is retained without seepage within a
watertight lining of opus signinum.

2.     The analemma of Book IX: geometric projection in gnomonics:
Chapter VII of Book IX is a scientific core for the study of regulated space. The
analemma is not an artistic drawing; it is a pure geometric construction that
projects the apparent annual motion of the Sun, mapping it onto the two-
dimensional plane of the dial. By mastering the analemma, the Roman architect
could calculate the exact shadow a building would cast at any time of day and
on any day of the year (equinoxes and solstices). The method thus allowed the
architect to represent, on a plane surface, the geometry governing the Sun's
apparent course throughout the year.
3.     The Inverted Siphon (Venter) and the Mastery of Gravity: In
Book VIII, Chapter VII, the description of the lead pipes crossing the valleys
demonstrates that Roman engineers understood the physics of communicating
vessels. To prevent water pressure from breaking the pipes at the bottom of the
valley, they constructed a horizontal section called a venter (belly). Roman
engineering did not evade the forces of gravity, but rather balanced them
through the symmetry of the watercourse.

This final book distils Vitruvius’s pragmatism in its purest form — that of a
legionary military engineer. One technical term calls for care: the Latin cochlea
must be rendered as the Archimedes’ screw (the water-screw, or auger pump for
raising fluids), not by any popular nineteenth-century equivalent. We also
systematise the direct influence of this book on the seminal treatises of antiquity
and the Renaissance.
Book X of De architectura crowns the work not as a technical appendix, but as
the dynamic manifestation of physics and geometry applied to the service of the
Roman  state. Vitruvius breaks down the laws of elementary kinematics,
distinguishing between large traction machines and precision devices, before
turning  to  industrial  hydraulics and  military  torsion  ballistics, whose
mathematical calibration depended directly on the geometric solution of
doubling the cube.

Vitruvian Tradition and the Family Tree of Architectural Theory
The disappearance of the original figures (estimated at a minimum of ten
modular plates affixed to the ends of the papyrus scrolls by Vitruvius himself)
forced 16th-century editors to undertake a colossal graphic reconstruction. This
hermeneutical effort gave rise to the creation of the great modern treatises,
which adopted the Vitruvian theoretical framework and adapted it to the needs
of their respective eras.

•       Pliny  the  Elder (Natural  History,  1st  century AD): An
immediate contemporary in the historiographical record. Pliny absorbed and
indexed Vitruvius's mineralogical and metallurgical investigations (particularly
the data in Book VII on cinnabar, lime, and marbles) within his books dedicated
to geology and the plastic arts, validating the soundness of science during the
time of Augustus.
•      Leon Battista Alberti (De re aedificatoria, 1452): The first great
treatise of Renaissance humanism. Alberti adopts the decemviral structure (ten
books) and cardinal concepts of Vitruvius, but purifies the medievalized
technical Latin of the Roman under the lens of Ciceronian prose and Platonic
philosophy, transforming the Vitruvian triad into the supreme concept of
Concinnitas.
•      Andrea Palladio (I quattro libri dell'architettura, 1570): The
apotheosis of visual codification. Palladio synthesizes Vitruvius's abstract
theory and translates it into a practical system illustrated with engravings of
perfect geometric symmetry. Through his four books, Palladio applies the
module and proportions of Vitruvian temples (Books III and IV) to the design
of urban palaces and residential villas, universalizing the classical canon in
Western architecture.

Critical Notes
1.     The cochlea (Archimedes’ screw): the Latin cochlea designates the
water-screw and must be rendered accordingly, not by any popular nineteenth-
century term. It effects the transformation of continuous circular motion into
an upward linear flow of fluid — one of the great achievements of applied helical
geometry, showing that the Roman architect had mastered the principles of
hydraulics.

2.     Music as a regulator of warfare: Chapter XII of Book X. Vitruvius
details how military engineers had to tune the catapult strings by musical ear. If
one arm of the ballista was tighter than the other, the projectile would be
deflected. This demonstrates that the harmonic music of Book V (designed for
theaters) and the physics of warfare in Book X share the same mathematical
framework. Music is not an art of entertainment; it is the physical law that
balances both the voice in the sacred space and destructive energy on the
battlefield.
3.     Odometry as the Metric of the Empire: The invention of the
odometer (Chapter IX) is the materialization of the control of Roman space. By
inventing a machine that mechanically counts miles, architecture aligns itself
with Agrippa's cartography: the untamed territory of the barbarian provinces is
fragmented, measured, and dominated by the geometric regularity of the
odometer. Measured space is space conquered by Ratio.

De architectura, Marcus Vitruvius Pollio; c. 80 – 70 BCE – d. after
15 BCE), probably written around 15 BCE
The chronology agreed upon by modern philologists (such as Pierre Gros and
Louis Callebat) places the birth of Marcus Vitruvius Pollio around 80–70 BCE
and his death around 15 BCE. His magnum opus, De architectura, was written
progressively and dedicated to Octavian Augustus between 27 BCE and 23 BCE
(coinciding with the consolidation of the Principate and the great urban renewal
program of Rome), although some technical appendices could be revised until
15 BCE.
" The treatise De architectura, the only theoretical corpus of Greco-Roman
architecture preserved in its entirety, was composed by the engineer and military
architect Marcus Vitruvius Pollio (c. 80/70 BCE – 15 BCE). The internal
chronology of the text places its main phase of writing between 27 BCE and 23
BCE, a critical period in the history of the West marked by the transition from
the Roman Republic to the Principate of Octavian Augustus."
Vitruvius conceived his ten books not as a descriptive manual a posteriori, but
as a programmatic and legitimizing manifesto of the new political order. By
dedicating the work to the Imperator, the author aligned geometric science and
construction  techniques  with  the  official  program  of  the  Restitutio
Reipublicae. The  treatise  served  as  the  conceptual framework  for  the

                           192

PRELIMINARY STUDY

monumentalization of public space, providing Augustus with the architectural
tools necessary to fulfill his celebrated historiographical maxim: to have received
a Rome built of brick (latericia) and to bequeath to posterity a metropolis clad
in marble (marmorea). The dating of the work, fixed in its definitive edition
around 15 BCE, closes the era of Hellenistic influence on the Italian peninsula
and inaugurates the construction canon of the global Empire.

Critical Notes
1.     The significance of 27 BCE: In this year, Octavian received the
sacred title of Augustus from the Senate. This is the precise moment
when Vitruvius decided to present him with the treatise. This is not a
chronological coincidence: Vitruvius knew that a new Empire needed a
new architecture that reflected stability, order, and eternity (firmitas). It
should be emphasized that the ten books constitute the geometric
constitution of Augustus's Empire.
2.     The Pax Romana as a technical requirement: Vitruvius confesses
in the Proem of Book I that, while the Roman state was mired in civil wars
(against Julius Caesar, Mark Antony, and Pompey), he dedicated himself to
artillery and legionary ballistics. Only when Augustus pacified the world (Pax
Romana) could the architect withdraw the siege engines and devote himself to
theorizing about temples and forums. The order of sacred space was only
possible when the chaos of war ceased.
3.     The transition from the papyrus scroll (volumina) to the modern
book: around 15 BCE, Vitruvius presented Augustus with ten separate
papyrus scrolls (volumina). The concept of a single bound book is a late
antique and medieval development. This physical separation explains
why each book has its own independent preface (proemium): each scroll
was opened and read before the emperor as a separate discursive and
scientific unit.

Exegetical notes
1.     Claude Perrault's theoretical fracture: this point is crucial for
assessing the persistence of a sacred geometry or cosmic order. Perrault
opens a wound in the history of architecture: he argues that the golden
ratio and the homo bene figuratus are not divine truths. For Perrault,
the eyes become accustomed to seeing buildings in a certain way, and that
is why they seem beautiful to us, not because they reflect the order of
heaven (Book IX). Perrault thus marks the shift from architecture as
mysticism and cosmology to architecture as an engineering science and
cultural convention.

2.     The Royal Printing Press and the Political Control of Order:
The Ortiz y Sanz edition (1787) was not a  literary whim. The
enlightened Spanish state needed to standardize architecture to control
its territory (just as Augustus did in 15 BCE). By decreeing that all
churches, town halls, and hospitals in the Spanish Empire (including
Spanish America) had to follow the 56 plates of Ortiz y Sanz, the Crown
used Vitruvian principles to visually standardize the urban landscape
and bury the Churrigueresque style. Geometry once again became an
instrument of political sovereignty and the ordering of matter.
3.     The value of the 56 plates by Ortiz and Sanz: Unlike the
Renaissance  illustrations of Cesare Cesariano or  Palladio (who adapted
Vitruvius to their own architectural tastes), the plates by Ortiz and Sanz are
characterized by obsessive philological  rigor. The Spanish Enlightenment

PRELIMINARY STUDY

Praefatio editoris · Editorial principles

This section sets out, for the benefit of the scholarly reader, the nature of the
present edition, the text that underlies it, the scope of its critical apparatus, and
the orthographic and translational conventions adopted throughout.

Nature and base text
This is a bilingual reading edition with a selective critical apparatus. The
authorial Spanish translation by Diego Kurilo is the source of the English
translation. Its Latin base is Fritz Krohn’s edition (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912),
checked against Valentin Rose (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899); the Budé volumes
provide further critical and architectural reference by book. A printed or
electronic edition  is distinguished from a direct reading of an individual
manuscript. Where the text departs from the adopted edition, or where a reading
remains disputed, the difference must be identified in the apparatus.

Scope of the apparatus
The critical apparatus of this edition is selective and illustrative rather than
exhaustive. It does not record every variant of every witness lemma by lemma,
as the great systematic editions (Teubner, Budé) do; instead it concentrates on
the passages of decisive importance for the constitution, the dating or the
interpretation of the text, which are treated in the Apparatus criticus (Appendix
M) and in the analytical restitution of the Greek vocabulary (Appendix N). The
reader who requires a full positive apparatus is referred to the editions of Rose,
Krohn and the Collection Budé. This limitation is stated openly so that the
edition may be judged for what it is: a critical reading edition addressed to the
architect and the historian of architecture, uniting the philological apparatus
with the technical and architectural analysis.

Orthographic conventions
In the running Latin text the consonantal u/v is normalized in the modern
manner (utilitas, Vitruvius), the classical majuscule V being retained only in
display titles and rubrics that reproduce the epigraphic and manuscript usage
(DE ARCHITECTVRA). The diphthong ae is written in full; consonantal i is
not distinguished as j. Greek words are given in their restored polytonic form,

with the correct breathings and accents, accompanied where useful by a Latin
transliteration; the principles of restitution are set out in Appendix N.

Translation
The  English  translation  derives from Diego  Kurilo’s  original  Spanish
translation, itself made directly from Latin. Its governing aim is fidelity to that
authorial interpretation, with Latin used to check doubtful technical terms,
concepts and numbers. Granger and Rowland–Howe  are  comparative
references rather than replacement source translations. Technical terms without
exact modern equivalents—firmitas, utilitas, venustas, symmetria, ordinatio
and dispositio—are retained in Latin where necessary and defined in the Glossary
(Appendix A).

ARGUMENTUM LIBRI  I — AFTER THE dedicatory proem  to Augustus,
Vitruvius  defines  the  encyclopedic  training  of  the  architect and  the  six
fundamental  principles  of the  discipline (ordinatio,  dispositio, eurythmia,
symmetria, decor, distributio); he explains the parts of architecture, the choice of
healthy sites, the layout of walls and towers, the orientation of streets according to
the compass rose and the arrangement of public buildings.

Note. —  Book  I  establishes  the  architect’s  education and  professional
competence, sets out the six categories of I.2.1 (ordinatio, dispositio, eurythmia,
symmetria, decor and distributio), formulates the triad firmitas–utilitas–
venustas in I.3.2, and then develops questions of health, fortification, winds and
urban planning. Its importance for subsequent architectural theory is exceptional,
but its categories must be read within their ancient technical and linguistic
context.

The meaning of the Text (Academic Analysis)
In this first paragraph of the preface, Vitruvius uses an extremely elaborate Latin
period (a typical construction of rhetorical prose) to address Augustus with
great reverence.

The fundamental meaning is as follows:
Vitruvius justifies the delay in publishing his work De architectura. He explains
that, while Augustus was at the height of his power — having pacified the
Roman world after the civil wars — he did not dare to distract him with his
writings on architecture.
The author uses language laden with courtly flattery (typical of Augustan
literature):

   •   He describes Augustus's mind as divine and mentions his numen
        (divine force).
   •    His undefeated military virtus stands out.
•         It presents the emperor as absolute ruler of the world (imperio potiretur
orbis terrarum).
•     He describes how the Roman people and the Senate, freed from fear,
are guided by Augustus’s judgment.

With this rich rhetoric, Vitruvius achieves two objectives:
   1.   Demonstrate humility and respect before the princeps.
2.       Carefully choosing the moment to dedicate his work: precisely when
Augustus has achieved universal peace and can dedicate himself to cultural and
construction projects.
This introduction sets the tone for the entire treatise: a technical work presented
under imperial protection and seeking to contribute to Augustus's program of
architectural and cultural renewal.

Explanation of the Meaning of the Text (Academic Analysis)
In this second paragraph of the preface, Vitruvius explains the reasons that
prompted him to dedicate his work to Augustus.




                           210

The text develops two main ideas:
1.     Thematic justification: Augustus not only concerns himself with
military and  political  matters, but  also with urban  beautification and
architectural monumentality. Vitruvius thus links his treatise to Augustus's
political and propagandistic program, centered on the maiestas imperii through
public works.
2.      Personal justification: Vitruvius reveals his career path. He appears to
have served as a military engineer in the time of Julius Caesar (parenti tuo),
worked alongside three colleagues in the manufacture and repair of artillery
(ballistae,  scorpiones and tormenta), and received rewards that Augustus
maintained even after Caesar's death, thanks to the recommendation of Octavia
(Augustus' sister).

Comparative apparatus — I.1.1. “Architecti est scientia…” is the lemma under
discussion. Scientia is translated as “knowledge” or “disciplinary knowledge”
wherever “science” might suggest a modern institution. Fabrica and ratiocinatio
are not isolated theory and practice, but two dimensions whose conjunction
defines the competence of the architectus.

Architecti est scientia pluribus disciplinis et variis eruditionibus ornata, cuius
iudicio probantur omnia106quae ab ceteris artibus perficiuntur opera. Ea nascitur
ex fabrica et ratiocinatione. Fabrica est continuata ac trita usus meditatio, quae
manibus perficit[ur] e materia cuiuscumque generis opus [est] ad propositum
deformationis. Ratiocinatio autem est, quae res fabricatas sollertiae ac rationis
pro portione demonstrare atque explicare potest.
The architect’s knowledge embraces many disciplines and varied forms of
learning; by its judgment, all works accomplished by the other arts are assessed.
It arises from fabrica and ratiocinatio. Fabrica is the continuous, practised
exercise of making: through manual work and materials of whatever kind, it
brings a work into being according to its intended design. Ratiocinatio, by
contrast, enables one to demonstrate and explain constructed works according
to the proper proportion of skill and reason.

Explanation of the Meaning of the Text (Academic Analysis)
This is one of the most important and frequently cited paragraphs in all of
Vitruvius's work. In it, he establishes the dual nature of architecture:

•       Fabrica → The practical and manual dimension of the architect’s
work: construction informed by accumulated experience.
•       Ratiocinatio → Theoretical, intellectual aspect: the ability to explain,
justify and project works through reason, mathematics and proportion.
From the outset, Vitruvius argues that architecture is not merely a trade, but a
scientia (an  intellectual  discipline)  requiring encyclopedic  training. The
architect must possess profound knowledge in multiple fields (which will be
detailed later), as their judgment serves as the supreme criterion for validating
the works of other arts.

Key concepts:
   •    Architecture as a synthesis between praxis and theoria.
   •   The importance of the proportio (proportion) as a rational
        principle.
   •   The architect as an intellectual figure and not just as a builder.
This paragraph lays the theoretical foundations of the entire treatise and exerted
an enormous influence on Renaissance architectural theory (Alberti, Palladio,
etc.).

In this paragraph, Vitruvius develops and exemplifies the thesis presented in the
previous section. He establishes a clear typology of architects and defends an
intermediate position:

dexterity, but lack intellectual authority and social prestige.

•         It reinforces the Vitruvian ideal of the architect as a complete and

Explanation of the Meaning of the Text (Academic Analysis)
This paragraph is of great importance because Vitruvius delves into the semiotic
and  epistemological nature  of  architecture and  establishes  the  ideal
educational program for the architect.

Main ideas:
1.      Theoretical distinction: Vitruvius introduces the conceptual pair
quod significatur (the real object, the thing itself) and quod significat (the
theoretical  representation,  the  rational  demonstration). This  distinction
underscores that architecture is both a material reality and a body of knowledge
that must be able to be rationally explained and justified.
2.      Balance between talent and instruction: Neither innate genius
(ingenium) without systematic training, nor study without natural ability, is
sufficient. A combination of both is required.
3.      Encyclopedia of the Architect: Vitruvius presents the first known list
of knowledge that an architect must master. This encyclopedic training
includes:

              •    Humanities (litteratus, history, philosophy)
              •    Arts (graphics, music)
              •    Exact sciences (geometry, astrology, caeli rationes)
              •    knowledge (medicine, law)

" Here are the reasons why this is so. The architect must know how to read and
write, in order to strengthen his memory through written notes. Likewise, he
must have knowledge of drawing, so that he can more easily represent, through
exemplary drawings, the appearance of the work he wishes to design."
Geometry, for its part, provides architecture with numerous aids: firstly, it
teaches the use of the ruler and compass, thanks to which the plans of buildings,
as well as the directions of set squares, levels, and lines, can be drawn much more

Explanation of the Meaning of the Text
In this paragraph, Vitruvius begins to justify in detail why the architect must
master each of the disciplines mentioned.

Main points:
1.      Letters (Litterae): They are used to take notes and consolidate
memory (commentarii).
2.     Drawing (Graphidos  scientia): An  essential  tool  for  visually
materializing the ideas of the project.
3.     Geometry: A fundamental discipline that provides practical tools
(ruler, compass,  set  square,  level)  for drawing  plans and  carrying out
construction work.
4.      Optics: Allows for the correct management of natural lighting
in buildings according to their orientation.
5.      Arithmetic: Necessary for  calculating  costs, measurements and,
especially, for solving problems of symmetria (harmonic proportion), one of
the most important concepts of Vitruvian theory.

Explanation of the Meaning of the Text
This paragraph is one of Vitruvius' most famous and constitutes the legendary
origin of the caryatids.

Key points:
1.     The Usefulness of History: The architect must not only know how
to build, but also provide cultural and historical justification for the ornamental
elements he employs. For Vitruvius, architecture is an eloquent art that “speaks”
through its forms.
2.     The caryatid narrative: Vitruvius gives an aetiological explanation
for the architectural figure. He names Caryae in the Peloponnese, which must
be distinguished from Caria in Asia Minor. His account presents the load-
bearing women as an enduring image of the punishment and humiliation
imposed on their city. The historical status of that account remains distinct
from its symbolic function in the treatise.
3.     Symbolic value: This passage illustrates how Roman (and Greek)
architecture used figurative elements with a strong moral and commemorative
content.

Key points:
1.      Historical context: Vitruvius refers to the Greek victory at the
Battle of Plataea (479 BCE), which ended the Persian Wars. The

must know their origin in order to explain them and justify their use.

cultured man, capable of endowing his works with intellectual and symbolic

Academic translation
“Philosophy, for its part, perfects the architect in spirit, so that he is not
arrogant, but rather gentle, fair, and loyal, and — most importantly — free from
avarice. For no work can truly be accomplished without loyalty and integrity.
Let him not be covetous or preoccupied with receiving gifts, but let him uphold
his dignity with gravity, maintaining a good reputation. And this is precisely
what philosophy prescribes.”
Furthermore, philosophy explains the nature of things, what in Greek is called
physiologia, a body of knowledge that must be mastered with special dedication,
since it encompasses many and varied natural matters, as is also the case with
water management. Indeed, the impulses, circulations, and pressures of natural
air occur in very different ways depending on the differences in elevation and
forced conduits; and no one will be able to solve their problems without
knowing, thanks to philosophy, the principles of nature. Likewise, whoever
reads the precepts written by Ctesibius, Archimedes, and other authors of the
same kind will not be able to fully understand them unless they have been
instructed in these matters by philosophers.

Explanation of the Meaning of the Text
In this paragraph, Vitruvius explains the fundamental role of philosophy in the
training of the architect, dividing it into two main aspects:
1.     Moral  (ethical)  formation:  Philosophy  shapes  the  architect's
character, instilling essential virtues such as humility, fairness, fidelity, and above
all, the absence of greed. Vitruvius emphasizes that moral integrity (fides et
castitas) is indispensable for practising the profession with dignity.
2.       Scientific  training  (physics  /  physiology):  Architects  need
knowledge of natural philosophy to understand complex physical phenomena,
especially in hydraulics (aqueducts, water and air pressure). Without these
principles, they would be unable to solve real-world technical problems.
Vitruvius further links theory with practice by mentioning great Hellenistic
engineers (Ctesibius and Archimedes), whose treatises can only be properly
understood with a philosophical basis.
This passage reinforces the Vitruvian ideal of the architect as a complete
professional: not just a technician, but a cultured, ethical and scientifically
trained man.

Explanation of the Meaning of the Text (Academic Analysis)
In this paragraph, Vitruvius justifies the need for the architect to master music
(understood as harmonic and acoustic theory) for an eminently practical reason:
the calibration of torsion war machines.

Key points:
1.     Connection between music and mechanics: Vitruvius establishes a
direct relationship between musical theory (harmonic proportions, tones,
intervals) and military engineering. The correct tension of the machine's strings
is achieved by ear, applying acoustic principles (sonitus certos et aequales).
2.     Key technical concept: Homoton (equal pitch/equal tension). If the
two halves of the torsion engine are not perfectly balanced, the weapon will lose
accuracy and the projectile will deviate from its trajectory.
3.      vision  of  architecture:  This  example  perfectly  illustrates  the
Vitruvian thesis: the architect is not only a builder, but a technician -scientist
who must apply knowledge from different disciplines (in this case, music) to
concrete problems of design and execution.
This passage  is especially interesting because  it shows how, in Antiquity,
disciplines that we now consider separate (music and military art) were closely
linked through mathematics and the theory of proportions.

Explanatory note — Bk. 5.4–5.5 (the echea and theater acoustics).
Vitruvius founds theater acoustics on the Harmonics of Aristoxenus of
Tarentum: in 5.4 he sets out the three genera —enharmonic, chromatic,
and diatonic— and the division of the voice into tones, semitones, and
tetrachords; in 5.5 he applies that theory to architecture through the
echea (ἠχεῖα), bronze vessels —or clay ones, in modest theaters— tuned
to the notes of the scale and set in niches under the seating to reinforce
the actors' voices by resonance. The exact scheme of their positions
(5.5.6) is lost in transmission. Vitruvius notes that wooden theaters need
none, since the boarding itself resonates; masonry, stone, or marble
theaters do. He admits he has seen none in Rome, citing as witness Lucius
Mummius, who after destroying Corinth (146 BCE) brought the bronze
echea of its theater to Rome and dedicated them at the temple of Luna.
Archaeology has found almost no trace of them in ancient theaters; they
reappear, however, in some two hundred medieval churches.
Comparative note — Bk. 5.4–5.5 (echea). In the Budé, Book V is the work
of Catherine Saliou (2009), whose commentary on the theater and its acoustics
is standard. In the Cambridge commentary, Thomas N. Howe observes that
Vitruvius here singles out an uncommon Greek technical feature, for which
only between eight and sixteen possible sites are known. Granger (Loeb)
preserves the Greek musical terminology (nete, paramese, mese, hypate); Corso–
Romano and Tavernor–Schofield accompany the passage with diagrams of the
scale. In 5.5 the manuscript tradition presents a crux (diatessaron for diapente
in the series of intervals), discussed since Rose; this edition follows Rose's text
and translates in its own voice.
Nor could anyone build hydraulic machines or other instruments similar to
these organs without knowing the principles of music.

Explanation of the Meaning of the Text
In  this paragraph, Vitruvius continues to  justify the need  for musical
knowledge for the architect, now moving from the military field to the acoustic
- architectural field.

Key points:
1.     Theater acoustics: Vitruvius describes one of the most sophisticated
acoustic systems of Antiquity: the echeia, or bronze resonating vessels. These

were strategically placed under the seating tiers of theaters to amplify and
enhance the sound quality of the actors.
2.     Mathematical -musical foundation: The tuning of these vessels was
carried out according to the Greek harmonic intervals (diatessaron = fourth,
diapente = fifth, diapason = octave), demonstrating the practical application of
Pythagorean musical theory in architecture.
3.     Comprehensive vision: Music is not a cultural embellishment, but an
indispensable technical tool. Without it, an architect could not properly design
theaters or build complex instruments like the hydraulic organ.
This passage is one of the most important sources we have on acoustics in
ancient theaters and demonstrates the high degree of technical and scientific
sophistication that Vitruvius demanded of the architect.
