Explanation of the Meaning of the Text
In this paragraph, Vitruvius concludes the enumeration of the disciplines that
the architect must master, highlighting three areas of great practical importance:
1.     Environmental Medicine / Hygiene: The architect must know how
to choose healthy sites according to the climate (klimata), air quality, soil and
water, anticipating health problems (a very Roman theme).
2.     Law: Basic legal knowledge to avoid litigation related to construction
(common walls, easements for light, water, rainwater runoff, sewers, etc.).
Vitruvius emphasizes the architect's responsibility in preventing legal conflicts.
3.      Astrology / Astronomy: Necessary for the correct orientation of
buildings and, especially, for the design of sundials (horology).
This chapter (I.1) presents the Vitruvian ideal of the architect as an encyclopedic
professional, capable of  integrating  technical,  scientific, humanistic, and
juridical knowledge. None of these disciplines is accessory: they all respond to
the concrete needs of his office.

Critical and Hermeneutic Translation
“12. Those unfamiliar with the subject (inperitis) may find it surprising that
human nature can master and retain so many disciplines. Once they recognize
the close connection and mutual exchange among all branches of knowledge,
however, they will readily believe it possible. Encyclopedic education (encyclios
disciplina) forms a single body composed of these members. Those trained in
different fields from an early age therefore recognize the same features and the
connections shared by all the disciplines, and so understand everything more
readily. For this reason Pytheos, the distinguished architect of Minerva’s temple
at Priene, states in his commentaries that an architect should be able to
accomplish more in every art and discipline than specialists who, through
sustained practice, have brought a single field to the highest distinction.”

However, the latter is not feasible in reality.
Exegetical Notes
1.     The Encyclios Disciplina as a mystical body: Vitruvius uses a metaphor
of Stoic and Platonic origin: education is a living organism (uti corpus unum),
where geometry, music, and astronomy are not isolated sciences, but rather the
"members" (membris) of a single being. This is fundamental: the architect does
not accumulate knowledge in a fragmented way; the architect understands the
common mathematical root that unites sound (music) with space (geometry)
and time (astronomy).
2.     The rectification of Pytheus (The tension between Idea and Matter):
Pytheus (the great Hellenistic architect of the Temple of Priene and the
Mausoleum at Halicarnassus) was a radical in his theory; he asserted that the
architect should know more about painting than a painter and more about
sculpture than a sculptor. Vitruvius, with the Roman pragmatism that
characterizes his framework, reins him in by closing the paragraph: Id autem re
non expeditur. Vitruvius knows that human beings have physical limitations.



112Encyclios disciplina concerns an interconnected general education. The expression  is

plastic arts (rationis plasticae non ignarus); nor should he be a physician like
Hippocrates, but that does not mean he should be ignorant of the principles of

medicine (aniatrologetos); finally, he is not required to excel in the other sciences,
but he must have a knowledge of them that is not inexperienced (non inperitus).”
In the midst of such a vast variety of subjects, no one can achieve singular
mastery or refinement (elegantias singulares), since knowing and thoroughly
assimilating its theoretical principles (ratiocinationes) is something that barely
falls within the capabilities of the human intellect.

Exegetical notes
1.     The constellation of Hellenistic archetypes: Vitruvius here maps
out the greatest sages of the classical world to define the boundaries of
architecture. He cites Aristarchus (the great grammarian of Alexandria who
standardized Homer's text), Aristoxenus (the great theorist of music and the
harmonic scale), Apelles (Alexander the Great's favorite painter), Myron and
Polyclitus (the fathers of the canon of Greek sculpture), and Hippocrates (the
father of medicine). By contrasting the architect with these giants,
Vitruvius demonstrates that architecture  is an integrative discipline: the
architect does not displace the specialist, but rather acts as the conductor who
coordinates all these areas of knowledge within the realm of the building.

2.     The structure of double negations (non agrammatos, non
amusos): This philological subtlety is relevant. Vitruvius does not use Vulgar
Latin; he  resorts to negated Hellenisms to  indicate a  state of  critical
competence. The architect does not have to compose a symphony  like
Aristoxenus, but he cannot be amusos (deaf to harmony), because if he were, he
would not know how to place the acoustic vessels in the theater (Book V). He
does not have to sculpt the Doryphoros like Polyclitus, but he must understand
ratio plastica so that the statues of the caryatids maintain the modular
proportion with the entablature. It  is an apologia for the knowledge of
synthesis.
3.     The Limit of Human Power: The paragraph's conclusion is a lesson
in epistemological humility in the face of Pytheus’s abstract intellectualism.
Vitruvius acknowledges that the absolute mastery of the singular refinements
(elegantias singulares) of each science eludes the power (potestas) of human
understanding. Architecture, therefore, is defined as the science of the possible
and the harmonious: it prioritizes the balance of the whole over the hyper-

specialized obsession with the fragment. This aligns with the thesis on Sophia:
the true sage is the one who unifies, not the one who atomizes.
This fragment (I, 1, 14) masterfully concludes Vitruvius's syllogism on the
nature of architectural knowledge. Vitruvius introduces an a fortiori argument
(from lesser to greater): if specialists themselves — who dedicate their entire lives
to a single discipline — rarely achieve universal acclaim, then demanding that
the architect surpass them all in their respective fields is a logical contradiction.
The architect's role is not competition, but technical coordination and self-
sufficiency (ne quid indigeat).
The  transmitted  text  exhibits  deficiencies  in  textual  cohesion  and
decontextualized turns of phrase such as " in private the properties of the arts, "
which is an erroneous translation of privatim proprietates tenent artium (which
refers to " those who possess the exclusive mastery of a particular art "). Similarly,
aevo perpetuo does not allude to " the nobility of the time," but to an "
imperishable celebrity / immortal fame. "

Critical and Hermeneutic Translation
“14. And yet, not only are architects unable to achieve supreme perfection
(summum effectum) in all matters, but even those who possess exclusive mastery
of a particular art (privatim proprietates tenent artium) do not, in their entirety,
attain the highest principality of glory. Therefore, if in individual sciences
particular artists — and of them not all, but only a few throughout the ages
(aevo perpetuo) —have barely achieved renown, how  is  it possible that an
architect, who must be skilled in multiple arts, accomplishes the prodigious and
admirable feat not only of lacking none of the necessary knowledge in them (ne
quid ex is indigeat), but of surpassing even all those artisans and specialists who
have devoted absolute assiduity and the utmost industry to a single doctrine? ”

Exegetical notes
1.      Deconstructing the Myth of the Absolute Sage: This passage is a
compelling argument for disassociating Vitruvius from the hyperbolic readings
of the Renaissance. While the humanists of the Quattrocento sought to find in
this chapter the justification for the absolute "universal man" (the unattainable
polymath), Vitruvius's actual text is a lesson in Roman pragmatism and legal
moderation. Vitruvius argues that the  architect's goal  is elemental  self-
sufficiency: "ne quid ex is indigeat " (that nothing should be foreign or lacking to
him). The architect should not be a rival to the painter or the musician, but a
valid interlocutor who understands the codes of each craft.
2.      Specialized diligence versus spatial synthesis: Vitruvius contrasts
adsiduitas (the specialist's obsessive and constant dedication to a single thing)
with the architect's panoramic vision. The genius of architectural design lies not
in fragmentary execution, but in symphonic coordination. The specialist works
on the detail; the architect works on the relationship between the details. This
distinction  is fundamental to your theoretical framework, as  it positions
architecture as a second-order science or meta-discipline, whose object of study
is not isolated matter, but the order that unifies the parts.
3.     The Status of Nobility in the Arts: The use of the terms nobilitatem
and laudis principatum reflects the Augustan mindset regarding the social status
of the intellectual and the artisan. Vitruvius  is attempting to elevate the
profession of architecture above purely manual (fabrica) or servile labor. By
demonstrating that the architect operates with the theory of all the arts, he

grants him a rank of intellectual nobility comparable to that of philosophers or
high-ranking officials of the Empire, thus justifying why the treatise is dedicated
directly to the Imperator.
This passage (I, 1, 15) is the epistemological keystone of the entire Book I. Here
Vitruvius definitively dismantles the error of Pytheus by introducing a binary
Platonic-Aristotelian  distinction:  the  opus  the  material,  empirical and
specialized execution and the ratiocinatio the theoretical, scientific and universal
principle).

“15. Consequently, at this point Pythius’s error is evident, for he failed to
recognize that all the arts are composed of two factors: the material execution
(opus) and the theory that underpins it (ratiocinatio). Of these two elements, the
first — that is, the completion of the physical work (operis effectus) —is the
exclusive domain of those who have practised a particular discipline; the second
— the theory or rational principle (ratiocinatio) —is common to all men of

share theoretical knowledge about the rhythm of blood pulses and its analogy
with the movement of metric feet; however, if it is necessary to heal a wound or
save a sick person from imminent danger, the musician will not come to the
rescue, but such a task will be the proper and exclusive work of the physician. ”

Exegetical notes
1.     The Anatomy  of  Knowledge:  Opus  versus  Ratiocinatio:
Vitruvius here establishes a division that elevates architecture to the rank of a
liberal science. Opus is blind; it is the mechanical repetition of the craftsman
who knows how to move his hands but does not know why the structure works.
Ratiocinatio is the logos, the mathematical matrix that governs the phenomenon
physically and formally. The architect's value lies in the fact that, although he
shares ratiocinatio with other scholars (commune cum omnibus doctis), he has
the unique ability to project it onto the constructive opus.
2.     The analogy of the pulse and the cosmic metronome (de venarum
rhythmo et ad pedem motu) is an exceptional archaeological testimony of the
Hellenistic medicine of Herophilus of Alexandria, who measured the body's
pulse using water clocks and the metrical feet of Greek poetry and music.
Vitruvius  illustrates  the  thesis  on  Sophia:  the  physical  universe   is
interconnected. Blood flows through the veins with the same numerical and
harmonic law with which a musician composes a measure and with which an
architect calculates the distances of the intercolumniations (modulatio) of a
temple (Book III).
3.     The delimitation of the professional field: At the end of the
fragment, Vitruvius prioritizes common sense over theoretical utopia. The
architect must possess the ratiocinatio of acoustics to design the theater (Book
V), but when it comes to playing the instrument (organ), he takes a step back
and  yields  the  position  to  the  practical  musician. This  distinction  is
methodologically important: architecture does not devour the other arts; it
conceptually assimilates them to create the spatial container where these arts can
coexist harmoniously. The physician heals bodies and the musician delights

This passage (I, 1, 16) definitively closes the great epistemological introduction

of synthetic knowledge by linking astronomy, music and geometry through
the laws of cosmic consonance and optics, and then decrees the real goal of the
professional: to achieve a moderate but sufficient knowledge (mediocriter)
that allows him to judge with technical authority without needing to be a
manual craftsman.

but the practical execution (opus) belongs to the specialists in each field.

Critical and Hermeneutic Translation
“16. Similarly, there exists a common sphere of debate (disputatio communis)
between astrologers and musicians regarding the cosmic sympathy of the stars
and musical consonances, structured according to the relationships of squares
and trigons, and the intervals of fourth (diatessaron) and fifth (diapente);
likewise, the architect shares with geometers the science of vision, which in
Greek is called λόγος ὀπτικός (logos optikos or perspective). In short, in all
branches of knowledge, many subjects — if not all — are common to scholars
exclusively on the level of theoretical argumentation (ad disputandum).” On
the contrary, the practical execution of works (operum vero ingressus), which are
brought to perfection and elegance by the hands and the skilled manipulation,
belongs exclusively to those who have been properly trained and instructed in a
single manual craft. Consequently, it is to be considered that an architect who
possesses a moderate knowledge (mediocriter) of the principles and parts of
each science—those strictly necessary for architecture—is more than adequately
fulfilling (satis abunde) his duty, so that if it were necessary to issue a technical
judgment or approve a project governed by these arts, his authority would not
be deficient (ne deficiat).

Exegetical notes
1.      Astrology and Cosmic Aspects: This passage constitutes one of the
most fascinating pieces of documentary evidence of Roman architectural
Pythagoreanism.  Vitruvius  equates  the  musical  intervals  of  a  fourth
(diatessaron, ratio 4:3) and a fifth (diapente, ratio 3:2) with the geometric
configurations traced by the stars in the firmament when they form squares
(square aspect, 90 °) and trines (trine aspect, 120 °). This fact confirms that
Vitruvian architectural space is a resonant microcosm: temples and theaters
are designed imitating the same metric proportions with which God tensions
the strings of the heavens and the planets.

2.     Logos  optikos  and  architectural  perception.  The  Greek
expression λόγος ὀπτικός provides an important conceptual context for
the optical adjustments discussed in Books III and IV. Greek geometric
perspective taught that the human eye distorts the material line (making it

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I

appear concave or convex). The architect, sharing this ratiocinatio with the
geometers, does not design for the abstract plane of the paper, but for the retina
of the viewer. Architecture intentionally alters the actual geometry (thickening
the corner columns or curving the stylobate) so that the logos optikos of the eye
perceives the building with perfect symmetry and visual stability.
3.     The Canon of the Mean (Mediocriter notes): Vitruvius coined the
definitive concept of the architect's professional training. The word mediocriter
does not have the modern derogatory sense of "mediocre," but rather the
classical sense of Aristotelian mediocritas: the golden mean, moderation, and
temperance. The excellent architect does not fall into the error of excessive
artisanal specialization (manu tractionibus); their domain is that of critical
intellect. They must possess instrumental knowledge sharp enough to be an
infallible judge of the work (iudicare et probare) and ensure that no contractor
or specialist deceives the state administration. Architecture is, ultimately, the
triumph of theoretical oversight over the brute force of the worker.

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I

Exegetical Notes
1.     The ontological distinction: Architect versus Mathematician:
Vitruvius defines the boundaries of the profession in relation to pure science.
The architect needs theory to order physical matter, but his ultimate goal is the
building, the structure. The mathematician, on the other hand, operates on a
purely intellectual plane; he transcends the need to build because his mind
masters the abstract laws that govern the universe. By placing mathematicians
above the architect, Vitruvius demonstrates brilliant epistemological honesty:
architecture is not the queen of the sciences because it is the most abstract, but
because it synthesizes abstract thought for the benefit of civilization.
2.     The  pantheon  of  Hellenistic  polymaths: The names  cited
constitute the canon of the Hellenistic scientific revolution analyzed here:

◦       Aristarchus of Samos: The first to propose the heliocentric model
of the universe.
◦       Philolaus and Archytas of Tarentum: Pythagorean philosophers;
Archytas was the father of mathematical mechanics and a friend of Plato.
◦      Apollonius of Perga: The geometer who revolutionized the study of
conic sections (ellipse, parabola and hyperbola).
◦       Eratosthenes of Cyrene: The sage who calculated the circumference
of the Earth with astonishing accuracy by measuring the shadows at the solstice.
◦      Archimedes of Syracuse: The greatest mechanical and hydrostatic
genius of antiquity, inventor of the burning mirrors and the claws that defended
Syracuse.
◦      Scopinas of Syracuse: Famous inventor of complex sundials and
linear gnomonic mechanisms.
3.     The Duality of the Organic and the Gnonomic: Vitruvius closes
the chapter by connecting this ending with the books that complete his treatise:
the machines of Book X  (res  organicas) and the  clocks of Book IX
(gnomonicas). By pointing out that these inventions were explained by numero
naturalibusque rationibus, Vitruvius offers us the interpretive key to his treatise:
the machine and the clock are not products of chance or blind craftsmanship;
they are the material crystallization of the mathematical laws of nature. The
mathematician discovers them in the heavens, and the architect applies them on
Earth.

Aware that his prose does not possess the refinement of a philosopher or a
rhetorician, the author asserts his status as an enlightened architect (architectus

grammatical liberties, promising in return an unshakeable theoretical and

Critical and Hermeneutic Translation
“18. Therefore, since the possession of such intellectual gifts and natural
ingenuity is not granted indiscriminately to all nations but to a small number of
exceptional men, and since the architect's craft must be practised within the full
range of liberal arts, the very nature of the discipline — due to its colossal
scope (propter amplitudinem rei) —allows for the possession not necessarily of
the highest degree in these sciences, but rather a moderate knowledge (mediocres
scientias) of them. For this reason, I beg you, Caesar, both you and all those who

been explained in a manner that does not conform to the rules of grammatical
composition.” I have endeavored to write these pages not in the style of an
eminent philosopher, nor of an eloquent rhetorician, nor of a grammarian
trained in the subtlest rules of his art, but rigorously like an architect steeped in
literature. Nevertheless, with regard to the intrinsic power of the profession
(artis  potestate) and the rational principles that are integrated within  it
(ratiocinationes), I firmly commit myself — or so I hope — to offering in these
volumes an unquestionable authority (maxima auctoritate), useful not only to
builders (aedificantibus), but also to all scholars.

Exegetical notes
1.     The material form of reading. Roman volumina were commonly
papyrus rolls rather than bound codices. This historical context helps explain
the material act of reading, but the adopted wording is volumina sunt lecturi,
“those who  will read these volumes”.  It neither  prescribes a  particular
movement of the hands nor supports an emendation to levaturi.
2.     The legitimization of technical prose: Vitruvius here constructs a
manifesto in favor of specialized technical language. By contrasting his style
with that of the summus philosophus or the rhetor disertus, the author argues that
architecture possesses its own syntax. The beauty of his text does not lie in the
ornamentation of words (political or literary rhetoric), but in the precision with
which the words reflect the ratiocinatio of the building. It is a defense of
scientific literature: the architect writes as he builds, with solidity (firmitas) and
structural clarity, renouncing the artifices of sophistical eloquence.

3.     The universal scope of the treatise (Omnibus sapientibus): The
closing paragraph is the argument that unifies the thesis on Sophia. Vitruvius
proudly proclaims that his work is not a mere catalog of constructions for
masons or laborers (non modo aedificantibus). By including the sapientibus (the
wise, the philosophers, the intellectual elite of the Empire), the treatise claims its
place in the high culture of the Pax Romana. Vitruvius demonstrates that
architecture  is a knowledge of the State, a branch of applied philosophy
indispensable for the ordering of the civilized world. The emperor governs men,
the philosopher governs souls, and the architect builds the material space where
both exercise their power.

Chapter 2

Chapter 2 of Book I sets out the six principles of architectural composition. The
enumeration at I.2.1 provides the conceptual framework for the definitions that
follow.

Latin text
«[1.2.1] Architectura autem constat ex ordinatione, quae graece τάξις dicitur, et
ex  dispositione, hanc autem  Graeci  διάθεσιν  vocitant,  et  eurythmia  et
symmetria et decore et distributione, quae graece οἰκονομία dicitur.»
« [1.2.1] Architecture rests upon Order (ordinatio), which the Greeks call τάξις;
Arrangement  (dispositio), which they term  διάθεσιν; and  further upon
Eurythmy, Symmetry, Propriety (decor), and Economy (distributio), which in
Greek is called οἰκονομία. »

Critical and Hermeneutic Translation
Translation note — I.2.1. Vitruvius explicitly gives Greek equivalents for
ordinatio (τάξις), dispositio (διάθεσις) and distributio (οἰκονομία). Eurythmia
and symmetria are themselves Greek loans incorporated into technical Latin;
the passage provides no Greek equivalent for decor here. All six Latin terms are
therefore retained and explained in context, without presenting τὸ πρέπον as
though it formed part of the text of I.2.1.
Comparative apparatus — I.2.1. Fleury’s Budé edition confirms that I.2 forms
the core of the general definitions in Book I. Ordinatio/τάξις, dispositio/διάθεσις
and  distributio/οἰκονομία  are  retained  as  technical  pairs; eurythmia and
symmetria remain technical terms of Greek origin. Decor is not automatically
replaced by “decoration”: it expresses the suitability or propriety of the work’s
appearance according to rule, custom and nature.
Architectural and philological note — Dispositio. Ichnographia, orthographia
and scaenographia are species dispositionis: graphic ways of conceiving and
representing a project. Dispositio should not be reduced to the functional
allocation of rooms, since the passage explicitly includes plan, elevation and
perspective or scenographic representation.
Comparative critical apparatus — I.2.1–2. The enumeration ordinatio/τάξις,
dispositio/διάθεσις, eurythmia, symmetria, decor and distributio/οἰκονομία is
stable in  its general structure, but  I.2.2 presents  real differences in the

constitution of the text. The modern critical edition consulted marks [modica]
and [commoditas] as doubtful, whereas other editions print them without
reservation. The reconstruction of the definition of quantitas also varies: some
critical  texts  introduce <membris>.  These  differences  are  not  silently
harmonized: the base text of the author’s manuscript  is retained and the
alternative recorded in the apparatus.
Textual note — I.2.2. Krohn marks [modica] and [commoditas] as doubtful in
the definition of ordinatio. This edition keeps them visibly marked wherever
they occur in the adopted critical text and avoids building on them a doctrine
dependent on their authenticity. Transmitted wording, editorial deletion, and
supplementation are distinct philological categories and must be identified
separately.
Terminological note. Ordinatio cannot be equated without qualification with
modern “order”, nor dispositio with ordinary “arrangement”. In this context,
ordinatio concerns modulation and the correspondence of parts; dispositio
concerns their concrete ordering and the modes of representing the project. The
Greek terms  τάξις,  διάθεσις, ποσότης and  ἰδέαι are retained because they
contribute to Vitruvius’s conceptual precision.

Exegesis Notes
1.    The Ontology of Design: The Verb Constat: Vitruvius does not
use the verbs habere (to have) or comprehendere (to understand). The use of
constat ex implies that architecture emerges and subsists only when these six
principles  coexist  simultaneously.  If even one of them  is  missing, the
constructed object ceases to be architecture (architecture) and degrades to a mere
utilitarian building (fabrica). This nuance is important: the six principles are
not optional tools, but rather the formal and efficient causes of sacred and civil
space.

2.     Vitruvius’s Greco-Roman biculturalism: It is highly significant
that Vitruvius immediately translated his concepts into Greek (τάξις, διάθεσις,
οἰκονομία). This demonstrates that the Latin of the 1st century BC still lacked an
abstract vocabulary mature enough for the theory of art. By anchoring his
treatise in Hellenistic terminology, Vitruvius sought to endow the new
architecture of the Roman Empire with the same philosophical and scientific


                           256

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I

dignity that the arts possessed in classical Greece. The Roman architect is not a
mere builder; he is the heir to Hellenic paideia.

3.     Preliminary conceptual map of the Six Axioms: For clarity of
exposition, it is convenient to set out in synthetic form the order and hierarchy
of these six concepts, which Vitruvius defines in the following paragraphs of the
chapter:

◦     The Ordination (Ordinatio / τάξις): The establishment of the
mathematical module and the general scale.

◦     The Arrangement (Dispositio / διάθεσις): The geometric and spatial
representation on the plane through the plan, the elevation and the perspective.

◦      Eurythmy: The visual and harmonious beauty that the eye
perceives in the proportions of the finished work.

◦     Symmetry  (Symmetria):  The  regular  metric  correspondence
between the parts and the whole based on a common unit of measurement (the
module).

◦     The Decorum (Decor): The ethical, social and liturgical suitability of
the building according to its function and the divinity to which it is consecrated.

◦      Distribution (Distributio / οἰκονομία): Economic management,
administration of materials and adaptation of the work to the status of the
owner.
This fragment (I, 2, 2) is of colossal theoretical density, as it defines the first two
axioms  of  architecture:  Ordination  (Ordinatio)  and  Arrangement
(Dispositio). Furthermore, it introduces the celebrated triad of architectural
representational forms (plan, elevation, and perspective), which constitutes the
basis of Western technical drawing.

These categories arise from meditation (cogitation) and invention (invention).
Meditation is attentive reflection, full of assiduity, industry, and vigilance,
which pursues the effect of the devised purpose with intellectual delight.
Invention, on the other hand, is the resolution of obscure problems and the
discovery of a new constructive principle through agile and vigorous ingenuity.

Exegetical Notes
1.      Quantitas as the Birth of the Module: Vitruvius defines quantitas
(ποσότης) not as an absolute metric dimension (meters or fixed feet), but as a
relative and modular dimension (modulorum sumptio). The architect takes
a part of the building — for example, the diameter of the column — and that
part becomes the module M. All the rest of the temple (height, width of the
forum, intercolumniations) will be a multiple or submultiple of that module.
Ordering is the abstract order that reduces the complexity of matter to a single
generating number.

2.     The restoration of the three Ideas of drawing: Vitruvius uses the
Platonic word ἰδέαι to refer to the plan, the elevation, and the perspective. This
means  that  for  the Roman,  technical  plans  are not mere commercial
illustrations; they are the mental forms or abstract archetypes that the
architect projects onto paper before the building exists in material reality.
◦      The ichnographia (ground plan) is defined by the footprint on the
ground (in solis arearum).
◦      The orthographia (elevation) is the rigorous orthogonal projection
(erecta frontis imago).
◦       Scaenographia is a representation of the front and receding sides, with
the lines answering to a center. Its precise geometric interpretation belongs to
the history of the passage’s reception; the wording alone does not establish
the complete system of Renaissance linear perspective.

3.     The Psychology of Design: Cogitatio and Inventio: The closing
of the paragraph connects technical drawing with the architect's mind.
Vitruvius details that plans do not arise from nothing; they spring from cogitatio
(the analytical, obsessive, and vigilant analysis of the site) and inventio (the
creative spark, the vigore mobili, that elegantly resolves the technical problem).
He emphasizes that meditation should result in an effect cum voluptate (with
pleasure/delight). Architectural design  is a  joyful  intellectual  act: reason
dominating the chaos of spatial limitations.
This fragment (I, 2, 3) defines the third axiom of Vitruvius' treatise: Eurythmy.
This principle shifts the theory of design from the purely numerical or abstract
plane  to  the  realm  of  visual  perception and  subjective  aesthetics,
establishing that architectural beauty  is consummated in the gaze of the
spectator (aspectus).
To render the Latin as “all things correspond to their own magnitude” is a gross
error. In Vitruvius, symmetria does not denote magnitude (absolute size) but
rather modular proportionality—the internal metric correspondence between
the parts.

Exegetical Notes
1.     The Aesthetics of the Retina: The Weight of Aspectus: Unlike
Ordinatio (which is a cold, mathematical calculation on papyrus), Eurythmy is
defined exclusively through visual experience (aspectus and species). Vitruvius
introduces here the psychological component of perception: the building must
not only be geometrically exact, but it must also appear so to the human eye.
Eurythmy is responsible for transforming the rigidity of number into visual
grace  (venusta),  guaranteeing  the  aesthetic  delight  of  the  citizen who
contemplates the work from street level.
2.     modulation (X:Y:Z): Vitruvius defines eurhythmy as a system of

establishes a clear design principle: height must be related to width (H→W),
width to length (W→L), and this dimensional trinity must ultimately be subject
to the general rule of modular symmetry (suae symmetriae). This passage is vital
to your conceptual framework, as  it demonstrates that Roman classicism
conceived of space in a volumetric and unitary way, preventing a façade from
being designed independently of the depth of the building's body.

3.     The preamble to Optical Corrections: Vitruvius will detail these in

perspective, the architect is obliged to apply the laws of eurhythmy to correct
these illusions. Sometimes, for a temple to appear perfectly symmetrical, it is
necessary to alter the actual measurements of its elements. Eurythmy, therefore,
represents the triumph of optical design over the rigidity of pure geometric
rules.
This fragment (I, 2, 4) defines the fourth axiom of classical design: Symmetry
(Symmetria).  This  concept,  along  with  the module,  is  the  absolute
mathematical core of Roman architecture during the Augustan period.

Critical and Hermeneutic Translation
« 4. Likewise, symmetry (symmetria) consists in the convenient consonance
(conveniens consensus) of the members of a work considered in themselves, and

Just as the human body possesses the eurhythmic quality of symmetry, derived
from the forearm, the foot, the palm, the finger, and other smaller parts, the
same is true for the perfect execution of buildings. This is evident, first and
foremost, in sacred temples, calculated either from the diameter or thickness of
the columns (columnarum crassitudinibus), or from the triglyph (triglypho), or
from the module (embater); similarly, it is found in military ballistics, derived
from the diameter of the torsion opening in the capital (e foramine capituli),
which the Greeks call περίτρητον (perítreton); and in ships, from the space
between the oars, or interscalmus, called διάπηγμα (diapegma). Similarly, the
analytical principle of symmetries (symmetriarum ratiocinatio) is discovered in
any other type of work by examining its own members.
Comparative  critical  apparatus —  I.2.4. Embatere  is adopted and  the
supplement <capituli> is made visible in ballista e foramine <capituli>, as in
Krohn’s printed text (1912, 10, lines 18–20). The Greek terms require particular
care: περίτρητον denotes the machine’s torsion opening. For the naval module
associated with interscalmium, the Spanish edition’s running text has διάπηγμα,
whereas  its comparative note  gives διπηχυια. Krohn’s printed  text  gives
διπηχυαια and Rose (1899, 11, line 17) gives διάπηγμα. the authorial Spanish
edition’s running reading is retained here, and the disagreement within the
Spanish source is recorded rather than silently harmonized; the current Perseus
transcription must not be assumed to reproduce every detail of Krohn’s Greek.
Conceptual note — Symmetria. Here symmetria means commensurability or
the modular correspondence of parts to a whole, rather than bilateral symmetry.
The variety of examples—temple, ballista and ship—shows that Vitruvius
formulates a principle of relative dimensioning applicable to different technical
fields, rather than a single universal proportion.

Exegetical Notes
1.     Ancient symmetry does not mean the same as modern symmetry (a
mirror image with respect to an axis). For Vitruvius, symmetry is the conveniens
consensus (shared mathematical harmony). It is the proportional relationship
that unites the parts with the whole. Its operational key is the rata pars (the
aliquot or fixed part), which acts as the common metric divisor of the entire
project. If the module (rata pars) measures 50 cm, the columns will measure
10×50 cm, the pediment 6×50 cm, and the forum 40×50 cm.

2.    Anthropomorphic  Metrological  Canon:  Vitruvius  bases  the
validity of architectural symmetry on the human body. God or nature has
designed the body in such a way that the finger is a fraction of the palm, the
palm a fraction of the foot, and the foot a fraction of the cubit. Therefore, the
classical metric system does not use impersonal abstractions, but organic and
corporeal units. The building is a reflection of the biological order.

3.    The Transdisciplinary Modular Unit: The recovered  section
confirms that the treatise unifies all engineering disciplines under a single
scientific framework. Vitruvius demonstrates that the same mathematical
thinking governs three seemingly unrelated fields:

◦      Sacred Architecture: Uses as a module the lower diameter of the
column (crassitudo), the module of the Doric triglyph or the embatés (the space
of the grid).

◦       Military Engineering (Siegecraft): The ballistae in Book X are not
designed "by eye." Their full scale depends on the foramen (the hole through
which the siege cords pass). The diameter of that hole is the rata pars, which
determines the size of the entire siege machine.

◦      Engineering: Warships are designed based on the diapegma (the
interscalm), the fixed distance that must exist between the seat of one rower and
the next.
For the High Empire, a temple, a war machine, and a naval vessel are,
ontologically, the same geometric structure applied to different materials.
The architect is the universal sage because he masters that symmetriarum
ratiocinatio that unifies the world.
This fragment (I, 2, 5) defines the fifth axiom of classical architecture: Decorum.
This principle introduces the ethical, theological, and semiotic dimension into
architectural design, decreeing that a building must not only be geometrically
perfect and perceptually eurhythmic, but also politically correct and sacredly
appropriate to its function and context.

Exegetical Notes
1.      Philological note on probatis rebus. The transmitted text and
modern  critical  editions  read  probatis  rebus,  “approved  elements”  or

corruption is asserted here without an identified manuscript witness.
2.      Architecture as Theological and Semiotic Anthropomorphism:
This passage constitutes the birth certificate of the theory of architectural
genres or characters. Vitruvius demonstrates that the classical orders
(Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian) are not mere decorative systems interchangeable
at whim, but the tectonic transposition of the identity of the god who inhabits
the cella:

◦     The  Doric  order  represents  masculine  Virtus:  Devoid  of
superfluous ornamentation (sine deliciis), it embodies the robust musculature
and severity of the soldier. It is the order of war and defensive wisdom (Mars,
Minerva, Hercules).
◦     The Corinthian is the feminine Teneritas: Slender, ornamented
with acanthus leaves and sinuous volutes, it represents the grace and fertility of
the young woman (Venus, Flora).
◦     The Ionic order is the matronly Mediocritas: The just mean (ratio
mediocritatis). It is neither as austere as the Doric nor as ornamental as the
Corinthian; its volutes imitate the curly hair of the mother of the family or of
deities who demand a solemn but balanced worship (Juno, Diana).
3.     Hypaethra Architecture and the Cosmos as Temple: The rule of
statio explained at the beginning demonstrates the indissoluble link between the
gnomonics of Book IX and building typology. Building hypaethra (roofless)
temples for the Sun, the Moon, or Jupiter is a cosmic imperative. It would be a
theoretical affront to enclose, under an artificial wooden roof, the deities whose
essence is infinite light and the ray of the firmament (in aperto mundo atque
lucenti). Roman architecture submits to the laws of physics and the astronomy
of the sky; the building breaks its own material boundary to merge with the
celestial vault.
This fragment (I, 2, 6) addresses the second dimension of decorum: Custom
(Consuetudo). Vitruvius momentarily abandons theology to focus on the
internal coherence  of  the  building, formulating two  universal laws  of
architecture: spatial congruence (the dignified correspondence between the
exterior and the interior) and tectonic orthodoxy (strict respect for the rules
of combining the orders).
The Latin term consuetudinibus (meaning customs/traditions) and ordinis
(meaning architectural order, not " order"). Likewise,  epistyliis are not
"epistles", but epistyles or architraves, and offendetur aspectus means that "
the viewer's sight will be offended/the gaze will be scandalized ".

“6. Furthermore, decorum is expressed according to custom (consuetudinem) in
the following way: when magnificent residential interiors are accompanied by
vestibules (vestibula) executed with identical propriety and elegance. Indeed, if
the internal rooms offer elegant views but the entrances are low, meager, or
indecorous (humiles et inhonestos), the work will lack decorum.”
Similarly,  if  dentils  (denticuli) were carved  into the  cornices of Doric
entablatures, or if triglyphs were sculpted on Ionic architraves attached to
columns with pulvinatis capitals, a grave offense would be committed. By
transferring the specific features of one structural logic to another type of work,
the viewer's sight would be seriously offended  (offendetur  aspectus),
because the traditions and customs previously established for each architectural
order (ordinis consuetudinibus) would have been violated.

to social status. In the Rome of the High Empire, the vestibule of the domus or

for the salutatio matutina. Designing a luxurious interior preceded by a squalid

2.    Grammar and Syntax Errors: Vitruvius defines the architectural
orders not as a collection of whimsical ornaments, but as languages with a
grammar and syntax of their own (an interpretive analogy).
◦      The Doric order imitates the primitive structure of wooden beams: the
triglyphs represent the ends of the crossbeams. Placing dentils (which belong to
the Ionic tradition of light reed roofs) on a Doric cornice  is an aberrant
structural contradiction.
◦      Mixing Doric triglyphs with architraves and Ionic columns with
pulvinated volute capitals (pulvinatis) destroys the veracity of the building.
3.      Sight as Moral Judge (Offendetur aspectus): For the thesis on
Sophia, the paragraph's conclusion is providential. Vitruvius points out that the
spurious mixture of the orders produces an immediate visual offense: offendetur
aspectus. This demonstrates that for the Romans, the eye of a cultivated
spectator is not passive; it possesses an aesthetic education rooted in custom
(consuetudo). Seeing a syntactic error in stone provokes the same intellectual
rejection as hearing a serious grammatical mistake in a speech in the Forum.
Architecture, therefore, is consolidated as a discipline regulated by cultural laws
as strict as those of law or rhetoric.
This fragment (I, 2, 7) defines the third and final dimension of decorum: Nature
(Natura). With this passage, Vitruvius masterfully connects the theory of
design with Galenic and Hippocratic medicine (ancient hygienism) and with
astronomy applied to climatic orientation (bioclimatics).

Critical and Hermeneutic Translation
7. For its part, natural decorum (naturalis decor) will be manifested if, above all,
the most healthy regions and suitable springs of water are chosen for the
foundation of the sanctuaries (fana) in those locations where the temples are to
be erected; this should be applied especially to Aesculapius and Salus, deities
whose medical arts seem to heal a great number of sick people. Indeed, when
bodies weakened by disease are moved from pestilent places to healthy
environments, and are given access to water from wholesome springs, they

recover their health more quickly. In this way, through the influence of the very
nature of the place (ex natura loci), the deity will receive increased worship and
veneration invested with the highest dignity.
Likewise, the decorum of nature will be respected if bedrooms (cubiculis) and
libraries receive light from the east; bathrooms (balineis) and winter
quarters (hibernaculis), from the winter west (west/southwest); and art galleries
(pinacothecis), together with those rooms that require constant illumination, from
the north, since that region of the firmament neither dazzles nor darkens with
the course of the sun, but remains fixed, homogeneous, and immutable
throughout the day (die perpetuo).

Exegetical Notes
1.     Hygienic  Urbanism  and  Medical  Theology:   Vitruvius
demonstrates that Roman sacred architecture is neither capricious nor purely
aesthetic; it is subject to the biological laws of nature. Placing a sanctuary
(fanum) dedicated to healing deities like Asclepius or Salus in an unhealthy
swamp would destroy the god's credibility. If the sick person recovers thanks to
the pure air and clean water of the place (ex natura loci), they will miraculously
attribute their cure to divine intervention, increasing the dignity and political
prestige of the state religion. Architecture here acts as a strategic ally of
preventive medicine.

2.     Bioclimatic Architecture and Solar Orientation: This paragraph
constitutes the first manual of thermal orientation in Western history. Vitruvius
distributes the program of needs of the domus following the movement of the
sun and the needs of the mind and body:

◦       East: For bedrooms and  libraries. The morning  light  prevents
dampness in books and awakens the intellect early.

◦      Winter West (Southwest): For winter bathrooms and lounges
(hibernaculis). By opening towards the west, these rooms capture the heat
accumulated throughout the afternoon, warming the space precisely during the
hours when they will be used during the cold months.

3.    The North as the Space of Absolute Light (Die perpetuo): The
recommendation to orient art galleries and studios towards the north (a

septentrione)  is overwhelmingly scientifically sound. Since in the Northern
Hemisphere the sun travels through the south, the light entering through north-
facing windows is reflected, indirect, diffuse, and constant. Vitruvius points out
that this illumination is neither clear nor obscured (it suffers neither the glare of
midday nor the long shadows of sunset). It  is an immutable light (certa
immutabilis), ideal for painters to work and for viewers to contemplate the true
colors of works of art without optical distortions.

impeccable and without impediments". The term emendata suggests a plan
that is corrected, refined, and free of design flaws.
•     ad regiones... distributio: Vitruvius refers not only to the "category
" of the building, but also to its climatic and geographical orientation. The
regions in this passage are the cardinal points and the zones of the sky (sun
exposure and prevailing winds).
•     membrorumque commensus: This translates as "the proportion of
the members" (or architectural elements). Commensus is the mutual metric
correspondence between the parts and the whole.
•      symmetriarum ratiocinationes: The term symmetria in the classical
world does not equate to the modern concept of bilateral mirror reflection. It
means "modular relation". It is therefore translated as "the just calculation of
symmetries ", that is, mathematical modulation based on a control member (the
diameter of a column, for example).
1.3.2 These constructions must be achieved in such a way as to attend to
solidity,  utility, and beauty.  Solidity  will be ensured by deepening the
foundations to the firm stratum and by diligently choosing the materials
without sparing any expense; utility, when the arrangement of the spaces
presents no impediment and their distribution is comfortable and suitable for
each type of building; and beauty, when the appearance of the work is pleasing
and the proportion of its members maintains a just calculation of symmetries
(Vitruvius, De architectura 1.3.2).
Comparative apparatus — I.3.1–2. Aedificatio, gnomonice and machinatio are
operational divisions of the discipline; firmitas, utilitas and venustas are criteria
Vitruvius requires of the works described. The triad is translated without
turning it into a modern slogan: firmitas includes foundations and the choice of
materials; utilitas, arrangement suited to use; venustas, a pleasing appearance
and proportional relationships.
Reception note — Firmitas, utilitas and venustas. The triad’s exceptional
subsequent influence should not be projected back on to the lemma. In I.3.2 the
three terms occur within a concrete explanation of how works should be
executed; their canonisation as a universal formula belongs to the history of
reception.

Critical Interlineation
Explanatory note: the στοιχεῖα and salubrity. In grounding the choice of
site upon the balance of the elements, Vitruvius adopts the Greek doctrine of
the στοιχεῖα —the “elements” or constituent principles of bodies—, which he
enumerates in Latin as calor, umor, terra, and aer (heat, moisture, earth, and
air). This conception derives from Greek natural philosophy (the four “roots”
of Empedocles,  later systematized by  Aristotle) and  is interwoven with
Hippocratic medicine, particularly the treatise Airs, Waters, Places, which links
climate and place to the health of the body. Vitruvius’s originality lies in making
this physiology the foundation of urban site selection (salubritas): the architect
must choose elevated, temperate sites far from marshes so that the elemental
mixture  (temperatura)  of  the  inhabitants’  bodies  remains  in  balance.
Architecture is thereby bound to medicine—a connection Vitruvius himself
claims when he requires the architect to know medicine propter inclinationes
caeli (1.1.10).
Textual note — I.4.5. The adopted text transmits στοιχεῖα, “elements” or
“principles”. This edition retains the reading and confines its commentary to its
role in Vitruvius’s argument, without reconstructing a history of manuscript
corruption that has not been checked directly against the witnesses.

Exegetical Analysis of De architectura 1.4.9
1. The Legacy of Tradition: Mos Maiorum and Roman Pragmatism
Vitruvius opens the passage with a forceful methodological statement: “Etiam
atque etiam veterem revocandam  censeo rationem ”  (“I believe that the
methodology of our ancestors must be recovered, again and again ”). This
recourse is not merely nostalgic; it corresponds to the Roman concept of mos
maiorum (the custom of the ancestors) as a legitimate source of technical and
moral knowledge.
In contrast to the abstract speculation of the Hellenistic philosophical schools,
the author champions ancient ratio: a profoundly empirical criterion, based on
continuous observation and accumulated success. For Vitruvius, the architect is
a steward of public space and, as such, inherited tradition is a safety protocol
tested by generations.

Ritual Aruspicin to Empirical Health Control
The core of the passage describes the examination of cattle entrails (inspicere
iocinera), a practice formally identical to haruspicy, the ancient divinatory


                           298

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I

discipline of Etruscan origin regulated by haruspices. However, Vitruvius
performs a radical demythologization of the ritual:
•      Absence of the sacred: Livers are not examined to look for signs of
the gods (such as caputiocineris or prophetic lines), but to check their objective
physiological state (integram et solidam naturam).
•       Livestock as a bioindicator: Vitruvius understood that animals
grazing in a fixed location act as a biological laboratory that metabolizes and
concentrates the properties of the soil, the pastures (pabulum), and the water
(aqua). If the liver shows necrosis or discoloration (livida  et vitiosa), the
ecosystem is corrupted.
•     The preliminary scientific method: The author describes a two-
step verification protocol. If the first liver is damaged, more cattle are sacrificed
(alia immolabant) to rule out an isolated pathology of the specimen (morbo)
versus an endemic environmental poisoning (pabuli vitio).

3. The Theory of Miasma Contamination and Human Ecology
The passage demonstrates the connection between Roman architecture and the
medical theories of the Hippocratic school, specifically the treatise On Airs,
Waters, and Places. Vitruvius establishes a direct correlation between animal
and human health: the territory that destroys the organs of livestock will, sooner
or later, destroy the constitution of the urban inhabitant (item humanis
corporibus pestilentem futuram).
The conclusion of the passage introduces a criterion for urban planning
subordinated to ecology: if the environment is unhealthy, the solution is not
constructive,  but  migratory  (transmigrabant   et  mutabant   regiones).
Architecture cannot defeat nature;  it must ally itself with its thermal and
hydrological cycles.

4. Military Application: Castra Stativa
The explicit mention of castra stativa (permanent camps or winter quarters)
underscores the strategic importance of hygiene in Roman engineering. The
Roman army could not afford epidemiological outbreaks in the legions
stationed on the frontiers (limes). Analysis of the terrain using haruspicy
(wisdom for livestock) was a mandatory step before the deployment of fixed
defenses (munitiones), thus equating the rigor of military architecture with that
of the founding of large civilian cities (oppida).

technical value of " to stagnate" (water that does not flow). Correctly translated
it is: "when they stagnate, they spoil. "

but to "dense exhalations", miasmas or vapors laden with corrupted particles
that floated on the air of the swamp affecting respiration.
•     M. Hostilium: the Marcus Hostilius named in Vitruvius’s
account of the relocation of  Salpia. The passage  gives no  office,
cognomen, or precise date for his intervention.
•       areas divisit: "divided the territories". In Roman urban planning,
areas are the "plots" or parcels of land designated for the construction of houses
within the new orthogonal layout of the city.
•    nummo sestertio … mancipio dedit: Hostilius conveyed each
building plot by mancipatio for a nominal sestertius. The legal formula
denotes a formal transfer of ownership. The passage does not specify a
beneficiary class or supply the full legal circumstances of the transaction.

become corrupted, emitting pestilent miasmas. This affected ancient Salpia in
Apulia, where its citizens fell ill annually until Marcus Hostilius, through a
rigorous technical study, moved the city to a healthy location by the sea.

provide the municipality with a functional port (Vitruvius, De architectura

Comparative critical apparatus — I.4.1–12. The chapter has been compared
with Krohn (1912) and Philippe Fleury’s Budé edition. The general structure is
stable, but several points require caution: in I.4.1 moenia must be understood
in relation to the urban enclosure, not merely the physical wall; spiritus
bestiarum palustrium belongs to an ancient environmental explanation of
disease and does not justify a microbiological reading; in I.4.2 lumina capere is
architectural language for opening or arranging apertures for light; in I.4.5
στοιχεῖα denotes constituent principles or elements; and in I.4.10 the Cretan
example contains a lacuna that should not be completed without editorial
support.  The  notes  consistently  distinguish  Latin  reading,  historical
interpretation and modern reception.
Historical and medical note — I.4. The chapter combines environmental
observation, the theory of four principles, material analogies, animal feeding
and sacrificial practices as criteria for a healthy site. Its historical value lies in
showing how Vitruvius  integrates the medicine, climatology and urban
planning of his time; it should not be presented as anticipating contemporary
epidemiology or environmental hygiene.
Comparative apparatus —  I.4. The siting of a city  is organized around
salubritas, exposure, moisture, marshes and climatic conditions. The critical text
confirms “electio loci saluberrimi… excelsus et non nebulosus, non pruinosus…
temperatas…  palustris  vicinitas”. The  translation  preserves  this  ancient
environmental medicine without presenting it as contemporary epidemiology.
Medical and historical note — Salubritas. Explanations of airs, bodies, humours
and  diseases  belong  to an  ancient  physiological  framework. Where  a
topographical  observation—drainage,  moisture  or  insolation—can  be
compared with modern environmental criteria, that comparison is offered as
technical reception, not as literal validation of Vitruvius’s aetiology.
Textual note — Inspection of viscera. The use of sacrificed animals to assess the
healthiness of pastures and waters is retained as an ancient practice described by
Vitruvius. It is neither recast as a modern diagnostic method nor omitted
because it lies outside present architectural practice.

refers to the "open" or unprotected flanks of a battle formation. The
projecting arrangement of the towers allowed for a deadly crossfire that battered
the flanks of the attacking troops.
•        itinera... non sint directa sed scaeva: A literal version erred in
translating scaeva as "accident-ridden." Scaevus means "oblique," "deviated to

force the enemy to approach by turning to the left.
•         erit tectum: A literal version suffered a notable lexical confusion by
translating scuto (shield) as "roof" (tectum is here the participle of the verb tegere,
to protect). Since Roman and Hellenistic soldiers carried the shield (scutum) on
their left arm, the right flank was completely unprotected. If the route
forced them to march with their right side exposed towards the wall, the
defenders could easily shoot them with arrows.
•       circumitionibus: Not " Circles." Vitruvius does not demand perfectly
circular cities, but rather layouts "in continuous curved lines" or organic
shapes that follow the topography of the land, avoiding straight lines and
corners that create blind spots.
•      angulus magis hostem tuetur quam civem: Geometric explanation
of blind spots in fortifications. A salient angle (procurrentibus angulis) provides
a sheltered space or " blind spot " where the attacker can take cover from
projectiles falling from the top of adjacent walls.

Vitruvius prescribed that the wood be singed or charred superficially (ustilatae).
This thermal process removes the internal moisture from the wood and alters
the organic compounds that attract wood-boring insects, acting as an ancient
and effective method of waterproofing and biological preservation.
•     quemadmodum fibulis: In this context of construction engineering,
the term fibula designates a clamp, connector, or locking key. Roman walls
typically consisted of two outer faces of ashlar or masonry (frontes) filled
internally with a core of loose stones and mortar (caementicium). Olive beams
acted as transverse tensioners that tied both faces of the wall together,
preventing the internal pressure of the fill from causing the structure to burst.
•      In earthly and underwater environments: Vitruvius praises the
rot-resistant properties of olive wood treated with  fire.  Its resistance in
underground and underwater environments made it ideal for substructures
(retaining foundations or embankments), where constant humidity usually
rotted other types of construction wood.

vault, and so dissipating the kinetic energy of the enemy engine.
•       aggeribus coniunctae: The agger was a traditional defensive element
of Roman military engineering, consisting of a massive earthen ramp or
embankment supported against the inner face of the wall. By filling the interior

absorbing the vibrations of battering ram blows without cracking.

which were then set on fire to cause the wall to collapse under its own weight.
The presence of a  large earthen embankment (agger) discouraged these
operations, as the massive weight of the structure caused the attackers' galleries

Critical Interlineation
Explanatory note: round towers and the fracture of angles. Vitruvius’s
preference for round or polygonal towers over square ones (1.5.5) rests on a
structural and ballistic principle: the ram and the siege engines concentrate their
blow upon the corners, where the masonry, lacking mass to distribute the
impact, splinters and collapses quickly. On a curved surface, by contrast, the
blocks are wedged towards the center and the blow is dispersed tangentially, so
that the stone cannot easily be dislodged. The same reasoning—avoiding the
weak point of the angle—recurs in the rounded circuit of the walls, which
moreover removes the dead angles and allows the assailant to be watched from
several flanks.

absorbed by the stone buttresses.

main danger of large fills of clayey or humic soil was the failure of the retaining

foundations and comb walls physically prevented this type of structural

Notes (Explanation of Vitruvius's Text)
1. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.5.8. For the textual tradition of

•     non est praefiniendum... copiae: Vitruvius here states the principle
of material autarky or adaptation to the geological environment. The Roman
architect and engineer should not impose an abstract theoretical design, but
rather critically evaluate the resources of the quarry and the local deposits
(copiae). The economy of transport in the ancient world made the large-scale
importation of stone for perimeter fortifications unfeasible.
•      Saxa quadrata / flint / caementum: Typological classification of
stone in Roman construction. Saxa quadrata are perfectly squared ashlar
blocks with parallel faces, typical of monumental architecture. Flint refers to
extremely hard stones, such as flint or basaltic volcanic rocks (frequently used in
roads and foundations). Caementum designates rubble masonry, fragmented
and irregular stones that were joined with mortar to form the core of the wall
(opus caementicium).
•       coctus later sive crudus: Vitruvius equates the use of industrialized
clay. Later crudus (adobe or sun-dried brick) remained common in domestic
architecture and secondary walls of the Republican periphery, while later coctus
(kiln-fired  brick)  represented maximum  resistance  to  compression and
humidity.
•       Babylon... liquid bitumen for lime: Historical mention of the
Mesopotamian construction technique,  also documented by Herodotus.
Babylon lacked limestone quarries for making lime (calx) and suitable sand
(harena), but it had natural outcrops of asphalt or bitumen from Hit. This
viscous hydrocarbon acted as a fast-setting mortar and waterproofing agent with
exceptional adhesion, fixing the courses of fired brick against river floods.
Vitruvius classifies it as a fortunate geographical anomaly (locorum proprietates),
inapplicable to the soil of the Italian peninsula.
1.5.8 It is not possible to prescribe a universal material for the construction of
walls, since the suitable resources vary according to the region. The architect will

Architectural and military note — I.5. The prescriptions for projecting towers,

ancient defensive logic. The edition avoids making them universal rules of

Comparative apparatus — I.5. Fortification requires foundations on firm
ground, proportionate thicknesses, projecting towers and layouts that hinder a
frontal assault. Agger, fossa, murus, turris, intervallum and emplecton are
checked  according  to   their  constructional  functions.  The  military
recommendations  are discussed  historically rather than  as contemporary
instructions.

distinguishes foundations, wall mass, transverse bonding and tower position.

consumption or tuberculosis; and sanguinis eectio is the expulsion of blood
through the respiratory tract (hemoptysis).
•     Non  detractionibus  sed  adiectionibus: A  fundamental
therapeutic concept of Galenic and Hippocratic medicine. Bodies suffered from

ailments due to excess (plethora) or deficiency. Diseases requiring detractions
(evacuations, bloodletting, or purges) were those caused by excess humours. In
contrast, chronic pulmonary pathologies generated malnutrition and physical
deterioration, thus requiring adiectiones: therapies of reconstitution, rest,
warmth, and nutrition.
•      aer agitatus... detrahit sucum: Vitruvius offers a microclimatic
explanation based on physical evaporation. The air agitated by the wind
becomes thinner or more subtle (extenuatur) and acts by increasing the rate of
perspiration and drying of the patient's mucous membranes. By stripping away
the sucus (the bodily juices or fluids that maintained the flexibility and defense
of the tissues), the wind accelerates the emaciation or malnutrition (exiliora) of
the patients.
•        lenis et crassus aer: The paradox of "thick or dense air." While
modern urban planning  prioritizes constant  ventilation, ancient  science
considered that still, warm, and dense (crassus) air inside sheltered alleyways
acted as a physical balm for damaged lungs. Lacking turbulence (perflatus), this
stable air provided an environmental rest that allowed the body to absorb
nutrients and recover lost energy.
1.6.3 The exclusion of winds in urban design generates optimal thermal
stability (temperature) for the recovery from chronic respiratory pathologies,
such as catarrh (gravedo), bronchitis (arteriace), tuberculosis (phthisis), and
hemoptysis. Since these diseases require restorative therapies (adictiones) rather
than evacuation therapies, dynamic and agitated air is detrimental because it
accelerates dehydration and  loss of  vital  fluids (sucum)  in the  patient.
Conversely, dense, stable air free of drafts (crassus aer) nourishes and restores
weakened organisms (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.6.3).

Archaeological note — Bk. 1.6 (the winds and the Tower of the Winds).
The layout of the city, Vitruvius says, must orient the streets by the
winds: along the lines dividing the eight winds —Solanus (E), Auster (S),
Favonius (W), Septentrio (N) and, at the corners, Eurus (SE), Africus
(SW), Caurus or Corus (NW), and Aquilo (NE)— so that no street
channels the wind against the houses. Against those who counted only
four winds, Vitruvius praises those who recognized eight, and cites as a
living witness Andronicus of Cyrrhus, who  raised  at Athens an
octagonal marble tower with a figure of each wind on its face and, at the
apex, a bronze Triton turning to point to the quarter from which the
wind blew. This is the Tower of the Winds (Horologion) in the Roman
Agora of Athens (c. 50 BCE), of Pentelic marble, with nine sundials and
a water-clock within: one of the very few buildings of classical antiquity
to survive almost intact —and one that links this chapter to the
gnomonics of Book IX.

monument confirms the octagonal plan and wind reliefs; the bronze weather-
vane does not survive.

•      East/West  Equinoctiali:  Vitruvius  uses Roman  astronomical
terminology to pinpoint the exact cardinal directions. The orient aequinoctiali
(equinoctial east) and octenoctiali (equinoctial west) refer to the points on the
horizon where the sun rises and sets during the spring and autumn equinoxes,
as distinct from the solstitial points (summer and winter). The associated
primordial winds are the Solanus (east wind) and the Favonius (the Greek
zephyr, west wind).
•      Andronicus Cyrrestes: Andronicus of Cyrrhus (Syrian by origin),
astronomer and mathematician of the 1st century BC. His tower in the Roman
Agora of Athens combined a multiple sundial, an internal water clock
(clepsydra) for cloudy days and the weathervane system described by Vitruvius,
constituting a compendium of the sciences of astronomy and gnomonics of the
time.
•      Imagines excalptas contra suos flatus: The eight friezes sculpted in
bas-relief at the top of the tower are  still preserved. Each wind deity  is
represented  anthropomorphically  and  flying,  carrying  specific  climatic
attributes and oriented exactly towards the geographical direction from which
its wind originates (e.g., Boreas in the north, Notus in the south).
•     metam marmoream: The meta refers to the conical or pyramidal
shape that crowns the roof of the tower, constructed with interlocking Pentelic
marble slabs. Its design imitated the meta of Roman circuses, serving as a solid
and elevated base for the automaton's axis.
•      Tritonem aereum... indicem virgam: The description of this
bronze Triton  represents  the  first  historical  record  of an automated
anemoscope or weathervane. The mythological marine figure functioned under
simple static and aerodynamic principles: as the air current acted upon the
Triton's tail or folds, it rotated on a central pivot until it offered the least
resistance to the wind, aligning its torso and the indicator rod (virga) towards
the exact quadrant from which the wind originated, pointing to the sculpted
deity that generated it.
1.6.4 In contrast to the traditional theory of the four cardinal winds, Vitruvius
adopted the scientific system of eight winds proposed by Andronicus of
Cyrrhus. As empirical proof, Andronicus erected an octagonal marble tower in
Athens with the effigies of the Aeolian deities sculpted on its respective faces.
The monument was crowned by a bronze Triton (Tritonem aereum) which,

Critical Notes (Explanation of the Vitruvius Text)

•       Eratosthenes of Cyrene... rationibus mathematicis: Vitruvius
testifies to the geodetic method of Eratosthenes (c. 276 – 194 BCE). This
consisted  of  simultaneously  measuring  the  difference  in  the
inclination of the sun's rays at midday during the summer solstice in
two cities located on the same meridian: Syene (Aswan), where the sun
reached its zenith and cast no shadow on the bottom of a well, and
Alexandria, where, using the shadow of a gnomon (or scaphe), he
determined an angle of inclination equivalent to 7.2 ° (one fiftieth of
the total circumference of 360 °). Multiplying the physical distance
between the two cities by 50, he obtained the global dimension of the
planet.
•      ducentorum quinquaginta duum milium stadium: The figure
of 252 000 stadia adopted by Vitruvius represents the practical correction
attributed to Eratosthenes (or his successors) to make the number perfectly
divisible by 360 ° from the division of the circle, assigning exactly 700 stades per
geographical degree. Depending on the stadium module used (probably the
Egyptian stadium of ≈ 157.5 m), the calculation yields a circumference of about
39 690 km, a value astonishingly close to modern satellite measurement (≈
40 075 km).
•      quae fiunt passuum CCCXV milia: Conversion to the official
metrological system of the Roman Empire. A double Roman step (passus) is
equivalent to 5 feet (≈ 1.48 m). Since a standard stadium contained 125 double

The figure expresses the total planetary perimeter in military and surveying units

•       huius autem octava pars: mathematical division of the aeolian horizon.
Dividing the 31,500,000 paces of the Earth’s circumference among the 8
principal angular sectors of the compass rose, each 45° wind quadrant has a
linear width at the equator of 31,500,000 ÷ 8 = 3,937,500 Roman paces
(approximately 5,827 kilometers).
•       Inclinations and Recessions: Vitruvius resolves a debate in ancient
physics and geography: the proliferation of local names for winds (such as the
Iapyx in Apulia or the Cecias in Athens). By mathematically demonstrating that
the front of origin of a single wind measures almost 6000 kilometers wide, he
argues  that  it  is  physically  inevitable  that  currents undergo  deviations
(inclinations) due to topography, mountains or valleys, or thermal oscillations
(recessions), changing their character and name according to the region, without
invalidating the scientific basis of the eight principal winds.
1.6.9 To silence the criticism of those who catalog an excessive amount of winds,
Vitruvius appeals to the geodetic scale of the planet established by Eratosthenes
of Cyrene. Based on the shadows of the gnomon, Eratosthenes calculated the
earth's circumference in 252 000 stadia (31 500 000 Roman paces). Since one-
eighth of this perimeter — the frontage allocated to each main wind — is
equivalent to a monumental arch of 3 937 500 Roman paces, the subtle thermal
and geographical variations of the relief cause deviations (inclinations) and local
oscillations in the gusts, multiplying the regional nomenclatures without
altering the octagonal macroscopic order (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.6.9).

Academic translation
1.7.1 Once the alleyways have been divided and the main avenues established,
the allocation of building plots (areae) intended for the convenience and
common use of the citizenry must proceed: the sacred temples, the forum, and
the remaining public spaces. If the walls are situated by the sea, the plot for the
forum should be chosen in the vicinity of the port; if, on the contrary, the city
is located inland, the forum will be situated in the very center of the urban area.
For the sacred temples of those gods under whose principal protection the city
appears to be placed — such as Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva — plots will be
distributed in the highest place (in excelsissimo loco), from where most of the
perimeter of the walls can be seen. In contrast, the temple of Mercury was
located in the forum or the market (emporium), as were those of Isis and Serapis;
the temple of Apollo and that of Father Liberus (Bacchus), next to the theater;
the temple of Hercules, in those cities lacking gymnasiums or amphitheaters, in
the vicinity of the circus; the temple of Mars, outside the city but next to the
training ground (campus); and likewise the temple of Venus, near the port. This
arrangement is similarly prescribed in the texts containing the discipline of the
Etruscan haruspices: the sanctuaries (fana) of Venus, Vulcan, and Mars must
be erected outside the city walls so that neither young men nor mothers become
accustomed to sexual lust within the city. Likewise, by banishing Vulcan's
destructive power from the city walls through rituals and sacrifices, public
buildings appear to be freed from the fear of fire. Finally, by consecrating the
divinity of Mars outside the walls, armed conflicts among the citizens are
prevented, protecting the community and preserving it from the dangers of war
against external enemies.

•        electio arearum  / foro... proxime portum: Vitruvius applies a
functional and typological criterion for the distribution of space (areae). The
forum (forum) is the economic, legal, and political center. In a maritime colony,
its position must correspond to the logistics of overseas trade (proxime portum),
connecting the port with the road axis. In continental cities (mediterranea), the
geometry of the military model is applied: the forum occupies the intersection
of the cardo and the decumanus, in the geographical heart of the settlement (ino
oppido medio).

•       Iovi et Iunoni et Minervae in excelsissimo loco: This  is the
urbanistic translation of the model of the Capitoline Triad of Rome. The
main temple, dedicated to the state cult, must preside over the city from the
acropolis or the highest topographical point (excelsissimus locus). This position
not only corresponds to a theological hierarchy, but also to a defensive-visual
function: the gods act as sentinels guarding the curtain of the walls (moenium
maxima pars conspiciatur).

•      Theological  - Functional Zoning:  Vitruvius  details  a  sacred
geography where the function of the god coincides with the socio-economic
nature of the neighborhood:

◦      Mercury,  Isis and Serapis: Gods of commerce and navigation,
located where money and merchandise flow (in foro aut in emporio).

◦      Apollo and Father Liberus: Deities linked to the lyric arts, music,
drama and wine, assigned to the leisure district, adjacent to the theater structure.

◦       Hercules: Patron of physical strength and athletic effort, linked to the
circus due to a lack of traditional Greek infrastructure (gymnasia).

•       Etruscis haruspicibus... extra murum: Vitruvius justifies zoning
restrictions through Etruscan tradition, the legal and religious framework that
conditioned Roman urban planning. The haruspices segregated three specific

  •    Veneris, Volcani, Martis fana:
◦      Venus: By placing her cult outside the walls (generally linked to the
port or marginal areas), the State sought to mitigate prostitution and preserve
the morality of young people and matrons (matres familiarum), containing
erotic passions on the periphery.

◦      Vulcan: A pragmatic risk prevention measure. By ritually expelling the
power of destructive fire (Volcani vi) from the high-density construction of the
timber and masonry neighborhoods, the city was protected from catastrophic
fires (timore incendiorum).

◦      Mars: The god of war must reside in the Campus Martius, the outdoor
military training ground. Keeping the worship of weapons outside the domestic
walls psychologically avoided internal violence,  civil war, or coups d'état
(armigera dissensio), projecting martial aggression exclusively towards the
foreign enemy (ab hostibus ea defensa).
1.7.1 Once the road network was delimited, Vitruvius established the zoning of
public plots (areae), combining commercial functionality with the Etruscan
sacred tradition. While the forum was located at the port or the city center
according to its geography, the Capitoline Triad (Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva)
had to crown the highest point of the terrain for purposes of representation and
surveillance. The sanctuaries of Mercury, Apollo, and Hercules were integrated
into their respective economic and leisure districts. Conversely, following the
writings of the haruspices, the temples of Venus, Vulcan, and Mars were
segregated outside the city walls; This territorial planning policy sought to
safeguard public morality, avert the danger of urban fires, and channel military
force exclusively towards external defense against the enemy (Vitruvius, De
architectura 1.7.1).

LIBER II

ARGUMENTUM LIBRI II — On the origin of architecture and civil life, and on
building materials: brick, sand, lime, pozzolana, quarry stone, wall patterns
(reticulatum, incertum, isódomon, pseudisódomon, émplecton) and woods, with
their virtues and defects according to the proportion of natural elements.

Notice. — Book II turns from theory to matter. After an anthropological
preface on the origins of building — the primitive hut, society born around fire —
it treats the materials of construction: brick, sand, lime, the volcanic pozzolana
that  sets under water,  stone and quarries, the methods  of walling (opus
reticulatum, incertum, the Greek emplekton) and timber. It is the foundational
ancient source for Roman building technology, and modern materials science has
confirmed much of its account of lime and pozzolanic mortar.
