II.Pr.1 Dinocrates132 the architect, trusting in his ideas and ingenuity, left
Macedonia for the army while Alexander was in power, eager to win the king’s
favor. He brought letters from relatives and friends at home to the leading
officers and courtiers, hoping to gain easier access. They received him kindly,
and he asked to be brought before Alexander as soon as possible. Although they
promised to do so, they delayed while waiting for a suitable occasion. Thinking
that they were making a fool of him, Dinocrates sought a resource within
himself. He was very tall, with a pleasing face and an impressive, dignified
physique. Trusting in these natural gifts, he left his clothes at the inn, anointed
his body with oil, crowned his head with poplar leaves, draped a lion’s skin over
his left shoulder and, holding a club in his right hand, advanced towards the
tribunal where the king was administering justice.
1. Dinocrates: Name of the celebrated Hellenistic architect and urban
planner of the late 4th century BC, the architect of Alexandria's urban plan. In
other ancient sources (such as Plutarch or Strabo) his name appears spelled with
phonetic variants such as Deinocrates, Stasicrates, or Cheiromocrates. — 2.
purpuratos: Technical term from the Macedonian court and the Hellenistic
kingdoms (philoi or diadochos) that designated the high dignitaries, ministers,
and generals of the king's utmost confidence, who possessed the privilege of
wearing robes dyed royal purple. The popular medieval translation confused the
adjective with "purple-colored letters." — 3. ab se: Philological emendation of
the main manuscript tradition. The expression indicates that Dinocrates, seeing
the mediation of the courtiers thwarted, decided to rely on his own means and
initiative, resorting to his own person as his only shield or "protection "
(praesidium).


132 Dinocrates (Δεινοκράτης; transmitted forms Dinocrates and Deinochares) was a Greek
architect contemporary with Alexander the Great. Vitruvius devotes the preface to Book II
(2.pref.1–4) to him, recounting how he presented himself to the king and proposed carving
Mount Athos into a colossal statue, with a city in its left hand and, in its right, a basin collecting
the mountain’s waters and discharging them into the sea. Alexander rejected the project after
asking about land capable of feeding the city, but retained its author. Tradition attributes to
Dinocrates the plan of Alexandria, founded in 331 BC, and its orthogonal Hippodamian layout.
His identification with the Chirocrates mentioned by Strabo remains disputed, as do the
attribution of Hephaestion’s funeral pyre at Babylon and of work on the temple of Artemis at
Ephesus. In Vitruvius the episode serves an argumentative purpose: it contrasts princely favor
with professional competence alone and introduces the author’s vindication of his own position.

signed by his relatives and friends, addressed to the leading officers and high
court dignitaries (purpurati), in order to facilitate his access to the sovereign.
Having been received by them courteously, he begged them to present him to
Alexander as soon as possible; however, although they promised to do so, they
were indolent and dilatory, waiting for a moment they deemed opportune.
Therefore, Dinocrates, suspecting that these officers were making a mockery of
him, decided to take matters into his own hands. Since he possessed an imposing
stature, a graceful face, and a presence of extraordinary beauty and dignity,
trusting in these gifts of nature, he stripped off his clothes at the inn, anointed
his entire body with oil, crowned his head with poplar fronds, covered his left
shoulder with a lion skin, and, wielding a mace in his right hand, advanced with
a firm step directly to the tribunal where the king dispensed justice.

security and inevitably forces Alexander's direct attention, breaking through the
filter of secretaries and generals.

Dinocrates burst into the public court where the monarch dispensed justice (ius

•      Novitas populum cum avertisset: Dinocrates's astute performance
has an immediate effect. The term novitas (the eccentricity or strangeness of the
spectacle) breaks the monotony of the royal court. In Greco-Roman culture,
attracting the attention of the crowd (populus) was the indispensable first step
to capture the interest of the monarch, who operated under the gaze of the
public.

•      Cogitationes  et formas:  Vitruvius employs  a  key  conceptual
binomial in his own architectural theory. Cogitationes represent the theoretical
ideas or mental conception of the design, while forms refer to the models, plans,
or tangible perspective representations that the architect brought with him to
visually persuade the king.

•     Athon montem in statuae virilis figuram: The Mount Athos
project constitutes the first major documented example of anthropomorphic
architecture on a territorial scale, or land art, in antiquity. Dinocrates
proposed sculpting a mountain over 2000 meters high to mold the figure of
Alexander himself (implicitly assimilated to Hercules, reinforcing the disguise
with which he presented himself).

•    manu  laeva  moenia...  dextra  pateram:  The  iconographic
distribution of the macrostatue follows the conventions of Greek divine and
heroic statuary:

◦       Left hand (The city): Holds the walls of a great city (civitatis
amplissimae moenia). This image symbolizes the sovereign as ecumenical
founder, protector and physical container of civilization over untamed nature.

◦      Right hand (The patera): Holds a ceremonial bowl or libation dish
(patera). The technical function of this piece is to act as a gigantic dam or
collection vessel that unifies the mountain's hydrographic basins (omnium
fluminum... aquam). By channeling the water and  artistically directing  it
towards the sea, the monarch is presented not only as a conqueror of peoples,
but as an organizer of the forces of nature and the hydrological cycle.

Translation and Commentary
II.Pr.2 After capturing the attention of Alexander the Great thanks to his
theatrical entrance, Dinocrates identified himself as a Macedonian architect and
presented him with a revolutionary model of colossal urbanism (forms). His
proposal consisted of carving the promontory of Mount Athos with the
physiognomy of a Herculean male colossus that would hold in its left hand the
walled enclosure of a great city, while in its right it would hold a monumental
collecting patera in charge of unifying the river channels of the mountain to
pour them aesthetically into the ocean, linking the glory of the sovereign with
the absolute dominion of the natural landscape (Vitruvius, De architectura
2.Pr.2).

whom he will later entrust a task where formal genius and ideal geographical
conditions will coincide: the founding of Alexandria in Egypt.

fascinated by the aesthetics of the colossus of Mount Athos, Alexander the
Great rejected the project due to the absence of a peripheral agricultural territory
capable of guaranteeing the sustenance of the population (frumentaria ratio).

unviability of colonies exclusively dependent on unstable maritime supply lines
(transmarinis subvectionibus), although he does incorporate Dinocrates into his
entourage of state engineers (Vitruvius, De architectura 2.Pr.3).

•     Mihi autem... faciem deformavit aetas, valetudo detraxit vires:
The Autobiographical Turn and the Rhetoric of Physical Decline. Vitruvius
presents himself to Augustus as the exact opposite of Dinocrates: an old man
(aetas), marked by illness (valetudo) and devoid of visual appeal or athletic
prowess. This confession does not seek compassion, but rather operates under a
classical  literary convention:  the devaluation of the body to  extol the
imperishable value of the intellect.
•      Per auxilia scientiae scriptaque: The thesis of Vitruvius's treatise.
The author proposes to Emperor Augustus a new model of patronage based not
on the immediate visual appeal of megalomaniacal projects, but on the solidity
of scientific knowledge and the written codification of the laws of architecture.
His ten books are, therefore, his own "lion's skin" and his "club": the intellectual
instruments with which he aspires to earn immortality and the commendation
(commendatio) of the sovereign of Rome.
II.Pr.4 The prologue concludes by linking Dinocrates' definitive success with
the founding of Alexandria, a site that, unlike Mount Athos, combined a safe
natural harbour with the agricultural and logistical potential of the Nile River.
Vitruvius takes advantage of this historical resolution to articulate a sharp
autobiographical contrast directed at Augustus (imperator); acknowledging his
lack of the youth, stature, and physical presence that elevated the Macedonian
master, the Roman writer claims state patronage based strictly on the rigor of
technical knowledge (scientia) and the enduring value of his written work as his
sole title of architectural nobility (Vitruvius, De architectura 2.Pr.4).

forests, caves, and groves, and passed their  lives feeding upon wild fare.

winds, and rubbing their branches one against another, kindled fire; and those
who were about that place, terrified by the fierce flame, were put to flight.
Afterwards, when it had grown quiet, drawing nearer they perceived that the
warmth of the fire was of great comfort to their bodies; and, adding wood and
so keeping it alive, they brought others to it, and by signs made plain what
advantages they had from it. In that gathering of men, as their voices were
uttered in differing ways with the breath, they established by daily use words as
chance had brought them; then, signifying the things in more frequent use, they
came by chance to speak, and thus speech was born among them. 135

described as being in a state of wild animality, nomadic, scattered, and lacking

doctrine expounded by the Roman poet Lucretius in Book V of his work De
rerum natura.

•      demystification of fire. In contrast to the Greek myth of Prometheus
(who steals fire from the gods to give  it to humanity), Vitruvius offers a
naturalistic and mechanical explanation of the phenomenon: the accidental
friction of tree branches caused by the wind. The driving force of cultural
change is not divine intervention, but a physical and fortuitous meteorological
phenomenon.

•       ignis teporem / utilitates: Fire acts as the ultimate social catalyst.
Upon discovering the physical advantage of heat (commoditatem ad ignis
teporem), humans overcome their initial fear and learn to domesticate the
element by gathering firewood (ligna adicientes). Maintaining the hearth
requires temporary sedentary behavior and cooperation, forcing  isolated
individuals to gather in a common place (hominum congressus).

1.     Primary  cries: Modulations of the voice caused by spontaneous
physical or emotional impulses (profundebantur aliter spiritu voces).

2.      Arbitrariness and convention: The random assignment of names to

constituerunt), consolidated by collective habit (cotiedad consuetudine).

3.      articulation: The pragmatic repetition oriented towards utility that

2.1.1 Vitruvius opens the main body of his second book by presenting a
materialist and evolutionist theory on the origin of humanity, in line with
atomist and  Lucretian  schools  of  thought. The  passage  describes  the
fundamental transition from a wild and disconnected existence to social
cohesion, identifying the accidental domestication of fire — caused by the
friction of forest vegetation — and the subsequent gathering of human
communities around hearths (hominum congressus) as the driving force behind
this change. This shared space forced the abandonment of instinctive cries in
favor of the conventional establishment of arbitrary linguistic signs, giving rise
to the simultaneous birth of society and articulated language (Vitruvius, De
architectura 2.1.1).

•      naturae praemium  / non proni sed  erecti: The anatomical
foundation of culture. Vitruvius aligns himself with the Stoic and Ciceronian
tradition (cf. Cicero, De natura deorum II.150) in arguing that the erect posture

the stars, elevating thought) and a pragmatic /mechanical one (to free the
upper  limbs). Animals, being  proni  (looking towards the ground),  are
determined by their immediate biological needs; human beings, being erectus,
possess the visual and physical distance necessary to design their environment.
•     manibus et articulis... facilitater tractarent: The hand as a tool
of tools. Vitruvius anticipates modern theses of technical anthropology on
hominization. The human hand, endowed with versatile joints and digital
opposition, allows for tractatio (the skilful manipulation of raw materials).
Without  this anatomical advantage, human  intelligence could not have
materialized in physical culture or architecture.

•     Hirundinum  nests... imitators: The concept of Constructive
Mimesis. The origin of architecture does not stem from divine revelation, but
from careful observation and imitation of zoology. Primitive humans imitate
the technique of swallows (hirundines), which mix flexible organic elements
(branches, straw) with moist binders (mud, clay). This is the zero degree of
masonry: the transition from the simple appropriation of natural space (the
cave) to the manufacture of an artificial habitat through the combination of
materials.
•       observantes aliena tecta  / adicientes suis cogitationibus: The
engine of technical progress is social emulation and cognitive development.
Architecture evolves thanks to two interconnected factors:
1.      Observing  others: Community  contact  within  the  coetus  fosters
competition and learning through imitation. Human beings copy the successes
of their neighbors.
2.     Mental optimization: The design process  (cogitation) allows  for
projecting variations and improvements on what is observed, which generates a
constant morphological evolution (efficiebant in dies meliora genera casarum),
transforming the rough branch hut into a functional architectural typology.
2.1.2  Vitruvius  defines the  origin of  architecture  as stemming from a
concatenation of anatomical determinants and dynamics of social emulation.
Thanks to the evolutionary advantages of bipedalism (non proni sed erecti) and
the consequent motor versatility of the hands (manibus et articulis), primitive
humans managed to overcome the stage of gathering and become agents of
transformation of matter. The text places the genesis of building in zoological
imitation — particularly of swallows' nests through the amalgamation of mud
and reeds —, a primordial process that was accelerated thanks to social
coexistence, where  the  visual exchange  of  technical  solutions and  the
accumulation  of  individual  cognitive  experiences drove  the  progressive
improvement of the hut (meliora genera casarum) as a basic typology of human
habitat (Vitruvius, De architectura 2.1.2).

•      Competition as a catalyst: Vitruvius emphasizes that progress is not
only individual, but social; by competing with each other (exercentes ingenia
certationibus), individuals constantly raised their standards of constructive
quality.

  •    Material evolution:
◦     Framework system: The first step was the use of vertical posts (furcis)
and horizontal support elements (virgulis) covered with clay.

◦      Earth walls: The second stage consisted of the use of blocks or lumps
of dry clay (luteas glaebas).

the invention of the pitched roof (proclinatis tectis). When flat roofs failed
during the winter, humans understood the need to create slopes (fastigia) to
channel water away, thus preventing seepage and protecting the mud structure
from erosion.

Critical and Technical Analysis
•      Ethnography as evidence: Vitruvius uses the observation of "
barbarian " peoples (Gauls, Iberians, Colchians) not as a curiosity, but as


                           389

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II

empirical evidence for his evolutionary theory. By observing that these cultures
still used thatched roofs or log structures, he confirms that these were the
formative stages of human architecture.
•      Colchid technique: The description details a construction system
using interlocking logs  (log cabin construction). Whole trees are placed
horizontally and locked at the corners to form a self-supporting structure.
•      Space management: The use of schidiae (wood chips or wedges) and
mud to fill the gaps (intervalla) between cylindrical logs is a necessary technical
solution to guarantee thermal insulation and watertightness of the walls.
•      Evolution of the roof: The description of the roof describes a
truncated pyramidal covering (metas). By setting back the beams (gradatim
contrahentes), they manage to create a dome or sloping roof which, once sealed
with mud and foliage, acquires a "testudina-like" shape (similar to the shape of a
turtle's shell), characteristic of barbarian defensive or storage constructions.

•      tumulos naturales... distinguentes: Vitruvius describes here the
creation of semi-buried or excavated dwellings in mounds (tumuli), a logical
adaptation to climates where the lack of wood prevents the construction of
elevated structures.
•       metas: The term refers to the conical or pyramidal shape, similar to a
circus goal, which allows for an optimal distribution of the earth load on the
wooden structure.

•        Massiliae... subacta cum paleis terra: Vitruvius cites Marseille as a

•      Romuli casa: The hut of Romulus (casa Romuli) was a sacred site in

to commemorate the austere foundation of the city in contrast to the opulence
of the imperial era.

Critical Apparatus and Notes
•         tritiores manus: The term tritiores (from terere, to rub or wear down)
refers to the constant practice that softens or refines movements. It refers to the
transition from brute physical effort to refined manual technique.
•       studiosiores fabros: Vitruvius marks the birth of the specialized craft.
The architect or builder is no longer just any individual, but one who, through
study and practice (studiosiores), elevates his activity to the level of a recognized
profession.
•       cogitationibus et consiliis: Vitruvius establishes here a hierarchical
distinction between animal nature (endowed with senses) and human nature
(endowed with reflective reason and strategic planning).
•      mansuetam humanitatem: This term defines the  final stage of
civilization: humanitas as a state of gentleness (mansueta) that arises from social
life, the exchange of knowledge and the creation of a built environment.

Critical Apparatus and Notes

rural to the urban requires a new scale of thought: the architect no longer
improvises, but projects (prospicientes) with a long-term goal.
•      Foundation domes:  Vitruvius marks  a  fundamental  technical
milestone: the introduction of foundations (fundata). Civilized architecture

complex (use of stone and brick).
•       e vagantibus iudiciis... ad certas symmetriarum rationes: This is
the core of Vitruvian philosophy: the transition from empirical and uncertain

maturity when it is codified in mathematical rules and exact proportions.
•       voluptatibus  elegantiam  vitae:  Vitruvius  concludes  that  the
ultimate goal of construction technique  is human well-being  (voluptas),
elevating the mere need for shelter to the category of elegance and vital
refinement.
•       Virtues: In Vitruvian lexicon, the virtues of materials are not moral

combinations of their elements are moderated, so that they are not obscure, but

Critical Apparatus and Notes
•       Constitutio: In this context, it refers to the logical and organizational
structure of the treatise.
•      Principiorum coetu. Vitruvius here uses the vocabulary of the
physical principles that he immediately develops by summarizing several Greek
doctrines. Coetus and congressus denote the coming together or combination of
those principles. The passage should not be reduced to a single atomist doctrine,
since  the  chapter  juxtaposes  explanations  from  Thales,  Heraclitus,
Democritus/Epicurus and the Pythagorean tradition.
•       Praeceptis physicorum: Vitruvius demands for architecture the
scientific rigor of ancient physics. It is not enough to know the use of materials,
but  it  is essential to demonstrate their underlying causes through "subtle
reasoning" (subtilibus rationibus).
•      Methodology: The author emphasizes that his exposition must be
"clear to the readers" (perspicua legentibus), avoiding academic obscurity in favor
of a rational explanation of the physical properties.
Comparative critical apparatus — II.1. The account of fire, human assembly,
language and the first buildings is retained as a Vitruvian genealogy, although it
admits comparison with Lucretius and other ancient  traditions. Densae
crebritatibus is an awkward construction that should not be regularized merely
for elegance. Nutu and sermones mark the transition from gesture and voice to
shared  communication;  tritiores  manus,  studiosiores  fabri  and  certas
symmetriarum rationes articulate practice, specialization and proportional
rules.

different peoples are literary ethnographic testimonies, not a demonstrated
archaeological  sequence.  Their  argumentative  function   is  to  show

Architectural and hermeneutic note — The origins of building. Vitruvius
connects primitive architecture with observation and imitation: branches,
forked supports, mud, reeds, trunks and roofs precede progressively regularized
forms. Comparison with vernacular techniques may be illustrative, but does not
prove a universal historical sequence.

Academic translation

evenly. Those prepared during the solstice are defective because, when the sun
violently bakes their outer layer, it makes them appear dry, even though the
interior is not. Then, as they contract during the final drying, the already dry
crust breaks, leaving the bricks cracked and weakened. They are much more
useful, however, if they have been made two years in advance, since they cannot
dry completely before then. Therefore, if they are used when they are still fresh

bricks settle and cannot maintain the same height as the coating; as they move
due to contraction, they do not adhere to it and separate from their joint." Thus,
the facing, being separated from the structure, cannot support itself due to its
thinness and cracks, deteriorating the walls themselves as they settle unevenly.

structures if they are thoroughly dried, have been manufactured five years prior,
and have the approval of the magistrate.

Critical Apparatus and Notes
•      Ducendi (to be made): Vitruvius uses the verb ducere (to lead/form)
to refer to the technical process of molding clay.
•       Solstice (solstitium): Excessive summer heat is discouraged because it
causes uneven drying: the outer surface becomes brittle while the core retains
moisture, which generates cracks (rimosi) as the material contracts.
•      Settlement  (sidentes): The  author  warns  about  the  physical
contraction of fresh brick. If the facing (tectorio) hardens on damp bricks, the
subsequent shrinkage of these bricks causes a separation between the supporting
structure and the finishing layer, resulting in cracks.
•     The Utica model  (Uticenses):  Vitruvius  praises  the  technical
legislation of the city of Utica (in North Africa), which established a mandatory
five-year  drying  period and  quality  control  supervised by  magistrates,
guaranteeing structural safety.

The reason why lime, on receiving water and sand, strengthens masonry appears
to be that stones, like other bodies, are compounded from the elements. Those
containing more air are soft; those containing more water are pliant through
moisture; those containing more earth are hard; those containing more fire are
more brittle. If such stones, before firing, are finely crushed, mixed with sand
and put into masonry, they do not set and cannot hold it together. When placed
in a kiln and seized by the violent heat of the fire, however, they lose the strength
of their original solidity: their powers are burned out and exhausted, leaving
open pores and voids.

Editorial note. — Chapter 6 is the most celebrated passage on Roman concrete.
Vitruvius describes the powder (pulvis) of the country round Baiae and the
slopes of Vesuvius — pozzolana, a volcanic ash — which, mixed with lime and
rubble, sets into a mass so hard that it withstands not only the weather but the
waves of the sea, hardening even under water. He accounts for its action by the
latent fire, sulphur and alum of the volcanic ground. This hydraulic mortar
(with the pulvis Puteolanus of 5.12) is the technical foundation of the great
vaulted and maritime architecture of imperial Rome, and modern chemistry has
confirmed the reactive volcanic silica that he intuited. Cf. Pliny, Naturalis
historia 35.166, and the Glossarium, s.v. pulvis Puteolanus.
Comparative critical apparatus — II.6. Pulvis denotes the Campanian volcanic
material subsequently called pozzolana. Vitruvius states that it can acquire
solidity under water when mixed with lime and caementa; his ancient causal
explanation is kept separate from contemporary mineralogy.

Archaeological note —  II.8, masonry bonds. Vitruvius contrasts two
arrangements of wall facing: reticulatum, customary in his time, and the older
incertum. He considers the former more elegant (venustius), though more
prone to cracking because of the arrangement of beds and joints; the latter he
judges  less handsome but stronger. Vitruvian terminology has  decisively
influenced modern archaeological nomenclature, although that classification
should not be projected without qualification on to every phase of Roman
construction. Opus incertum uses irregular pieces visible in the facing; opus
reticulatum arranges cubilia with their faces forming a diagonal network. Later
or combined techniques, such as brick facings and so-called opus mixtum,
belong to developments beyond the passage’s immediate description. Vitruvius
subsequently compares  these  fabrics with Greek  procedures,  including
emplekton and the use of transverse elements (διάτονοι).
1. There are two kinds of masonry facing: the reticulatum now commonly used,
and the older kind called incertum. The reticulatum is more attractive but is
liable to crack because its bedding surfaces and joints are discontinuous in every
direction. In the incertum, irregular rubble stones rest upon and overlap one
another, producing masonry that  is less handsome but stronger than the
reticulatum.
      The  types  of  masonry  (structurae)  are  these:  the  reticulated
(reticulatum), which everyone uses now, and the ancient one, which is called
incertum. Of these, the most elegant is the reticulated, but it is prone to cracking
because its beds and joints settle in all directions. In contrast, the uncertain, with
its stones (camenta) interlocked course upon course, although less showy, is
more solid than the reticulated.

Born at Mylasa, he observed that Halicarnassus offered natural defenses, a

Editorial note. — Chapter 8 is the principal ancient source on wall construction.
Vitruvius contrasts the fashionable reticulate facing (opus reticulatum), elegant
but prone to cracking, with the older random facing (opus incertum), less
handsome but sounder; both, set in lime-and-sand mortar over a rubble core,
are weakened if the core is coarse. He commends Greek practice: the squared,
mortarless ashlar laid as isodomon (courses of equal height) or pseudisodomon
(unequal courses), and the emplekton (ἔμπλεκτον), faced on both sides with
bonding-stones (diatoni) tying the two leaves together — the weakness of the
Roman two-leaf wall being precisely the want of such  ties. The terms

reticulatum, incertum, isodomon, pseudisodomon and emplekton are retained,

Comparative  critical apparatus —  II.8. The terminological core requires
retaining opus reticulatum, opus incertum, isodomum, pseudisodomum and
ἔμπλεκτον as technical terms. In II.8.5–7 the critical text also transmits διατόνους
for the pieces that pass through and bond the wall’s thickness. Isodomum
denotes courses of equal height; pseudisodomum, unequal courses. Greek
ἔμπλεκτον is explained by the relation between facings, lengthwise pieces and
bonding through the thickness, not simply as “infill”.
Architectural  note —  II.8.  Vitruvius compares masonry  systems  with
simultaneous attention to appearance,  joints, beds, moisture absorption,
transverse bonding and speed of execution. A constructional reading must
preserve the distinctions between facing, core, cubilia, coagmenta and diatonoi;
reducing everything to modern categories of “masonry” or “concrete” erases
essential distinctions in the passage.
Textual and constructional note — II.8. The description of bonds distinguishes
transmitted terminology from graphic reconstruction. Ἰσόδομον, ψευδισόδομον,
ἔμπλεκτον and διάτονοι are retained as Greek technical terms accompanied by a
functional explanation. Equivalence with modern archaeological categories is
offered only where secure and is not used to alter the Latin.
Synthesis for architects —  II.8. The central problem  is not merely the
appearance of the facing: Vitruvius considers cubilia, coagmenta, continuity of
joints, transverse ties and the behavior of the core. The comparative apparatus
avoids equating opus reticulatum and incertum without qualification with any
visually similar modern construction.

building materials, the proportions of the natural elements that compose them,
and the virtues and defects of each, so that these may not be unknown to those

1.     Aedium   compositio   constat   ex   symmetria,   cuius   rationem

totiusque commodulatio, ex qua ratio efficitur symmetriarum. namque non
potest aedis ulla sine symmetria atque proportione rationem habere compositionis,
nisi uti hominis bene figurati <> membrorum habuerit exactam rationem.
The composition of temples depends on symmetria, whose principles architects
must observe with the greatest care. Symmetria arises from proportion, which
the Greeks call analogia (ἀναλογία). Proportion is the commensuration of the
members and the whole of a work with a determined part as their common
measure; from it the system of commensurability is established. No temple can
have a coherent composition without symmetria and proportion, unless its
members stand in an exact relationship comparable to that of a well-formed
human body.

described by the outstretched limbs; comparison with the square, by contrast,
proceeds from the equality of height and arm-span.
Architectural and philological note — Homo bene figuratus. The human body
serves as an analogy of commensurability: each member has a ratio to the whole.
The text does not prescribe that temples should literally reproduce a human
figure, nor does it contain the modern expression “Vitruvian Man”. Graphic
reconstructions of circle and square belong to the history of reception and must
be labeled accordingly.

Editorial note. — Chapter 1 contains the most famous proposition of the whole
treatise: that the design of a temple rests on symmetria (commensurability), and
that the model for it is the proportion of the well-formed human body (homo
bene figuratus). Vitruvius lists the canonical ratios — the face a tenth of the
height, the head an eighth, the foot a sixth — and observes that a man lying with
limbs outstretched can be inscribed in both a circle (centered on the navel) and

by fraction: facies, palma, pes, cubitus, pectus and total height. Equality

maintained in accordance with what the text explicitly states. Any additional

Philological note — Symmetria, proportio and analogia. In this chapter,
“proportion” must not absorb symmetria. The functional distinction between
the relationship of a part, the commensurability of members and a common
ratio   is  preserved. The  Spanish  version  avoids  arbitrarily  alternating
“symmetry”, “proportion” and “modulation” when the Latin changes its term.
Comparative   critical  apparatus —   III.1.1–9.  Symmetria,  proportio,
commodulatio and ἀναλογία are not reduced to modern synonyms. Proportio
denotes  a  measurable  relationship  of  parts;  symmetria,  the  ordered
commensurability  of members with one another and with  the whole;
commodulatio emphasizes their common reference to a module. In III.1.3 the
transmitted text places the bodily circle’s center at the navel, whereas the relation
to the square is constructed from equality between height and arm-span. The
edition preserves the sequence of six and ten as an ancient history of number
and measure, without attributing to it a universal mathematical theory foreign
to the passage.

Archaeological note — III.2, temple types. Vitruvius classifies temples by
the arrangement of their columns: in antis (naos en parastasin), prostyle,
amphiprostyle,   peripteral,   pseudodipteral,   dipteral  and   hypaethral.
Archaeology illustrates each type: Vitruvius himself exemplifies the in antis
temple, with two columns between the antae, by the “Three Fortunes” near
Rome’s Colline Gate; the peripteral scheme, with six columns at the front and
eleven on each side, is that of the canonical Greek temple; the pseudodipteral
arrangement, octastyle with a single row where a double row could stand, is
exemplified by the temple of Diana at Magnesia, by Hermogenes of Alabanda,
and that of Apollo, by Menesthes; the dipteral, with its double colonnade, and
the hypaethral, decastyle and open to the sky, complete the sequence. The
pseudoperipteral type—columns engaged in the  cella wall to simulate a
peripteral arrangement, defined by Vitruvius in 4.8—was the most widespread
in the Roman world. Its best-preserved examples are the temple of Portunus in
the Forum Boarium, Ionic and dating to the late second century BC, and above
all the Maison Carrée at Nîmes, a Corinthian hexastyle prostyle temple of
around AD 2, the world’s best-preserved Roman temple.
      The principles of temples, on which the aspect of  their forms
depends, are these: first the in antis, which in Greek is called ναὸς ἐν παραστάσιν
(a temple between antae); then the prostyle, the amphiprostyle, the peripteral,
the pseudodipteral, the dipteral, and the hypaethral. Their configurations are
expressed by the following rules.

intercolumniorum et imae crassitudinis columnae spatium erit ab parietibus
circa ad extremos ordines columnarum. Huius exemplar Romae non est, sed
Magnesiae Dianae Hermogenis Alabandei et Apollinis a Menesthe facta.
      The pseudodipteral is arranged with eight columns at the front and
rear, and fifteen on each side including the corner columns. The cella walls stand
opposite the four central columns at the front and rear. A space of two
intercolumniations plus the lower column diameter thus lies between the walls
and the outer rows of columns all around. There is no example at Rome, but
there is the temple of Diana at Magnesia, the work of Hermogenes of Alabanda,
and that of Apollo, built by Menesthes.
Textual note — III.2.5–6. Krohn (1912, 63), followed by the authorial Spanish
edition, transposes sine postico before the examples beginning in porticu
Metelli; Rose (1899, 68) places it after Honoris et Virtutis. The different scope
is preserved in the adopted translation rather than silently settled by an
archaeological identification. In III.2.6 Krohn prints Hermogenis Alabandei,
identifying Hermogenes as Alabandean; Rose prints Hermogenis, Alabandis
etiam Apollinis, locating the temple of Apollo at Alabanda. The Spanish edition
follows Krohn. Menesthes  is the named architect of Apollo’s temple, not
Hermogenes. These are differences in editorial constitution and punctuation,
not newly collated manuscript readings.
7. dipteros autem octastylos et pronao et postico, sed circa aedem duplices habet
ordines columnarum, uti est aedis Quirini dorica et Ephesi Dianae ionica a
Chersiphrone constituta.

                           480

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III

      The dipteral is octastyle both in the pronaos and at the rear, but about
the temple it has double rows of columns—as is the temple of Quirinus, of the
Doric order, and that of Diana at Ephesus, of the Ionic order, built by
Chersiphron.

8. hypaethros vero decastylos est in pronao et postico. reliqua omnia eadem habet
quae dipteros, sed interiore parte columnas in altitudine duplices, remotas a
parietibus ad circumitionem ut porticus peristyliorum. medium autem sub divo
est sine tecto. Aditus valvarum ex utraque parte in pronao et postico. huius item
exemplar Romae non est, sed Athenis octastylos ex templo Olympio.
      The hypaethral temple is decastyle in the pronaos and at the rear. In
all other respects it resembles the dipteral, but inside it has columns in two tiers,
set away from the walls to provide a circuit like the porticoes of peristyles. The
center is open to the sky and unroofed. There are doorways at both ends, in the
pronaos and at the rear. There is no example at Rome; at Athens the text gives
the octastyle temple of Olympian Zeus.
Note — Bk. 3.2. The typology (in antis, prostyle, amphiprostyle, peripteral,
pseudodipteral, dipteral, hypaethral) derives from Greek theory. The examples
range from Rome—the three Fortunes, the Tiber Island, the portico of Metellus
—to Asia Minor, where Hermogenes of Priene (2nd c. BC) fixed the symmetries
of the Ionic pseudodipteral, a recurring authority in this book.
Archaeological note —  III.2. Vitruvius’s  classification here  rests on the
arrangement of the colonnade in relation to the cella and its fronts. The ancient
technical   terms—in    antis,    prostylos,   amphiprostylos,    peripteros,
pseudodipteros, dipteros and hypaethros—should be retained, and each form
explained from the text’s own definition, without projecting later archaeological
taxonomies on to  Vitruvius. Krohn includes  dipteros  in the sequence;
hypaethros is defined subsequently by its particular arrangement and must not
be confused with a supposed “dipteral-epipteral” type.
Note —   III.2.  Vitruvian  typology  distinguishes  in  antis,  prostylos,
amphiprostylos, peripteros, pseudodipteros, dipteros and hypaethros according
to the arrangement of columns and cella. The examples combine Roman and
Greek buildings. Modern archaeological identifications and the chronology of
each monument must remain separate from the typological definition provided
by the Latin text.

1. Species autem aedium sunt quinque, quarum ea sunt vocabula: pycnostylos, id
est crebris columnis, systylos paulo remissioribus, diastylos amplius quam oportet
inter se diductis, araeostylos spatiis intercolumniorum patentibus rare, eustylos
intervallorum iusta distributione.
       There are five kinds of temples, whose names are these: pycnostyle,
with closely set columns; systyle, with somewhat greater spacing; diastyle, with
the columns farther apart than is fitting; araeostyle, with wide and sparse
intercolumniations; and eustyle, with a just distribution of the intervals.
Vitruvius distinguishes five kinds of temples by their intercolumniations:
pycnostyle (pycnostylos), with very closely set columns; systyle (systylos), with
somewhat more generous intervals; diastyle (diastylos), with wider separations;
araeostyle (araeostylos), with columns farther apart than is fitting; and eustyle
(eustylos), characterized by a proportionate distribution of the intervals.
Textual note — III.3.1, 5 and 9. The two Spanish formulations in the Spanish
edition do not distribute the qualification “farther apart than is fitting” in the
same way. Its running Latin and first translation follow Krohn (1912, 64),
attaching amplius quam oportet inter se diductis to diastylos. Rose (1899, 69)
instead attaches rarius quam oportet inter se diductis to araeostylos; the Spanish
edition’s explanatory parallel follows this  latter distribution. The English
preserves both authorial paragraphs separately and records the difference, rather
than merging the two editorial constitutions. The varicae restored in III.3.5
follows Krohn (1912, 65), whose apparatus attributes the reading to Turnebus;
⟨improviso⟩ in III.3.9 is marked as Krohn’s supplement (1912, 66). Both belong
to the authorial Spanish edition’s adopted constitution and are not presented as
newly verified manuscript words.

2. ergo pycnostylos  est cuius intercolumnio unius  et dimidiatae columnae
crassitudo interponi potest, quemadmodum est divi Iulii et in Caesaris foro
Veneris et si quae aliae sic sunt compositae. item systylos est in qua duarum
columnarum  crassitudo  in  intercolumnio  poterit  conlocari,  et  spirarum
plinthides aeque magnae sint  ei spatio quod fuerit inter duas plinthides,
quemadmodum  est Fortunae Equestris ad theatrum lapideum reliquaeque
quae eisdem rationibus sunt compositae.

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III

      Thus the pycnostyle is that in whose intercolumniation the thickness
of one and a half columns can be inserted, as in the temple of the Divine Julius,
that of Venus in Caesar's forum, and any others composed in this way. The
systyle, in turn, is that in whose intercolumniation the thickness of two columns
can be placed, and in which the plinths of the bases are as large as the space that
lies between two plinths, as in the temple of Fortuna Equestris, near the stone
theater, and the rest composed on the same principles.

3. haec utraque genera vitiosum habent usum. matres enim familiarum cum
ad  supplicationem  gradibus  ascendunt,  non  possunt  per  intercolumnia
amplexae adire  nisi ordines  fecerint, item valvarum aspectus abstruditur
columnarum crebritate ipsaque signa obscurantur, item circa aedem propter
angustias inpediuntur ambulationes.
       Both these kinds have a faulty use. For the matrons, when they mount
the steps in supplication, cannot pass through the intercolumniations arm in
arm, but only in single file; moreover, the view of the doors is obstructed by the
crowding of the columns, and the statues themselves are darkened; and likewise,
owing to the narrowness, the walks around the temple are impeded.

4. diastyli autem haec erit compositio, cum trium columnarum crassitudinem
intercolumnio interponere possumus, tamquam est Apollinis et Dianae aedis.
haec dispositio hanc habet difficultatem quod epistylia propter intervallorum
magnitudinem franguntur.
      The arrangement of the diastyle will be this: when we can interpose in
the intercolumniation the thickness of three columns, as in the temple of Apollo
and Diana. This disposition has the drawback that the architraves break on
account of the great width of the intervals.

5. In araeostylis autem nec lapideis nec marmoreis epistyliis uti datur, sed
inponendae de materia trabes perpetuae. Et ipsarum aedium species sunt varicae,
barycephalae, humiles, latae, ornanturque signis fictilibus aut aereis inauratis
earum fastigia tuscanico more, uti est ad Circum Maximum Cereris et Herculis
Pompeiani, item Capitolii.
        In araeostyles it is not possible to use architraves of stone or marble;
instead, continuous timber beams must be laid on. The very aspect of such
temples is splayed, top-heavy, low and broad, and their pediments are adorned
with figures of terracotta or gilded bronze, in the Tuscan manner—as in the

                           484

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III

temple of Ceres near the Circus Maximus, that of Hercules Pompeianus, and
the Capitol.
In araeostyle temples, stone or marble architraves cannot be used: continuous
timber beams must be placed on the columns. According to Vitruvius, these
temples have a barycephala appearance—a visually heavy upper part—and are
low and broad. Their pediments are adorned in the Tuscan manner with figures
of terracotta or gilded bronze. He cites as examples the temple of Ceres beside
the Circus Maximus, that of Hercules Pompeianus and the Capitol.
Note — Bk. 3.3 (araeostyle). The araeostyle—low, broad, and 'top-heavy,'
with wooden architraves and terracotta or gilt-bronze ornament 'in the Tuscan
manner' (tuscanico more)—is associated in the passage with the Tuscan manner
of building; the Republican Capitol is its chief example. Cf. Vitr. IV.7, where
the Tuscan temple is set out in detail.
Note — III.3.5. The Latin adjective transliterated from Greek, barycephala,
here describes the formal effect of low, broad buildings with a visually heavy
roof or crowning element. The passage should not become a general definition
of the “archaic Etruscan temple”: Vitruvius establishes a formal connection
with tuscanico more and supplies concrete examples; the  historical and
archaeological category is later.

6. Reddenda nunc est eustyli ratio, quae maxime probabilis et ad usum et ad
speciem et ad firmitatem rationes habet explicatas. namque facienda sunt in
intervallis  spatia  duarum  columnarum   et  quartae  partis  columnae
crassitudinis, mediumque intercolumnium unum quod erit in fronte, alterum
quod  in  postico,  trium columnarum  crassitudine.  sic enim  habebit  et
figurationis aspectum venustum et aditus usum sine inpeditionibus et circa
cellam ambulatio auctoritatem.
          It now remains to set forth the method of the eustyle, which is the
most commendable and has the principles of use, appearance, and stability fully
worked out. For in the intervals there must be made spaces of two and a quarter
column-thicknesses, and a single central intercolumniation—one at the front
and one at the rear—of three column-thicknesses. For thus it will have at once a
graceful aspect in its figure, a convenient and unhindered approach, and a
dignity in the walk about the cella.


                           485

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III

7. huius autem rei ratio explicabitur sic. frons loci quae in aede constituta fuerit,
si tetrastylos facienda fuerit, dividatur in partes XI S praeter crepidines et
proiecturas spirarum, si sex erit columnarum, in partes XVIII. si octastylos
constituetur, dividatur in XXIV et semissem. item ex his partibus sive tetrastyli
sive hexastyli sive octastyli una pars sumatur eaque erit modulus. cuius moduli
unus erit crassitudinis columnarum. intercolumnia singula, praeter media,
modulorum duorum et moduli quartae partis. mediana in fronte et postico
singula ternûm modulorum. ipsarum columnarum altitudo modulorum VIIII
et dimidiae moduli partis. ita ex ea divisione intercolumnia altitudinesque
columnarum habebunt iustam rationem.
The method of this will be explained as follows. The front of the site laid out for
the temple, if it is to be tetrastyle, let it be divided into 11½ parts, excluding the
crepidines (steps or platform margins) and the projections of the column
bases; if it is of six columns, into 18 parts; if octastyle is to be set out, into 24½.
Then, from these parts—whether of a tetrastyle, a hexastyle, or an octastyle—let
one be taken, and that will be the module. The thickness of the columns will be
one module. The intercolumniations, except the central ones, will each be two
and a quarter modules; the central ones, at front and rear, three modules each.
The height of the columns themselves will be nine and a half modules. Thus, by
this division, the intercolumniations and the heights of the columns will keep a
just proportion.

8. huius exemplar Romae nullum habemus, sed in Asia Teo hexastylon Liberi
Patris. Eas autem symmetrias constituit Hermogenes, qui etiam primus invenit
octastylon pseudodipterive rationem. ex dipteri enim aedis symmetria distulit
interiores  ordines columnarum XXXIV eaque  ratione sumptus operasque
compendii fecit. is in medio ambulationi laxamentum egregie circa cellam fecit,
de aspectuque nihil inminuit sed sine desiderio supervacuorum conservavit
auctoritatem totius operis distributione.
      Of this we have no example at Rome, but in Asia the hexastyle of
Father Liber at Teos. These symmetries were established by Hermogenes, who
was also the first to devise the method of the octastyle pseudodipteral. For from
the symmetry of the dipteral temple he removed the inner rows of columns,
thirty-four in number, and by this means he saved expense and labor. In the
middle he made an admirable open ambulatory about the cella, and in no way


                           486

diminished the appearance; rather, without any want of the superfluous, he
preserved the dignity of the whole work in its distribution.
Note — Bk. 3.3. Of the five kinds of intercolumniation Vitruvius prefers the
eustyle, whose modular system (front divided into equal parts; column = 1
module; intercolumniations of 2¼ and 3 modules) he attributes to Hermogenes,
whom he also credits with inventing the octastyle pseudodipteral, saving thirty-
four columns over the dipteral.
Textual note — III.3.8. the Spanish edition’s running Latin and Krohn’s
printed text (1912, 66, line 4) give XXXIV, thirty-four; Rose’s printed text
(1899, 71, line 13) gives XXXVIII, thirty-eight. Krohn’s apparatus explicitly
records “xxxiv Phil: xxxviii x”, identifying thirty-four as the editorial reading
associated with Philander and distinguishing it from the reading labeled x. This
confirms the choice of thirty-four in the authorial base and corrects the Spanish
comparative note’s attribution of thirty-eight to the current Perseus text of
Krohn. Neither H nor Cotton  is independently assigned a reading here.
Hermogenes’s  association  with  the  pseudodipteral  scheme  belongs  to
Vitruvius’s own account.

9. Pteromatos enim ratio et columnarum circum aedem dispositio ideo  est
inventa,   ut   aspectus   propter   asperitatem  intercolumniorum   habeat
auctoritatem, praeterea,  si ex ⟨improviso⟩ imbrium aquae vis occupaverit et
intercluserit hominum multitudinem, ut habeat in aede circaque cellam cum
laxamento liberam moram. Haec autem ut explicantur in pseudodipteris
aedium dispositionibus! Quare videtur acuta magnaque sollertia effectus operum
Hermogenes   fecisse  reliquisseque   fontes,  unde   posteri  possent  haurire
disciplinarum rationes.
       For the principle of the pteroma and the arrangement of columns
about the temple was devised so that the appearance might have dignity through
the relief created by the intercolumniations, and further, that if a sudden
downpour of rain should overtake and shut in a throng of people, they might
have within the temple and about the cella an ample and free place to wait. All
this  is worked out thus in the arrangements of pseudodipteral temples.
Wherefore Hermogenes seems to have acted with keen and great sagacity in the
execution of his works, and to have left springs from which posterity might draw
the principles of the disciplines.

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III

10. Aedibus araeostylis columnae sic sunt faciendae uti crassitudines earum sint
partis octavae ad altitudines. item in diastylo dimetienda est altitudo columnae
in partes octo et dimidiam et unius partis columnae crassitudo conlocetur. in
systylo altitudo dividatur in novem et dimidiam partem et ex eis una ad
crassitudinem columnae detur. item in pycnostylo dividenda est altitudo in
⟨partes⟩ decem et eius una pars facienda est columnae crassitudo. eustyli autem
aedis columnae, uti systyli, in novem partes altitudo dividatur et dimidiam
partem et eius una pars constituatur in crassitudine imi scapi. ita habebitur pro
rata parte intercolumniorum ratio.
        In araeostyle temples the columns are to be made so that their
thickness is an eighth part of their height. Likewise in the diastyle, let the height
of the column be divided into eight and a half parts, and let the thickness of the
column be one part. In the systyle, let the height be divided into nine and a
half parts, and of these let one be given to the thickness of the column. Likewise
in the pycnostyle, the height is to be divided into ten, and one part of it made
the thickness of the column. In the eustyle temple, as in the systyle, let the height
be divided into nine and a half parts, and let one of them be fixed as the thickness
of the lower shaft. Thus the proportion will be had according to the kind of
intercolumniation.
In araeostyle temples the columns must be made with a diameter equal to one-
eighth of their height. In the diastyle, divide the column height into eight and a
half parts and give one part to the diameter. In the systyle, divide the height into
nine and a half parts and give one to the diameter. In the pycnostyle, divide the
height into ten and give one part to the column diameter. In the eustyle, as in
the systyle, divide the height into nine and a half parts and assign one part to the
diameter at the bottom of the shaft. The proportion will thus correspond to the
class of intercolumniation.

11. quemadmodum enim  crescunt  spatia  inter columnas,  proportionibus
adaugendae sunt crassitudines scaporum. namque si in araeostylo nona aut
decima pars crassitudinis  fuerit, tenuis  et  exilis apparebit, ideo quod per
latitudinem intercolumniorum aer consumit et inminuit aspectu scaporum
crassitudinem; contra vero pycnostylis, si octava pars crassitudinis fuerit, propter
crebritatem et angustias intercolumniorum tumidam et invenustam efficiet
speciem. itaque generis operis oportet persequi symmetrias. etiamque angulares


                           488

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III

columnae crassiores faciendae sunt ex sua diametro quinquagesima parte, quod
eae ab aere circumciduntur et graciliores videntur esse aspicientibus. ergo quod
oculus fallit, ratiocinatione est exaequandum.
       For as the spaces between the columns increase, the thicknesses of the
shafts must be enlarged in proportion. For if in the araeostyle the thickness were
a ninth or a tenth part, the column will appear thin and slender, because through
the width of the intercolumniations the air consumes and diminishes the
diameter of their thickness to the view. Contrariwise, in pycnostyles, if the
thickness were an eighth part, on account of the frequency and narrowness of
the intercolumniations it will produce a swollen and graceless appearance. One
must therefore pursue the symmetries proper to each kind of work. Moreover,
the corner columns are to be made thicker by a fiftieth part of their diameter,
because they are cut round by the air and appear more slender to those who
behold them. Therefore what the eye deceives must be redressed by calculation.
Note — Bk. 3.3 (optical corrections). Vitruvius states here a cardinal
principle of his aesthetics: 'what the eye deceives must be redressed by
calculation' (quod oculus fallit ratiocinatione est exaequandum). From it derive
the thickening of the corner columns by 1/50 of their diameter and the
adjustment of thickness according to the width of the intercolumniation.
Note —  III.3.11. Quod  oculus  fallit,  ratiocinatione  est exaequandum
formulates Vitruvius’s principle of visual compensation with particular clarity:
perception may  require measurable adjustments  to  abstract  geometrical
regularity. Optical correction or compensation is the appropriate description,
without attributing to the passage a modern theory of perception that it does
not develop.

12. contracturae autem in summis columnarum hypotracheliis ita faciendae
videntur uti si columna sit ab minimo ad pedes quinos denos, ima crassitudo
dividatur in partes sex et earum partium quinque summa constituatur. item
quae erit ab quindecim pedibus ad pedes viginti, scapus imus in partes sex et
semissem dividatur earumque partium quinque et semisse superior crassitudo
columnae fiat. item quae erunt a pedibus viginti ad pedes triginta, scapus imus
dividatur in partes septem earumque sex summa contractura perficiatur. quae
autem ab triginta pedibus ad quadraginta alta erit, ima dividatur in partes
septem et dimidiam, ex his sex et dimidiam in summo habeat contracturae

                           489

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III

rationem. quae  erunt ab  quadraginta  pedibus ad  quinquaginta,  item
dividendae sunt in octo partes et earum septem in summo scapo sub capitulo
contrahantur. item si quae altiores erunt, eadem ratione pro rata constituantur
contracturae.
The diminution at the tops of columns, in the hypotrachelia, should be made as
follows. For a column up to fifteen feet high, divide the lower diameter into six
parts and make the upper diameter five of them. For a column from fifteen to
twenty feet, divide the lower shaft into six and a half parts and make the upper
diameter five and a half. For columns from twenty to thirty feet, divide the lower
shaft into seven parts and complete the upper diminution with six. For a column
from thirty to forty feet high, divide the lower diameter into seven and a half
parts and give the top six and a half. For columns from forty to fifty feet, divide
the lower diameter into eight parts and diminish the top of the shaft, below the
capital, to seven. For taller columns, establish the diminution proportionally by
the same principle.
The diminution of the diameter at the upper hypotrachelium is determined by
the column’s height. For a column up to fifteen feet, divide the lower diameter
into six parts and give the upper diameter five. Between fifteen and twenty feet,
divide it into six and a half and give the upper diameter five and a half. Between
twenty and thirty feet, divide it into seven and give the top six. Between thirty
and forty feet, divide it into seven and a half and give the top six and a half.
Between forty and fifty feet, divide it into eight and give the top seven. For
greater heights, establish the diminution proportionally by the same principle.
      The contractions at the tops of the columns, at the necks, are to be
made thus: if the column is up to fifteen feet, let the lower thickness be divided
into six parts, and let the top be made of five of them. Likewise for one from
fifteen feet to twenty, let the lower shaft be divided into six and a half parts, and
let the upper thickness of the column be made of five and a half. Likewise for
one from twenty to thirty feet, let the lower shaft be divided into seven parts,
and let the contraction at the top be completed with six of them. One that is
from thirty to forty feet high, let the lower part be divided into seven and a half
parts, and of these let it have six and a half at the top by the rule of contraction.
Those from forty to fifty feet are likewise to be divided into eight parts, and

seven of them contracted at the top of the shaft beneath the capital. Likewise, if
any are higher, let their contractions be fixed proportionally by the same rule.

13.  haec autem  propter  altitudinis  intervallum,  scandentis  oculi  species,
adiciuntur crassitudinibus temperaturae. venustates enim persequitur visus,
cuius si non blandimur voluptati proportione et modulorum adiectionibus, uti
quod fallitur temperatione adaugeatur, vastus et invenustus conspicientibus
remittetur aspectus. de adiectione quae adicitur in mediis columnis, quae apud
Graecos  ἔντασις  appellatur,  in  extremo  libro  erit forma  et  ratio  eius
quemadmodum mollis et conveniens efficiatur subscripta.
       These compensating adjustments are added to the thicknesses on
account of the interval of height, as the eye ascends. For sight pursues beauty,
and if we do not flatter its pleasure by proportion and by additions of modules—
so that what deceives may be augmented by compensation—the aspect will be
rendered coarse and graceless to beholders. As for the addition made in the
middle of the columns, which among the Greeks is called entasis (ἔντασις), at the
end of the book its form and method will be set down, showing how it is made
soft and fitting.
Comparative note — Bk. 3.3.13 (entasis). The entasis (ἔντασις)—the
slight swelling or adiectio of the shaft that corrects the optical illusion
of concavity—is, with the contractions and the inclination of the
members, one of the system's optical «temperings». Vitruvius defers its
drawing to a plate «at the end of the book» (in extremo libro), lost in
the manuscript tradition, which has made the exact profile an open
problem since the Renaissance (Fra Giocondo, Alberti, the practice of the
curves). The editions reflect this: Rose (Teubner, 1899) fixes the text
without restoring the figure; Granger (Loeb, 1931) renders adiectio as

shaft’s profile in its middle region. The surviving text refers to a forma et ratio at
the end of the book; the loss or incomplete transmission of the figures prevents
turning that reference into a single geometrical reconstruction. The edition
therefore retains the Greek term and distinguishes textual testimony from the
various reconstructions proposed since the Renaissance.
Technical note — Rhythm and module. The eustyle is not merely the “ideal
type”: Vitruvius presents it as a solution balancing usus, species and firmitas
through ordinary intercolumniations of two and a quarter diameters and a
wider   axial   intercolumniation.  A   comparative   table  must  show
intercolumniation, diameter-to-height ratio and examples separately, avoiding
confusion between measurements expressed in diameters and Roman feet.
Metrological note — Doron. Vitruvius explains doron by reference to the palm
and relates pentadoron/tetradoron to five/four palms. Any modern metric
equivalent is given as an approximation dependent on the standard adopted; the
ancient dimensions retain priority in the text.

semilateria is interpreted as a strategy for bonding facings and joints. Modern
explanation of the bond is kept separate from Vitruvius’s exact words and does
not turn a reasonable reconstruction into a textual reading.

araeostylos and eustylos depend on numerical relationships between diameter,
height and intercolumniation. Each fraction must be retained in ancient
notation in the base commentary before conversion to a decimal in auxiliary
tables.

thickening of corner columns are presented as devices described by Vitruvius.
No universal formula is attributed to these adjustments where the text refers to
a figure or leaves variables dependent on scale.

Krohn and with the Budé edition of Book III established, translated and
annotated by Pierre Gros. Pycnostylos, systylos, diastylos, araeostylos and

inwards at a distance of one and a half parts. Divide these lines so that four and
a half parts remain beneath the abacus. At the point separating those four and a
half parts from the remaining three and a half, establish the center of the eye

ARGUMENTUM LIBRI IV — On the orders: the origin of the Corinthian capital
(Callimachus), the rules of the Doric order and of the triglyphs and metopes, the
arrangement of temples according to their orientation, the classes of temples
according to their plan and the altars of the gods.

Notice. — Book IV completes the orders. It gives the aetiology of the three genera
— the Doric drawn from the male body, the Ionic from the matronly, the
Corinthian capital invented by Callimachus from an acanthus grown about a
votive basket — and the rules of the Doric, with the famous problem of the corner
triglyph. It then treats the parts of temples (cellae, doorways, the Tuscan and
round temples) and closes with the orientation of altars. With Book III it forms
the most influential ancient account of the classical orders.

There are also, set upon these same columns, kinds of capitals named by various
terms, whose properties of symmetry we cannot set out, nor assign them to
any other kind of column; but we see that their very names are borrowed and
adapted from the Corinthian, the cushioned (Ionic) and the Doric, whose
symmetries have been carried over into the refinement of new carvings.
Editorial note. — Chapter 1 gives the famous account of the origin of the orders
and, in particular, the aetiology of the Corinthian capital. Vitruvius reads the
orders anthropomorphically: the Doric drawn from the proportions of a man’s
body (at  first  six, later seven diameters high), the Ionic from a matron’s
slenderness — its volutes for the hair, its flutes for the folds of the robe — and
the Corinthian from the slight grace of a maiden. The capital itself he ascribes
to Callimachus, nicknamed by the Athenians κατατηξίτεχνος (“the refiner of his
art”), who, passing the grave of a Corinthian maiden, saw an acanthus grown
about a votive basket weighted by a roof-tile, its leaves curling into volutes, and
made of it the new capital. The tale is legend, not history; but it embodies the
Vitruvian principle that architectural form is an imitation of nature (cf. 2.1 and
4.2 on the timber origins of the stone members).
Critical and historical note — IV.1. The Corinthian column shares the Ionic
column’s proportions except for its capital; its upper members may follow
Doric or Ionic arrangements. A  rigid modern definition of a complete
Corinthian order should therefore not be imposed on the passage. Dorus, Ion,
the masculine and feminine analogies, and the story of the maiden’s basket and
acanthus belong  to  Vitruvius’s  aetiological  account. Prima  inventio …
memoratur presents the Callimachus story as a tradition of invention rather
than independently demonstrated biography.

Chapter 2

1.     Quoniam autem de generibus columnarum origines et inventiones supra
sunt scriptae, non alienum mihi videtur isdem rationibus de ornamentis eorum
quemadmodum sunt prognata et quibus principiis et originibus inventa dicere.
in aedificiis omnibus insuper conlocatur materiatio variis vocabulis nominata. ea
autem uti in nominationibus, ita in re varias habet utilitates. trabes enim supra
columnas et parastaticas et antas ponuntur, in contignationibus tigna et axes. sub
tectis, si maiora spatia sunt, et transtra et capreoli, si commoda, columen et
cantherii  prominentes ad extremam  suggrundationem.  supra  cantherios
templa,  deinde  insuper  sub  tegulas  asseres  ita  prominentes  uti  parietes
proiecturis eorum tegantur.
But since the origins and inventions of the kinds of columns have been set out
above, it does not seem out of place to treat in the same way of their ornaments:
how they arose and from what principles and origins they derive. In every
building there is set, above, a framework of timber called by various names; and
this framework, just as it varies in its names, so too it varies in its uses. For the
beams (trabes) rest upon the columns, the pilasters (parastaticae) and the antae;
in the floor-framing are placed the joists (tigna) and boards; under the roofs,
where the spans are larger, the cross-beams (transtra) and the braces (capreoli);
where they are moderate, the ridge-beam (columen) and the rafters (cantherii)
that project to the edge of the eaves (suggrundatio); over the rafters, the purlins
(templa); and then, above, beneath the tiles, the laths (asseres) projecting so that
the walls are covered by their overhang.

Thus each thing keeps its own place, kind, and order. Hence, taking their model
from timber carpentry, the craftsmen imitated in their carvings—in the stone
and marble construction of temples—the arrangement of those members, and
judged that such discoveries should be followed. For the ancient carpenters,
building in a certain place, once they had set the beams (tigna) projecting from
the inner walls out to the outermost parts, raised their structure between the
beams and, above, adorned the cornices and pediments with carpentry of more
graceful aspect; then they cut back the projections of the beams, as far as they
jutted out, to the line and the vertical of the walls. And since that aspect seemed

small tablets shaped as triglyphs are now made, and painted them with blue wax,

imitating the divisions of the beams, they began to have in Doric works the
arrangement of triglyphs and, between beam and beam, the metopes.

those between the triglyphs—are called metopes. For the Greeks call the sockets

Comparative note — Bk. 4.2 (structural truth). Here Vitruvius states one
of  the most  influential  doctrines  of  architectural  theory:  stone
ornaments  are  the  translation—petrification—of  timber  roofing
(triglyphs from beam-ends, mutules from rafters, dentils from laths), so
that they must not represent what cannot exist in constructional reality
(quod non potest in veritate fieri… non… certam rationem habere).
Hence his rejection of dentils beneath mutules. The editions fix the
passage without major divergence (Rose, Teubner 1899; Budé, dir.
Gros); Rowland and Howe (Cambridge, 1999) stress its scope as a
principle of «constructional truth». [Historical-architectural note] It is
the ancient root of modern structural rationalism: Laugier's «primitive
hut» (Essai sur l'architecture, 1753), Viollet-le-Duc's rationalism, and, in
the  twentieth  century,  «truth  to  materials» and «form  follows
function». Cf. the note on the angular triglyph (4.3.1–2).

And just as in the Doric the principle of triglyphs and mutules was found, so in
the Ionic the disposition of the dentils has its own basis in the works; and just as
the mutules reproduce the image of the projections of the rafters, so in the Ionic
the dentils imitate the projections of the laths (asseres). For this reason, in Greek
works no one sets dentils beneath mutules, since laths cannot lie beneath rafters.
So what in reality must be set above the rafters and the purlin, if in the images it
is placed below, will give the work a faulty design. The ancients, moreover, did
not approve or establish the making of ⟨mutules or⟩ dentils on the pediments,
but only plain cornices, because neither the rafters nor the laths are distributed
against the fronts of the pediments, nor can they project, but are set sloping
towards the drip. Thus, what cannot be done in reality, they judged could have
no sound design when done in the images.

Critical and architectural note — IV.2. The sequence tigna–triglyphi, cantherii
–mutuli and asseres–denticuli explains stone ornament through an ancient
theory of translation from timber construction. Opas, tignorum cubicula,
intertignium and metopa form a technical chain which must not be reduced to
generic decoration. Vitruvius explicitly rejects the explanation of triglyphs as
images of windows. His relation between veritas and imago  is historically
influential, but neither  its aetiology nor his proposed Greek derivations
independently  prove  the  archaeological  origin  of  every member. The
supplement ⟨met⟩oparum retains its editorial status.

1.      Nonnulli antiqui architecti negaverunt dorico genere aedes sacras

itaque negavit Arcesius, item Pytheos, non minus Hermogenes. nam is cum
paratam  habuisset marmoris copiam  in  doricae  aedis  perfectionem, <>

Critical note — Bk. 4.3.1–2. The 'angular triglyph conflict' is the chief
objection to the Doric in temples: the triglyph must fall at once over the
column's axis and at the corner of the frieze—incompatible demands that force
either the narrowing of the end intercolumniation or the distortion of the
metope. Hence Arcesius, Pytheos, and Hermogenes rejected  it. Vitruvius
nonetheless sets out the corrected system. It is one of the classic problems of
Greek architecture.
      Some ancient architects denied that sacred buildings should be built
in the Doric style, because they created false and inappropriate symmetries. And
so Arcesius denied it, Pythius as well, and Hermogenes no less. For when he had
prepared a supply of marble for the completion of the Doric building, he
changed  it from the same supply and made  it Ionic for the Free Father.

Explanatory note — Bk. 4.3 (the angular-triglyph problem). This is one
of the most famous passages in the treatise. Vitruvius sets out the structural
contradiction of the Doric order: the rule requires each triglyph to be centered
on the axis of its column and every metope to be square; yet at the corners the
triglyph must occupy the end of the frieze, so that the adjoining metope
becomes wider —by half a triglyph's width— and ceases to be square. The two
ancient remedies —widening the corner metope or contracting the outermost
intercolumniation— Vitruvius calls mendosum, 'faulty.' For this awkwardness,
he says, the ancients avoided the Doric order in temples; and he recalls that
Hermogenes, having already prepared the marble for a Doric temple, converted
it into an Ionic one dedicated to Father Bacchus (Liber Pater). The Roman
solution —leaving a half-metope at the corner— allowed columns and triglyphs
to be aligned once more. Collation confirms the transmitted Latin (namque
necesse est triglyphos constitui contra medios tetrantes columnarum… est
mendosum), with no variant affecting the sense.
Comparative note — Bk. 4.3 (angular triglyph). On the angular-triglyph
problem, Gros's Budé (1992) devotes an extended commentary to the 'errors'
that exegetes charge against Vitruvius, seeking to understand the logic of his
choices rather than to correct them, and sets the passage within Vitruvius's
polemic against the partisans of the Ionic order. Granger (Loeb) renders
mendosum literally; Rowland and Howe explain the Roman half-metope
solution with diagrams; Corso-Romano detail the terminology of tetrantes and
metopae. This edition keeps the transmitted Latin (namque necesse est… est
mendosum) unemended and translates in its own voice. The testimony of H
and of the codices collated by Gros offers no variant here that alters the sense:
the difficulty is doctrinal, not textual.

Editorial note. — Chapter 3 sets out the Doric order, which, Vitruvius reports,
some earlier architects had judged unfit for temples on account of its “faulty”
symmetries. The difficulty  is the celebrated corner-triglyph problem: each
triglyph must stand over the axis of its column, yet the frieze must also close
with a triglyph at the angle — two demands that cannot both be met without
contracting the end intercolumniation or widening the corner metopes.

Vitruvius gives the rules (the module system, the triglyph divided into six parts,
the half-metope at the corner) by which the conflict is managed; it would
exercise theorists from the Hellenistic age to the Renaissance. The Doric shaft is
fluted with twenty flutes, and the whole order, like the Ionic dentils, is read as
the stone image of an earlier timber construction (cf. 4.2).
Critical and metrological note — IV.3. The Doric difficulty concerns the
distribution of triglyphs, metopes and intercolumniations: the corner triglyph,
column axis and square metope cannot all be reconciled without adjustment.
Femur and μηρός here denote the vertical bands of the triglyph; a problematic
form such as femina must not yield an incoherent translation as ‘women’.
Modulus, tetrantes, hemitriglyphium and the series XIX S / XXIX S remain
ancient dimensional expressions. The twenty flutes and the arrangement of
guttae require control against the particular reconstruction, rather than decimal
normalization in the Latin.

ARGUMENTUM LIBRI V — ON public buildings: the forum and the basilica,
the treasury, the curia and the prison; the Greek and Latin theater, its acoustics
and the resonant bronze  vessels; musical  scales according  to the theory of
Aristoxenus; the porticoes, the palaestras, the ports and the shipyards.

Notice. — Book V concerns the public buildings of the forum. It
describes the forum and basilica — including the one Vitruvius himself
built at Fanum Fortunae, his only documented work — the treasury,
prison and senate-house, then the theater, with its harmonic theory and
the bronze sounding-vessels (echea) tuned to the Greek genera. Baths, the
palaestra and gymnasium, and harbors with their underwater concrete
complete the book. It  is a primary source for Roman urbanism,
acoustics and hydraulic engineering.

forum through dimensional correspondence. The curia’s height depends on

dispersal  of  the  voice. Modern  concepts  of  reflection,  absorption  or
reverberation may assist comparison, but are not quantities measured in the

pervenire.  et ad summam ita  est gubernandum uti linea cum ad imum
gradum et ad summum extenta fuerit, omnia cacumina graduum angulosque
tangat. ita vox non inpedietur.
      The praecinctiones (belts) should be made in proportion to the height
of the theaters, and no higher than the width of the passage of the praecinctio;
for if they were too high, they would drive the voice upward and would not let
the endings of words reach with clarity the ears of those seated above the
praecinctiones. In sum, it must be so governed that, when a line is drawn from
the lowest step to the highest, it touches all the summits and angles of the steps:
thus the voice will not be hindered.

connect the upper and lower ones, but to make them continuous and direct
from  all  areas without any  obstacles,  so  that when  people  leave  the
performances, they should not be cramped, but have separate exits from all areas
without obstruction. Care must also be taken to ensure that  it  is not a
soundproof space, but that the voice can travel through it as clearly as possible.

lingering.

through the canonical method of mathematics and music, that whatever voice

Critical note — V.3. The theater’s healthy site, avoidance of southern exposure
and cavea slope belong to Vitruvius’s environmental and medical framework.

avoid obstructions that impair intelligibility. A modern account of waves or the
acoustic field remains commentary rather than a replacement for his ancient

Harmonic theory is a difficult and obscure branch of learning, especially for
those unfamiliar with Greek. To explain it, we must use Greek terms, since some
have no Latin equivalents. I shall therefore interpret the writings of Aristoxenus
as clearly as I can and set out his diagram and the limits of the notes, so that
attentive readers may understand them more readily.

2. vox enim mutationibus cum flectitur alias fit acuta alias gravis, duobusque
modis movetur,  e quibus unus  effectus habet continuatos,  alter  distantes.
continuata vox neque in finitionibus consistit neque in loco ullo, efficitque
terminationes non apparentes, intervalla autem media apparentia, uti sermone
cum dicamus sol lux flos vox. nunc enim nec unde incipit nec ubi desinit
intellegitur, sed quod ex acuta facta est gravis et ex gravi acuta, apparet auribus.
per distantiam autem e contrario. namque cum flectitur inmutatione vox statuit
se in alicuius sonitus finitione, deinde in alterius, et id ultro citro crebre faciendo
⟨non⟩  constans apparet  sensibus,  uti in cantionibus cum  flectentes vocem

initium fecit et ubi desiit apparet in sonorum patentibus finitionibus, medianis
autem patentia intervallis obscurantur.
As the voice changes inflection, it becomes high or low and moves in two ways:
continuously or by distinct intervals. Continuous movement settles at no fixed
pitch; its boundaries are imperceptible, although the intervening movement is
audible, as when we say sol, lux, flos, vox in ordinary speech. We do not identify
its precise starting and stopping points, but the ear hears the change from high
to low and from low to high. Movement by intervals is different. The voice
settles at one definite pitch, then another, and repeatedly passes between them,
as in singing when changes of pitch produce melodic variety. The beginnings
and endings are then perceptible at the clearly defined notes, while the
intervening passage is obscured by the intervals.
