There are three genera of melody: the first, called harmonia by the Greeks, is the
enharmonic; the second is chroma, the chromatic; and the third is the diatonic.
The enharmonic is an artistic construction whose melody has a particularly
grave and distinguished character. The chromatic offers a gentler pleasure
through the subtle skill and closeness of its steps. The diatonic is natural and
its intervals are easier to grasp. The tetrachords are divided differently in the
three genera. The enharmonic contains two whole tones and two dieses; a diesis
is one-quarter of a tone, so two dieses make a semitone. The chromatic has two
successive semitones and a third interval of three semitones. The diatonic has
two successive whole tones, with a final semitone completing the tetrachord.
Each genus therefore spans two tones and a semitone, although the division of
that span differs.

4. igitur intervalla tonorum et hemitoniorum et ⟨diheseon⟩ tetrachordorum in
voce  divisit natura  finîtque terminationes eorum mensuris intervallorum

artifices qui organa fabricant ex natura constitutis utendo comparant ad
concentus convenientes eorum perfectiones.
Nature has divided the voice into the intervals of tones, semitones and dieses
within the tetrachords, fixing their limits by the size of the intervals and
establishing distinct qualities at definite distances. Instrument makers use these
natural divisions to bring their finished instruments into consonance.

The notes, called phthongoi (φθόγγοι) in Greek, number eighteen in each genus.
Eight remain fixed in all three genera; the other ten are movable when the genera
are considered together. The fixed notes, interposed among the movable ones,
maintain the connection of the tetrachords and retain their positions as the
genera change. Their names are proslambanomenos, hypate hypaton, hypate
meson, mese, nete synhemmenon, paramese, nete diezeugmenon and nete
hyperbolaeon. The movable notes occupy positions between the fixed notes
within a tetrachord and change their places with the genus. They are parhypate
hypaton,  lichanos  hypaton,  parhypate  meson,  lichanos  meson,   trite
synhemmenon,  ⟨paranete synhemmenon⟩,  trite  diezeugmenon,  paranete
diezeugmenon, trite hyperbolaeon and paranete hyperbolaeon.

of Aristoxenus of Tarentum (4th  c. BC): the three genera—enharmonic

harmonics;  its  highly  technical,  partly  Hellenizing terminology  requires
collation with Aristoxenus (Elementa harmonica) and Ptolemy. Cf. Barker,
Greek Musical Writings.

1.       Ita ex his indagationibus mathematicis rationibus fiant vasa aerea pro
ratione magnitudinis theatri eaque ita fabricentur ut cum tangantur, sonitum
facere possint inter se diatessaron diapente et ex ordine ad disdiapason. postea
inter sedes theatri constitutis cellis, ratione musica ibi conlocentur ita uti nullum
parietem tangant circaque habeant locum vacuum et ab summo capite spatium,
ponanturque inversa et habeant in parte quae spectat ad scaenam suppositos
cuneos ne minus altos semipede, contraque eas cellas relinquantur aperturae
inferiorum graduum cubilibus longae pedes duo, altae semipede.
On these principles, bronze vessels should be made by mathematical calculation
in proportion to the size of the theater. They must be fashioned so that, when
struck, they sound in relation to one another at a fourth, a fifth and successively
up to the double octave. Vaulted chambers should then be built among the seats
and the vessels placed in them according to musical principles. Each vessel must
touch none of the surrounding walls and must have free space around it and
above. Set the vessels upside down, supported on wedges at least half a foot high
on the side facing the stage. Opposite the chambers, leave openings in the beds
of the lower seating steps, two feet long and half a foot high.159

Editorial note. — The bronze vessels (echea, from the Greek ἠχεῖα) were
resonating jars set in niches beneath the theater’s seats and tuned to the intervals
of Greek musical theory — the enharmonic, chromatic and diatonic genera that
Vitruvius takes from Aristoxenus of Tarentum — so that they would vibrate in
sympathy with the actor’s voice and reinforce its clarity. It is one of the few
passages where Vitruvius sets out a precise acoustic application of Greek
harmonics. It should be noted, however, that the archaeological evidence for
such vessels is scant and disputed: niches and, in some theaters, jars that might
have served the purpose have been found, but no assemblage that confirms the
full system described here.

Someone may object that many theaters are built in Rome each year without
any provision of this kind. The objection overlooks the many boarded surfaces
in public wooden theaters, which necessarily resonate. The same effect can be
observed in cithara players: when they wish to sing in a higher register, they turn
toward the stage doors and obtain support for the resonance of their voices.
When theaters are built of solid materials—rubble masonry, stone or marble—
which do not resonate in this way, the system of sounding vessels must be
employed.

following the harmonic theory of Aristoxenus, to whose diagram — in the now-
lost end of the book — he refers. No vessels that are certainly Vitruvian survive,
and their efficacy has been questioned since the Renaissance; yet the resonating
niches found in several ancient theaters, and the acoustic jars built into medieval
church walls, attest the persistence of the idea. Whatever their practical effect,
this remains the fullest account of architectural acoustics to come down from
antiquity (cf. the theory of consonance in 5.4 and the Conspectus of Greek
Terms).

Explanatory note — Bk. 5.10 (the baths and the hypocaust). Vitruvius
gives the fullest ancient account of the Roman bath. The site is chosen as warm
as possible, facing south and west; the men's and women's baths are set side by
side to share a single furnace (praefurnium). The heating system  is the
hypocaust: the floor of the hot rooms —the suspensura— is raised on brick
piers, leaving a chamber through which the hot air of the furnace circulates and
then rises through clay pipes (tubuli) set in the walls. Over the hypocaust three
bronze cauldrons —caldarium, tepidarium, and frigidarium— are placed and
linked so that the water passes from the warm to the hot as it is drawn off. The
bathwater is further heated in a bronze vessel called the testudo ('tortoise'), from
its shape. Pompeian archaeology (the Forum Baths) confirms the scheme. The
text has been collated with no variant affecting the sense.

Editorial note. — Chapter 10 gives the earliest detailed account of the Roman
bath. Its technical core is the hypocaust: the floor of the hot rooms is raised on
small  pillars of  tile (suspensurae) so that the hot gases from a furnace
(hypocausis) circulate beneath it and, through flues, up the walls; the bronze
tanks (testudines alveolorum) are heated from the same source. Vitruvius
prescribes the warm orientation (away from the cold north), the sequence of

ARGUMENTUM LIBRI VI — On the private house: the influence of climate
and latitude on the arrangement of buildings, the proportions of atriums,
tablinums, peristyles and triclinia, the differences between the Greek and Roman
house, and the suitability (decor) of each room to its use and the condition of its
owner.

Notice. — Book VI treats the private house. After a preface on the worth of
learning above fortune, it relates domestic architecture to climate and latitude,
sets out the proportions of the atrium, tablinum, peristyle and the several oeci,
distinguishes the Greek house from the Roman, and turns to the working
farmstead (villa rustica). It closes with the principles of sound construction —
foundations, retaining walls and substructures. The book is the chief ancient
evidence for the Roman domus and its social use of space.

Historical and critical note — VI.1. The connections between latitude, climate,
voice, bodily constitution and national character belong to ancient medical
geography and ethnography. They explain Vitruvius’s architectural argument

modern populations. Their historical logic is preserved without endorsement or
retrospective scientific harmonization.

2.     The central courts of houses, or cava aedium, are divided into five types:
Tuscan, Corinthian, tetrastyle, displuviate and testudinate. In the Tuscan type,
beams spanning the width of the atrium carry the cross-members and valleys
that run from the corners of the walls to the corners of the beams; the rafters
direct the rain toward the central compluvium. In the Corinthian type, the
beams and compluvium are arranged on the same principles, but the beams are
set back from the walls and supported on columns around the opening. The
tetrastyle type has columns beneath the beams at the corners, giving practical
support and stability: the beams need neither span so great a distance nor bear
the load of the intervening members unsupported.
Explanatory note — Bk. 6.3. Vitruvius distinguishes five forms of the central
court by their roof construction. The Tuscan type spans the atrium without
columns; the Corinthian uses a colonnade around the opening; the tetrastyle
places four columns at its corners. The displuviate sheds water outward and, in
Vitruvius’s account, is vulnerable to overflowing gutters. The testudinate is fully
covered and permits accommodation above  it. The identification of an
excavated house with one of  these  literary  categories  requires  its own
architectural evidence; the word testudinatum alone does not establish the
material or geometry of a masonry vault.

Explanatory note — Bk. 6.7 (the Greek house). Vitruvius describes the
Greek house by contrast with the Roman: the Greeks use no atrium. From the
gate a passage —the thyroreion (θυρωρεῖον), between the two doors, with the
stable on one side and the porter's rooms on the other— leads to the peristyle,
porticoed on three sides; on the south side two antae carry beams and form a
recess called prostas (προστάς) or parastas. Within lies the great oecus where the
mistress  sits with the wool-spinners, flanked by the thalamus and the
amphithalamus; around the porticoes are triclinia, bedchambers, and servants'
quarters: this is the gynaeconitis (γυναικωνῖτις), the women's area. Adjoining it
is a larger house with a more spacious peristyle (four equal porticoes, or the
southern one higher —the 'Rhodian peristyle'—), with cyzicene oeci, triclinia,
and picture-galleries: the andronitis (ἀνδρωνῖτις), reserved for men, since women
did not recline at table. Between the two peristyles run the mesaulae, which the
Romans call andrones. The text has been collated with no variant affecting the
sense.
Comparative note — Bk. 6.7 (Greek house). In the Budé, Louis Callebat
(2004) treats this chapter as a key witness to the Greco-Latin domestic
vocabulary and discusses the terminological mismatches Vitruvius himself flags
(andron, xystus, prothyrum/diathyron). Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe
(Cambridge, 1999) recall that the Vitruvian account served as the basis for
reconstructions of the Greek house before excavation, and that the finds at
Delos, Priene, and Olynthus show plans more open and less rigid in the
separation of the sexes than the text implies (as recent studies of the gynaeconitis
and the andron, e.g. by S. Weir and H. Franks, have qualified). This edition
translates in its own voice and keeps the Greek spelling of the technical terms;
the gynaeconitis/andronitis division is presented as a Vitruvian category, not as
secure archaeological fact.

chapter treats substructiones: foundations carried down to solid ground and,
above  all, retaining walls able to resist the thrust of the earth. Vitruvius

and diagonal walls at the corners, so that the thrust does not bear on the wall as
a single mass but is distributed: the same principle as the 'comb-like' rampart of

text has been collated with no variant affecting the sense.

Editorial note. — Chapter 8 closes Book VI with the principles of sound
construction (firmitas): foundations carried to solid ground; relieving arches
(fornicationes) and voussoirs (cunei) to lighten the load over  lintels and
openings; the strict perpendicular of every wall. Its most technical passage
concerns substructures and retaining walls against the thrust of earth: Vitruvius
prescribes buttresses on the face — anterides, in Greek erismae — and, on the
inner side, counterforts toothed into the wall (serratim), each spaced from it by
a distance equal to the height of the substructure, so that the earth’s pressure is
resisted as if by the teeth of a saw. The chapter ends with the famous maxim that
the architect should take counsel from craftsmen and laymen alike, for the
layman cannot judge a work until it is built, whereas the architect foresees its
grace, utility and propriety before it is begun.

ARGUMENTUM LIBRI VII — On finishes: the preparation of pavements and
stuccos, lime plasters, ceiling moldings; natural and artificial colors and pigments
(ochre, vermilion, purple, verdigris, ceruse) and their correct application.

Notice. — Book VII, after a learned preface on plagiarism and the history of
writing on architecture, treats the finishing of buildings: pavements and their
bedding, the preparation of stucco and the technique of fresco, and the pigments —
the natural earths and the manufactured colors, among them the synthetic
Egyptian blue (caeruleum) and the lead and copper pigments. It is the most
important ancient source on the technique of painting and the chemistry of
pigments.
Critical and structural note — VI.8. Foundations and substructures, uprights,
vaults, wedges, piers and anterides or erismae are presented as an ancient
constructional system. Modern distinctions between vertical loading, lintel
bending, arch thrust and retaining-wall action belong to the explanatory note.
Continuity of support can clarify Vitruvius’s principle without attributing
elastic theory or stress calculation to him. Buttress and tooth proportions
remain the prescriptions of the text.

technical knowledge, condemns plagiarism and constructs a genealogy of
writers on architecture, perspective and artistic theory. Its function in the
treatise is substantive, not an expendable digression. The Aristophanes anecdote
is read within that argument; ancient literary judgment and independently
verified library history remain distinct.

Archaeological note — Bk. 7.1 (pavements). Vitruvius transmits the ancient
recipe for the layered Roman floor, which archaeology confirms across the
Empire (from Fishbourne in Britain to Lod in Israel, from Zippori to Braga).
From the bottom up: the statumen (large stones forming the base and draining
ground moisture); the rudus or ruderatio (a mortar of broken brick and lime,
more than 20 cm thick, rammed down —three parts lime to one if fresh, five if
recycled—); the nucleus (a fine layer of three parts crushed potsherd to one of
lime, some 15 cm); and above it the setting bed where the tesserae of the
pavimentum were fixed. On upper floors the whole is laid over the joists. A key
material here is opus signinum (cocciopesto): lime with crushed terracotta,
waterproof, of Punic North African origin, spread through Sicily and Italy and
used both for floors and for cisterns. The Vitruvian stratigraphy remains the
reference framework for the archaeometry of mosaics.

2.      After the construction of pavements, lime finishing must be
explained. Soak the best lumps of lime well before they are needed. Any
lump insufficiently burned in the kiln can then be thoroughly slaked by
prolonged contact with water. Fresh lime used before it is fully soaked
contains hidden unslaked particles that form blisters after application. As
those particles finally slake within the work, they disrupt and break up
the plaster finish.

Explanatory note — Bk. 7.5 (the critique of wall-painting). This is one of
the most cited passages in the history of ancient art. Vitruvius condemns the
pictorial fashion of his own day —the so-called 'Second' and above all 'Third'
Pompeian style in August Mau's modern classification—: instead of images
drawn from real things, monstra ('monsters') are painted. He lists the fantasies:
reeds in place of columns; instead of pediments, curling stalks with leaves and
volutes; candelabra supporting little shrines; stalks from which figurines sprout
for no reason, half-figures with human or animal heads. His reproach is one of
truth and decorum: 'such things neither are, nor can be, nor have been' (haec
autem nec sunt nec fieri possunt nec fuerunt), since a reed cannot hold up a
roof. In time these very fantasies, found in the Domus Aurea, would inspire the
Renaissance grottesche. [The author's personal hermeneutic proposal: to read
the passage as proof of a general decline of taste belongs to interpretation, not
to the datum.] The text has been collated with no variant affecting the sense.
Comparative note — Bk. 7.5 (wall-painting). In the Budé, Book VII is the
work of Bernard Liou, Marie-Thérèse Cam, and Michel Zuinghedau, whose
commentary links the passage with Pompeian painting and the theory of decor.
Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) set  it within the
debate over the four Pompeian styles (Mau) and Vitruvius's relation to art
criticism; Corso–Romano detail the vocabulary (monstra, tectoria, coliculi).
Modern scholarship has debated whether Vitruvius is a reliable observer or a
conservative moralist; this edition translates in its own voice and keeps the
transmitted text, with no variant affecting the sense.
Editorial note. — This passage (7.5.3–4) is the locus classicus of ancient art
criticism. Vitruvius condemns the fanciful wall-painting of the Third Pompeian
Style — impossible architectures, hybrid figures, vegetal scrolls — as untruthful.
When such Roman decoration was rediscovered underground (in “grottoes”) at

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VII

the close of the fifteenth century, it gave rise to the Renaissance ornament
known as grottesche (whence “grotesque”); Vitruvius’s strictures became central
to the debate, taken up by Raphael, Daniele Barbaro, and later academic theory.

Explanatory note — Bk. 7.8–7.9 (minium, quicksilver, and ganosis).
Vitruvius describes minium, which for him is cinnabar (mercuric sulphide, the
ancient vermilion), not the red lead (minium secundarium) with which the
name was later confused. He calls the clod from which it is drawn anthrax; he
explains its working —drying, grinding, washing, and heating to bring out the
color— and its source (the Spanish deposits of Sisapo, alongside Ephesus). From
cinnabar comes hydrargyrum or argentum vivum, 'quicksilver,' which he
describes as gathered in 'tears' and used to recover gold by amalgam. He warns
that vermilion is unstable in light: exposed to the sun it blackens. Hence ganosis
(7.9): over the dry color, Punic wax melted with a little oil is applied, warmed
with coals, and polished with a cloth, sealing the surface as was done with the
marble of statues. It is a key chapter for the history of painting technique and of
ancient toxicology (mercury is poisonous). The text has been collated with no
variant affecting the sense.
Comparative note — Bk. 7.8–7.9 (minium and quicksilver). In the Budé,
Book VII is the work of Bernard Liou, Michel Zuinghedau, and Marie-Thérèse
Cam (1995), whose commentary collates the passage with Theophrastus (De
lapidibus 58), Pliny (Natural History 33.37–40), and Dioscorides (5.94).
Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) stress the distinction,
crucial for archaeometry, between Vitruvius's cinnabar (HgS) and red lead;
Corso–Romano fix the vocabulary (anthrax, hydrargyrum, ganosis). Modern
physico-chemical analysis of Pompeian frescoes confirms both the use of
cinnabar and its photochemical darkening —precisely the problem ganosis
sought to prevent. This edition keeps the transmitted text and translates in its
own voice, with no variant affecting the sense.

it becomes as it were flour; copper is filed with coarse files into shavings and
sprinkled over it; the mixture is moistened, rolled by hand into balls, dried, and
packed in an earthen jar, and the jars are placed in a furnace. So, when the copper
and the sand grow incandescent together by the fierceness of the fire, by giving
and receiving their properties from one another they take on a blue color.
Explanatory note — Bk. 7.11 (Egyptian blue, caeruleum). Vitruvius
transmits the only ancient recipe for the first synthetic pigment in history:
caeruleum or Egyptian blue (from caelum, 'sky'; hence 'cerulean'). Its formula
was invented at Alexandria and then established at Puteoli by Vestorius —a
Puteolan  banker,  correspondent  of Cicero and Atticus—, whence  the
'caeruleum Vestorianum.' The recipe: sand (harena) is ground with flower of
natron until it is as fine as flour; filings of Cyprian copper are sprinkled in; balls
are rolled by hand, dried, and fired in earthenware jars in a furnace, until copper
and sand, fused by the fire, take on the blue color. Modern chemistry identifies
the product as a calcium copper silicate (cuprorivaite, CaCuSi₄O₁₀), sintered at
about 850–1000 °C; the calcium comes from the sand itself, which Vitruvius
does not mention. The text has been collated with no variant affecting the sense.
Comparative note — Bk. 7.11 (Egyptian blue). The Budé of Liou,
Zuinghedau, and Cam (1995) comments on the recipe in the light of the
pigment's archaeometry; Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge,
1999) stress that it is the only ancient textual source on its manufacture. Corso–

finding of springs, the qualities of different waters and famous rivers, the leveling

Among the Seven Sages, Thales of Miletus held that water was the first principle
of all things; Heraclitus favored fire, and the priests of the Magi both water and
fire. Euripides, a pupil of Anaxagoras whom the Athenians called “the
philosopher of the stage”, proposed air and earth: the latter, fertilised by rain
from the heavens, brought forth human beings and other living creatures. What
arose from earth would return to it when dissolved by time, while what arose
from air would return to the regions of the sky, not perishing but reverting
through dissolution to its former nature. Pythagoras, Empedocles, Epicharmus
and other natural philosophers proposed four principles — air, fire, earth and
water — whose natural combination produces different qualities.

poterunt habere coctionis temperaturam. Item  si non terrestri cibo membra
corporis alantur, deficient et ita a terreni principii mixtione erunt deserta.

places trees and woods are first abundant, and the mountains themselves have
their shadows that block them, and the rays of the sun do not reach the earth
directly, nor can they burn the moisture.

The valleys between mountains receive the most rain. Dense woodland and the
shade of trees and mountains preserve the snow there for longer; when it melts,
it filters through veins in the earth and reaches the lowest mountain slopes,
where it gushes out in springs. In the plains, by contrast, supplies cannot be
abundant or wholesome. With no shade to obstruct it, the Sun’s fierce heat
draws moisture from the exposed ground. Of any water that remains visible, the
air carries away and disperses the lightest, finest and most wholesome parts,
leaving the heaviest, hardest and least pleasant components in the springs of the
plains.

Archaeological note — Bk. 8.6 (the Roman aqueducts). The chapter on
conduits is illuminated by the archaeology of the greatest hydraulic
system of antiquity. Rome came to have eleven aqueducts: the first was
the Aqua Appia (312 BCE, of Appius Claudius the Blind), mostly
underground; there followed the Anio Vetus, the Aqua Marcia (144
BCE) —the longest and famed for its purity— the Aqua Claudia and the
Anio Novus, whose arches still cross the Roman campagna. The chief
ancient source is the De aquaeductu of Sextus Julius Frontinus, curator
aquarum under Nerva and Trajan, half a century after Vitruvius. The
three methods Vitruvius describes are verified in the remains: masonry
channels (specus) in the great aqueducts, lead pipes (fistulae, stamped by
the plumbarius)  in the urban  distribution, and  terracotta  pipes.
Surviving monuments such as the Pont du Gard (Nîmes) and the
aqueduct of Segovia, and the network of Ostia, confirm the gentle
gradient and the engineering that Book VIII theorizes.

LIBER IX

ARGUMENTUM LIBRI IX — On gnomonics and astronomy: the doubling of the
square handed down by Plato and the right-angled triangle of Pythagoras; the
discovery of Archimedes concerning the adulterated crown; the course of the sun
through the twelve signs of the zodiac, the northern and southern constellations
and the doctrine of the astrologers; and the analemma, the construction of
sundials, and the water-clocks (clepsydrae) of Ctesibius.

Notice. — Book IX turns to gnomonics and astronomy. Its preface, a meditation
on the immortality of learning above athletic fame, is among the most quoted in
the treatise. The book expounds the geometry of the heavens, the zodiac and the
courses of sun, moon and planets, the phases and the analemma, and the
construction  of  sundials and  water-clocks.  It  preserves much  Hellenistic
astronomical lore and is the principal Latin source for ancient dialling.

Explanatory note — Bk. 9, preface (Archimedes and the crown). The
preface to Book IX contrasts the fleeting fame of athletes with the lasting glory
of the learned, and issues in the most famous anecdote of ancient science. Hiero
II of Syracuse, suspecting that the goldsmith had abstracted gold from a votive
crown and replaced it with silver without altering the weight, commissions
Archimedes to detect the fraud. On entering the bath, Archimedes observes that
the water overflows in proportion to the body immersed: he thus grasps that he
can measure the volume of an irregular body by the water it displaces. He runs
out naked, crying in Greek 'heureka, heureka' ('I have found it!'). Then, with
two masses of equal weight —one of gold, one of silver— and the crown, he
measures the water displaced by each and, by comparison, reveals the admixture
of silver. Vitruvius is the oldest ancient source for this story (some two centuries
after the event); Archimedes himself does not record it, and the exact method —
simple immersion or hydrostatic weighing— is debated. The text has been
collated with no variant affecting the sense.

1. We must set these matters aside and explain how the days shorten and
lengthen from month to month. At the equinox, when the Sun moves
through Aries or Libra, a gnomon nine units high casts a shadow eight
units long at the latitude of Rome. At Athens the corresponding ratio is
four to three; at Rhodes, seven to five; at Tarentum, eleven to nine; and
at ⟨Alexandria⟩, five to three. In other places the equinoctial shadows of
gnomons likewise differ according to their situation.

Explanatory note — Bk. 9.7–9.8 (the analemma and sundials). The
technical heart of Book IX  is gnomonics. In 9.7 Vitruvius sets out the
analemma: a geometric construction —a system of lines and curves built from
the shadow of the gnomon at noon on the equinox— that projects the celestial
sphere onto a plane and allows the hours and months to be marked on any dial,
without recourse to trigonometry (Ptolemy's more advanced method, in his On
the Analemma, is later). In 9.8 he gives the fullest ancient catalog of sundials
with their Greek inventors: the hemicyclium, hollowed from a block and
undercut to the latitude, by Berosus the Chaldean; the scaphe or hemisphere

Water entering evenly through the opening raises an inverted vessel, called a
phellos or tympanum by craftsmen. A toothed rack is attached to it beside a
revolving drum. The equally spaced teeth engage and produce controlled
rotations and movements. Other racks and drums, toothed in the same way and
driven by the same motion, produce a variety of effects: small figures move,
cones turn, pebbles or eggs are released, trumpets sound and other ornamental
devices operate.
      The water flowing steadily through this hole lifts the inverted vessel,

this. These rulers are perfectly aligned with teeth, making small turns and
movements by pushing against each other. Likewise, other rulers and drums,
turned in the same way, produce effects and a variety of movements when spun
with a forced motion, in which seals are moved, goalposts are spun, stones or
eggs are thrown, trumpets sound, and everything else that makes up the parade.

In the great and distinguished Greek city of Ephesus, the ancestors are
said to have established an ancient law, severe in its terms yet not unjust.
When an architect undertakes a public building, he declares its estimated
cost. Once that estimate has been submitted to the magistrate, his
property stands as security until the work is complete. If the final
expenditure agrees with the estimate, he receives public honors and
decrees of recognition. An overrun of no more than one quarter is
covered by the public treasury without penalty. If the excess exceeds one
quarter, however, the additional money required to complete the work
is recovered from the architect’s own property.
In the renowned and spacious Greek city of Ephesus an ancient law is said to
have been established by the men of old — harsh in its terms, yet founded in
justice rather than injustice. When an architect undertakes the charge of a public
work, he declares beforehand what its cost will be. The estimate being handed
to the magistrate, his property is pledged as security until the work is completed.
When it is finished, if the outlay has answered to his declaration, he is honored
with decrees and distinctions. Likewise, if the estimate is exceeded by no more
than a quarter, the excess is added to it and met from public funds, and he incurs
no penalty. But when more than a quarter is overspent, the money required to
complete the work is exacted from his own estate.

COMPARATIVE CRITICAL APPARATUS — X.15. Hegetor's tortoise is
described with one of the most unstable sets of numerals in Book X. Against a
textual tradition giving a base of LX × XIII feet and a ram of CIV feet, the

readings and does not reconstruct missing dimensions merely by proportional
inference.
NOTE ON HISTORICAL ENGINEERING — X.15. The importance of
this passage  lies  less in the possibility of reconstructing one machine to
millimetric accuracy than in its structural logic: a mobile base capable of
movement in several directions, layered protection against missiles and fire, a
platform for artillery, a suspended battering ram, and control over the approach
to the wall. The unstable numerals demonstrate why the description must be
read as a transmitted technical document rather than as a modern set of working
drawings.

ARGUMENTUM LIBRI X — VITRUVIUS DEFINES THE MACHINE AND
DISTINGUISHES IT FROM THE INSTRUMENT, THEN EXAMINES HOISTING
DEVICES AND THEIR TACKLE, WATER-RAISING MECHANISMS, THE WATER-
SCREW,  CTESIBIUS’S  PUMP,  THE  HYDRAULIC  ORGAN, AND  THE

ENGINES, INCLUDING RAMS AND TORTOISES, AND CONCLUDES WITH
METHODS OF DEFENSE.

Notice. — Book X treats machines. It distinguishes machina from organon, then
describes hoisting engines and their tackle, water-raising devices (the bucket-wheel,
the Archimedean screw, the water-organ and the water-mill), the odometer, and
finally the engines of war — catapults and ballistae, the tortoise and siege-towers
— closing with stratagems of defense. It is the fullest ancient account of classical
mechanical and military technology.

APPENDIX A

GLOSSARY OF VITRUVIAN TECHNICAL

TERMS
This glossary brings together the principal technical terms used by Vitruvius in
his De architectura, with their Latin form, the Greek spelling where appropriate,
and their academic definition. In each case, the relevant passage in the treatise
where the term is defined or appears with greater precision is indicated.
ARCHITECTURE. The discipline that arises from the union between fabrica
(constructive  practice) and  ratiocinatio  (theoretical  reasoning). Vitruvius
defines it in De architectura 1.1.1: “Architecture is a science furnished with
many disciplines and diverse fields of knowledge branches of learning.” Its
implicit Greek equivalent is ἀρχιτεκτονική (architektoniké).
CUBE [ κύβος ]. The cube, a geometrical figure of six equal square faces.
Vitruvius employs it in the preface to Book V to explain the Pythagorean cubic
ratio: The number 216 (= 6 ³) was the conventional measure of a writing
volume. « A cube is a body with sides of equal width on flat surfaces » (De
architectura 5.praef.3).
CYBICIS RATIONIBUS. « Cubic ratios ». Pythagorean expression that
designates the organization of knowledge in volumes of 216 verses (= 6 ³). Cf.
De architectura 5.praef.3; Krohn (1912), 100.
DECOR. The suitability or correctness of the appearance of a work, obtained
through the appropriate application of the principles of use, custom, and
nature. “Decor autem est emendatus operis aspectus probatis rebus compositi
cum auctoritate” (De architectura 1.2.5). It should not be confused with
“decoration” in the modern ornamental sense.
DISPOSITIO [ διάθεσις ]. Layout or conception of the plan, elevation and
perspective of a building.  It involves the three forms of representation:
ichnographia (plan), orthographia (elevation) and scaenographia (perspective).
Cf. De architectura 1.2.1 – 2.
DISTRIBUTIO  [ οἰκονομία  ]. The administration Suitable materials and
terrain, with economic balance. Includes adapting the design to the owner's
status and use. Cf. De architectura 1.2.8 – 9.

                           911

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

ECHEA [ ἠχεῖα, sing. ἠχεῖον ]. Bronze vessels (vasaenea) tuned according to
musical intervals, placed in niches under the tiers of theaters to amplify and
clarify the voices of the actors. They constitute the foundation of Vitruvian
acoustic architecture. Cf. De architectura 1.1.9 and 5.5.1 – 8.
ENCYCLIOS DISCIPLINA. Encyclopedic education. The comprehensive
training program that Vitruvius requires of the architect: writing, drawing,
geometry,  arithmetic,  history,  philosophy,  music,  medicine,  law,  and
astronomy. Cf. De architectura 1.1.12.
EURYTHMIA [ εὐρυθμία ]. The graceful and proportionate appearance in the
composition of the members of a work. It results from the correct application
of  symmetry.  «  Eurythmia   est  venusta  species  commodusque  in
compositionibus membrorum aspectus » (De architectura 1.2.3).
FABRICA. The constructive practice: " continuous and practised experience
of construction, by which the intended work is executed by hand." Together
with ratiocinatio, it constitutes the origin of architectura. Cf. De architectura
1.1.1.
FIRMITAS. Structural solidity. The first condition of all architectural work,
achieved "when the foundations are carried down to firm ground and when the
choice of materials is made without avarice. " Cf. De architectura 1.3.2.
GNOMONICS [ γνωμονική ]. The art of measuring time using the gnomon
(sundial) and other instruments. Vitruvius dedicates Book IX to  it. The
gnomon is the rod whose shadow indicates the time.
ICHNOGRAPHY [ ἰχνογραφία ]. Horizontal plan or projection of a building,
plotted with ruler and compass. One of the three forms of architectural
representation described by Vitruvius. Cf. De architectura 1.2.2.
ORDINATIO [ τάξις ]. The ordering or modular arrangement of the members
of a work, taking as a reference a unit of measurement (m o dule). “Ordinatio is t
he balanced adjustment of the members of a work taken separately, and of the
whole with regard to proportion” (De architectura 1.2.2).
ORTHOGRAPHY [ ὀρθογραφία ]. Elevation or vertical representation of the
façade of a building, at the correct scale. Second of the three forms of Vitruvian
representation. Cf. De architectura 1.2.2.



                           912

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER

RATA PARS. The " determined part " or reference module from which the
proportions of a work are established. In temples, the module is the semi -
diameter of the column. Cf. De architectura 1.2.4.
RATIOCINATIO. Theoretical reasoning applied to construction: " that
which can show and explain through skill, method and proportion the works
carried out. " Cf. De architectura 1.1.1.

SCAENOGRAPHIA  [ σκηνογραφία  ]. Perspective or foreshortened
representation of facades and lateral parts of a building. Third form of
Vitruvian representation. Cf. De architectura 1.2.2.
SCAMILLI IMPARES. The “irregular wedges” or curvilinear corrections of
the stylobate of temples, intended to compensate for the optical illusion of
sinking on long horizontal surfaces. Cf. De architectura 3.4.5 and Rowland and
Howe (1999), 51.
SYMMETRIA [ συμμετρία ]. The proportional correspondence between the
members of a work and the whole, taken from a rata pars (reference part). «
Symmetria  est  ex  ipsius  operis membris  conveniens  consensus » (De
architectura 1.2.4). It differs from the modern meaning of « bilateral symmetry
».
UTILITAS.  Functional  utility. The  second  Vitruvian  condition:  the
arrangement of spaces must be irreproachable and present no obstacles to use.
Cf. De architectura 1.3.2.
VENUSTAS.  Elegance  or beauty  of  appearance. The  third  Vitruvian
condition, achieved when " the appearance of the work is pleasing and in good
taste, and when the proportions of the members are calculated according to the
principles of symmetry. " Cf. De architectura 1.3.2. The term derives from
Venus (goddess of beauty) and connotes proportional  grace, not mere
ornamentation.
ABACUS [ἄβαξ]. The abacus: a square slab that crowns the capital and receives
the architrave. Its proportion varies according to the order.
ASTRAGALUS [Astragalus]. Small convex molding of semicircular section
(also tondino), used at the transition between fuste and capitel.

COLUMN. The vertical support composed of a base (except in the Vitruvian
Doric), shaft (scapus) and capital (capitulum). Its height/diameter ratio defines
the order.
CORINTHIUS (ordo). The Corinthian order, the most slender and ornate,
characterized by the acanthus leaf capital; Vitruvius recounts its invention by
Callimachus (4.1).
DIASTICLES [διάστυλος]. Wide intercolumniation, of three diameters
between columns (3.3).
DORICUS (ordo). The Doric order, the most robust, based on its Vitruvian
form, with a frieze of triglyphs and metopes (4.3).
ENTASIS [ἔντασις]. The slight bulging or convex tension of the column shaft,
intended to correct the optical illusion of concavity (3.3.13).
EUSTYLOS  [εὔστυλος]. The  optimal  intercolumniation  according  to
Vitruvius, of two and a quarter diameters, which reconciles beauty and solidity
(3.3.6).
IONICUS (ordo). The Ionic order, intermediate in slenderness, recognizable
by the volutes of the capital; Vitruvius dedicates the core of Book III to it.
MODULUS. The module: unit of measurement (in Vitruvius, generally the
radius or lower diameter of the column) with which the entire building is
dimensioned by symmetria.
MUTULUS. The mutule: projecting block under the Doric cornice, vestige of
the beam heads; it bears the guttae.
PERIPTERAL  [περίπτερος]. Temple surrounded by  a  single row  of
freestanding columns on its four sides (3.2).
PYCNOSTYLOS [πυκνόστυλος]. Narrow intercolumniation, one and a half
diameters between columns (3.3).
PRONAOS [πρόναος]. The portico or front vestibule of the temple, in front
of the cella.
STYLOBATA [στυλοβάτης]. The stylobate: upper platform or step on which

Vitruvius Today

The Continuing Life of a Canon
De architectura remains an active point of reference in architectural culture. Its
contemporary value lies in the questions it brings together: how a building
stands, how it serves its users, how its parts form an intelligible whole, and how
the architect acquires the knowledge needed to judge these relationships. Three
lines of reception connect that ancient inquiry with present practice.
The triad of  firmitas,  utilitas and venustas continues to offer a concise
framework for discussing durability, use and beauty. In the twentieth century,
Le Corbusier’s Modulor developed a modern system of measure around the
human body. It can be studied as a reinterpretation of the anthropometric
tradition, while its aims and proportional rules remain distinct from those of
Vitruvius.
Symmetria, understood as the commensurability of the parts and the whole
through  a  module,  also  invites  comparison  with  design  governed by
relationships and rules. Parametric modeling makes such relationships explicit;
Building  Information Modeling  coordinates  information  about  design,
construction and maintenance. These are contemporary analogies proposed by
the author. They do not establish a direct technical descent from the ancient
treatise.
The discussions of site, orientation, healthy air, materials and water in Books I,
VI and VIII likewise remain useful interlocutors for environmental design.
Ancient explanations must be assessed within their own scientific and social
setting. Reading firmitas today as durability and responsible use of resources
extends the historical concept to a modern ethical concern; it does not attribute
a present-day environmental agenda to Vitruvius.
His continuing relevance is therefore best tested through informed comparison.
The architect can learn from the relation between practical experience and
reasoned explanation while examining the limits of both the ancient evidence
and its later interpretations. That critical dialogue preserves the vitality of the
canon without turning it into a timeless rulebook.

The Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (architekton) combines ἀρχι- (archi-, “chief” or “master”)

prefix belongs to the word family of ἀρχή (archē, “beginning” or “authority”)
and ἄρχω (archō, “to begin” or “to rule”). In technical practice, the architect
directed and coordinated building work; the title alone does not establish a
priestly function. The numerical proposal in Figure 19 concerns ΑΡΧΩ and is

The geometry of the plane and the organization of sacred space
planimetric configuration of temples in Pharaonic Egypt — exemplified by the
complexes of Luxor, Karnak, and Edfu — responds to criteria of astronomical
and  topographical  precision. The  segmentation  of  space by  axial and
processional axes allowed for the systematic observation of  solstices and
equinoxes, fundamental for the civil and agricultural calendar. The structure of
the temple, divided between areas of restricted access (priestly cella) and public
spaces, was based on a logic of strictly functional spatial segregation.
It  is important to note that the use of complex geometries, such as the
intersection of right triangles to determine the layout on the ground, responds
to the needs of architectural layout to guarantee the symmetry and stability of

The architect as artifex: Evolution of professional titles.
The designation of architects in ancient Egypt, as in the case of Imhotep —
architect of the Step Pyramid of Saqqara — is linked to technical mastery in the
manipulation of materials. The epithet " potter" or similar titles should not be
interpreted under demiurgic categories, but rather as a technical metaphor for
the work of molding and construction. The allusion to the "potter's wheel" is an
analogy that describes the builder's skill in transforming raw materials (stone or
clay) into functional and structured volumes, a technique reflected in both
pottery and monumental architecture. <sup>4</sup>

2. Evolution of time computation
The development of calendars in ancient societies responded to a need for
administrative and agricultural organization. The recording of lunar phases
(lunae cursus) was, in effect, the primary method by which various civilizations,
including the Roman, structured their  initial time cycles, a process that
preceded the implementation of complex solar calendars.

Janus's association with architectural passageways and the management of time

although difficult to validate through official epigraphy.

Janus and dactylonomy: a hermeneutic reading

In the heart of the Forum Boarium, the Temple of Janus housed a statuary
whose gestural configuration transcended mere ornamentation. The deity's
hands were positioned according to the system of dactylonomy, configured to
represent the number 355 (the duration of the Roman lunar year), symbolically
adapting to the 365 - day cycle after the Julian reform. This codification was not
accidental: it symbolized Janus's absolute dominion over time and his nature as
absolute initium.
This capacity of the hand to articulate complex theological concepts through
coded gestures was a central component of Greco-Roman religiosity. A key
testimony to this communicative power is found in Apuleius's The Golden
Ass. In the description of the procession of Isis, the author recounts how a priest,
carrying the sacred attributes, addresses the crowd and performs a specific
gesture that was not a simple blessing, but a visual representation of secret
knowledge — an  initiatory  teaching  inaccessible  to  the  uninitiated —

demonstrating that gesture functioned as an encrypted code that protected and
transmitted the mysteries of the divine.
Janus, like those initiated into mystery cults, presides over the abstract principles
of the cosmos. As the "guardian of the gates," he maintains mediation with the
divine pantheon, which is why he must be invoked first in every rite, thus
establishing himself as the indispensable regent of human beginnings, historical
eras, and financial ventures.

hand functions as a mechanical computing instrument that positions the deity

2. The Gesture in Apuleius: In Metamorphoses (XI, 17), Apuleius describes
the Isiah procession where the priest, in presenting the sacred objects, performs
a gesture (adinstar) that encapsulates an arcane doctrine. The use of the term
"secret knowledge" (or arcanum) in this context underscores that, in antiquity,
the manual gesture could function as a hermeneutical signum; that is, a form of
communication that substituted for the forbidden word or one incapable of
explaining the magnitude of the sacred. This passage reinforces the idea that the
form of the hands in divine statuary was not only numerical but also carried a
deep and hidden semantics.

obligatory mediator, since "everything you see, you open or close. " This
function as intermediary justifies his privileged position both in the calendar
(giving his name to Ianuarius) and in the gestural language of the temples, where
the god's hand "opens" time before the eyes of men.

This edition stems from an extended study of the symbols, archetypes, and
technical traditions linked to architecture and the art of building in classical
antiquity. Through the figure of Marcus Vitruvius Pollio and his treatise De
architectura, an attempt has been made to offer a comprehensive approach that
combines historical and philological analysis with a hermeneutical reading of
the symbolic dimensions present in the Greco -Roman architectural tradition.
        Vitruvius is not only the only architectural theorist whose complete
works have survived from antiquity, but he also embodies a comprehensive
conception of technical knowledge in which *fabricatio* and *ratiocinatio * —
practice and theoretical reflection — are inextricably linked. His treatise,
structured in ten books, constitutes a true encyclopedic corpus that reflects both
the technical knowledge of his time and a vision of the architect as an intellectual
versed in the liberal arts.
      The  influence of De  architectura  far transcends  its  value  as a
construction manual. Its rediscovery and dissemination from the 15th century
onwards decisively contributed to shaping the architectural thought of the
Renaissance and the Modern Age. From Leon Battista Alberti to Andrea
Palladio and Le Corbusier, by way of Leonardo da Vinci, the Vitruvian tradition
has served as a guiding thread linking Antiquity with modernity.

     Vitruvius writes about the parts that make up the
discipline of architecture:
"There are three parts to Architecture: Building, Gnomonics, and the construction
of machines (machinatio). In turn, construction is divided into two parts: one part
deals with the arrangement of walls and common works in public places; the other
part deals with the development of private buildings. "

      Public buildings have three possible objectives: protection, worship, and
advantageous location:

     The protection refers to the structure of walls, towers and gates, with the
purpose of repelling enemy attacks at any time.

The cult refers to the location of the temples of the immortal gods and the sacred
sanctuaries.

The advantageous situation consists of the arrangement of common places
intended for public use, such as ports, forums, porticoes, public baths, theaters,
promenades and similar constructions, which are located in public places,
serving the same purpose of use.

        In the  first chapter of his initial book, Vitruvius reveals that the
architect's wisdom originates in "fabrica" (the practice of the  craft) and
"ratiocinatio" (intellectual work), thus enabling him to evaluate all other trades.

guild structures and building traditions, introducing a personal separation

devoted himself exclusively to creating plans and models, leaving the actual
construction of buildings to experienced project managers.

        Vitruvius prioritizes the ideal architect over the art of architecture,
thus restricting access to the realm of architecture. The architect embodies
architecture (a royal compendium of all things, united through art), but is only
perfected through a comprehensive training course in various disciplines, which
Vitruvius likens to a corpus. This discipline, the encyclios, 170has evoked the
liberal  arts for many readers, who imagine that Vitruvius invokes these
disciplines to "elevate" architecture or even Vitruvius himself. However, it is also
evident that architecture was already perceived as intellectually meticulous.

A related question is the relation between bodily measure and architectural
design.  Vitruvius’s  account  of human  proportion  in  3.1.2–3 may be
summarized as follows:

                           953

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

1. Commensurability as a governing principle
Vitruvius relates the proportional organization of a temple to that of a well-
formed human body. The analogy concerns the commensurable relation of
parts to the whole, rather than bilateral symmetry alone. He gives the following
ratios:
•     The face: The face, from the chin to the top of the forehead (where
the hair grows), should measure one - tenth of the man's total height.
•     The hand: The length of the hand, from the wrist to the tip of the
middle finger, is also equal to one - tenth of the total height.
•     The head: From the chin to the crown, it represents one-eighth of the
total height.
   •   The upper chest: The distance from the upper chest to the
       hairline is one-sixth of the body’s height; the distance from
       the upper chest to the crown is one-quarter.
2. The circle and the square
Vitruvius postulates that the human body has two inscribed geometric forms
that demonstrate its proportional perfection:
•     The square: If a man stands with his arms extended horizontally, the
distance between his fingertips (his wingspan) is equal to his total height. Thus,
inscribing the body in a square results in a figure with equal sides.
•     The  circle:  If a man  lies on his back with  his  legs and arms
outstretched, his navel is the center point of his body. If a circle is drawn by
placing a compass on his navel, the circumference will touch the tips of his
fingers and toes.

3. The body as a unit of measurement (The module)
Vitruvius insists that the measurements of the human body should be the basis
for establishing "modules" in architecture:

   •   The foot: It is equivalent to one sixth of the total height of a
      man.
•      The cubit (distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger):
Represents one-quarter of the height.

4. The purpose: Eurythmia
Vitruvius uses the relations between the parts of the human body as an analogy
for the commensurability required in temple design. His account of eurythmia

APPENDIX I

Testimonia veterum (Ancient Testimonies about
Vitruvius)

Antiquity and the early Middle Ages that mention Vitruvius or use his work
are gathered. They constitute the documentary basis for reconstructing his
biography and the fortune of De architectura, and explain why the treatise, far
from being completely forgotten, enjoyed continuous transmission.
Pliny the Elder, Natural History, indexes of books XVI and XXXV. He
includes Vitruvius among the sources (auctores) he uses for the chapters on
materials and pigments; it is the oldest testimony of the use of the work, barely
one or two generations after its composition.

Frontinus, De aquaeductu urbis Romae. The curator aquarum of Rome
(c. 97 CE) agrees with Vitruvius in the measurements of the pipes
(fistulae) and in the hydraulic doctrine, which proves the technical
circulation of the treatise in the field of public administration.
Faventino, De diversis fabricis architectonicae. Compendium from the
3rd-4th century AD that summarizes and transmits large portions of Vitruvius;
It is the main late antique link in the tradition.
Palladius, Opus agriculturae. He collects, through Faventinus, Vitruvian
prescriptions on rural construction, disseminating them in medieval agronomic
literature.
Servius, Commentarii in Vergilii Aeneidem. The grammarian quotes
Vitruvius on matters of architecture and religion, a sign of his authority in late
antique teaching.
Sidonius Apollinaris, Epistulae IV.3. He mentions Vitruvius as a model of
technical knowledge, proof of his prestige in 5th century Gaul.
Cassiodorus, Variae VII.5; Institutiones. He recommends the reading of
Vitruvius to the officials in charge of the public works of the Ostrogothic
kingdom (6th century), guaranteeing its survival.
Einhard, Epistulae. Charlemagne's biographer uses Vitruvian vocabulary
and concepts,  reflecting the  circulation of the  text  in the Carolingian
Renaissance that produced the Codex Harleianus.

Appendix K · Apparatus fontium: Vitruvius’ Greek
sources

Vitruvius states in the preface to Book VII (7.praef.11-14) that his
treatise is based on the works of the Greek architects and theorists who
preceded him, most of whose works are now lost. This appendix lists,
book by book, the principal Hellenic sources that scholars recognize as
underlying Vitruvian doctrine, distinguishing those Vitruvius himself
names from those inferred from the content. Unless otherwise indicated,
the attributions follow Gros (Budé) and Rowland-Howe.

Book I — Principles and training of the architect
The doctrine of principles (ordinatio, dispositio, eurythmia, symmetria,
decor, distributio) and the encyclopedic ideal of the architect reflect
Hellenistic architectural theory and Greek paideia. Vitruvius  cites
Pytheos of Priene as an authority on the architect's comprehensive
training  (1.1.12).  The  philosophical  background  refers  to  the
Pythagorean  tradition  and  the  pre-Socratic  physiologoi  (Thales,
Democritus), invoked in the proems.

Book II — Materials and Origins of Construction
The history of the origin of architecture and the primitive hut is linked
to  Greek  evolutionary  theories  (Democritus,  Epicurus,  and  the
Peripatetic tradition). For the doctrine of the elements and matter,
Vitruvius follows Thales, Heraclitus, Democritus, and the Greek physics
that he himself summarizes (2.2).

Books III-IV — Temples and the Orders
This  is the most densely Greek core of the work. Vitruvius relies
primarily on Hermogenes of Alabanda (2nd century BC), architect of the
pseudodipteral temple of Artemis at Magnesia on the Meander and the
monopteral temple of Dionysus at Teos, from whom he takes the rules
of the Ionic order, the eustyle, and the critique of the dipteral (3.2-3.3;
4.3). Also contributing are Pytheos, author of the temple of Athena at
Priene and, with Satyrus, of the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus; Arcesius,
on Corinthian proportions; and the archaic writers whom Vitruvius


                           979

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

himself  lists  in  7.praef.12  (Silenus, Theodorus, Chersiphron and
Metagenes, Ictinus and Carpio, Philo of Athens).

Book V — Public Buildings, Theater and Acoustics
For the theory of the acoustic vessels of the theater (echea) and the
harmonic arrangement of the seating, Vitruvius adapts the Greek
musical theory of Aristoxenus of Tarentum (5.4-5.5), whose doctrine of
tetrachords he explicitly summarizes. The design of the Greek theater
compared to the Latin one (5.7) derives directly from Hellenic models.

Book VI — Private Buildings and Climate
The theory of the suitability of housing to latitudes and climates (6.1) is
based on Greek ethnography and scientific geography, particularly on
the Hippocratic  tradition (On  Airs, Waters and  Places) and on
Posidonius.

Book VII — Finishes, stucco and painting
His preface is the main source for reconstructing Vitruvius's library: it
lists the Greek authors on proportions and machines. For  stage
perspective (scaenographia) he cites the works of Agatharchus of Samos
and  the commentaries  of Democritus and Anaxagoras on  optics
(7.praef.11).

Book VIII — Water
The doctrine on the search, properties and conduction of water follows
the Greek authors of natural sciences; Vitruvius invokes Thales (water as
a principle) and gathers material from the Peripatetic and Hippocratic
tradition on the qualities of waters (8.3).

Book IX — Gnomonics and Astronomy
The most dependent on Greek scientific sources. Vitruvius follows
Berossus  the  Chaldean  (who  introduced  astrology  to  Greece),
Aristarchus  of Samos  (to whom  he  attributes  the  sundial and
heliocentrism), Eudoxus of Cnidus, Eratosthenes (measurement of the
meridian), and Archimedes (9.praef.; 9.1-9.8). The anecdote about the
crown comes from the tradition surrounding Archimedes.

Book X — Machines
Vitruvian mechanics rests on the Alexandrian school. For pumps, the
hydraulic organ, and the water-lifting machine, Vitruvius follows
Ctesibius of Alexandria (10.7-10.8); for artillery and catapults, Philo of
Byzantium and Ctesibius; for the lifting screw, Archimedes (10.6); and
for siege engines, Diades (Alexander's engineer), Agesistratus, and the
Hellenistic siegecraft tradition (10.13-10.16).

Note.
The works of these authors have been almost entirely lost; they are
known primarily through Vitruvius himself, Pliny the Elder (Natural
History), and the surviving Greek mechanical  treatises (Heron of
Alexandria, Philo). This appendix does not aim to be exhaustive, but
rather to guide the reader towards the profound Hellenic roots of De
architectura.

Appendix L · Critical editions of Vitruvius: overview

The editions and translations that form the basis of the study of
Vitruvius today are listed here in chronological order, along with a brief
assessment of their usefulness. This list expands upon and formalizes
what was presented in the Preliminary Note.

Valentin Rose (Teubner, 1867; 2nd ed. 1899)
An important modern critical edition of the Latin text, without a facing
translation. Rose’s recension and apparatus remain valuable for comparison. In

following a different reading requires an explanation at its locus.

Fritz Krohn (Teubner, 1912)
Krohn’s critical edition is the declared reference text of this reading edition. It

and the relevant Budé volume at disputed passages, rather than reduced to a
mechanical rule of following the oldest witness.

Auguste Choisy (Paris, 1909)
A bilingual Latin-French edition in four volumes, the work of an
architect and construction historian. Without footnotes, it is notable for

editions geared towards architects.

A two-volume bilingual Latin-English edition, based on the Harleianus.

Appendix M · Stemma Codicum and the Manuscript
Transmission

This appendix sets out the genealogy of the surviving manuscripts of the De
architectura, traces the principal stages of its transmission from Antiquity to the
editio princeps, and explains the reasoning — the recensio — by which the two
main branches of the tradition are reconstructed. The classification rests not on
any single isolated error but on shared conjunctive errors (errores coniunctivi):
when two or more codices preserve the same improbable corruption, a common
ancestor may be inferred.

1. Chronology of the transmission (1st c. BC – 15th c. AD)

c. 27–23 BCE — Composition. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio composes the ten books of
the De architectura under Augustus, to whom the work is dedicated. It is the only
complete treatise on architecture to survive from classical Antiquity.

1st–3rd c. CE — Ancient circulation. The work was transmitted through
successive copies; the author’s autograph has not survived. The surviving
witnesses do not establish when it was lost.

Late Antiquity and the early Middle Ages — The text passed through
copies that are now lost. Shared lacunae and textual disturbances allow
editors to infer a common exemplar behind the surviving witnesses;
neither its physical form nor an exact date is established by that inference
alone.
6th–8th c. — The dark age of transmission. Documentation is extremely scarce.
The survival of the De architectura through these centuries is one of the most
remarkable episodes in the preservation of Roman literature.
9th c. — Carolingian Renaissance. Under Carolingian patronage, many ancient
works were copied afresh. Harley MS 2767 (H) is an important early witness to
De architectura. Its age and textual value do not establish that every surviving
manuscript descends from it. Krohn distinguishes the H–S grouping from the
Gudianus witnesses E and G; their relationships must be assessed through
shared readings, corrections and losses.
10th–13th c. — Monastic and scholastic preservation. The work circulates in
monastic  libraries and  cathedral  schools. New  copies  appear;  errors of

                           985

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

transcription, omissions and interpolations multiply, and some witnesses show
contamination through the collation of different exemplars.
14th–15th c. — Humanist rediscovery. Italian scholars revive their interest in
the technical literature of Antiquity; Poggio Bracciolini and others recover and
diffuse dispersed manuscripts. Vitruvius becomes essential reading for Alberti,
Francesco di Giorgio Martini and Leonardo da Vinci. Humanistic copies
circulate widely.
1486 — Editio princeps. The first printed edition of the De architectura,
published in Rome by Fra Giovanni Sulpicio da Veroli, marks the passage from
manuscript to print and opens the modern editorial tradition.

2. General scheme of the transmission
The surviving witnesses are commonly referred to a lost archetype, but the
relationships between their branches must be stated according to a named
critical edition. Krohn’s preface (1912, VIII) distinguishes H and S from E and
G. The age and authority of H do not justify treating every other witness as its
direct descendant.

Lost common exemplar (Ω): inferred from shared lacunae and textual
disturbance.
H–S: Harleianus 2767 and Selestadiensis.
E–G: Gudianus 132 and Gudianus 69.
These paired witnesses summarize Krohn’s grouping; they do not
assign direct descent to every copy.
The manuscript tradition passes into print in the Roman editio
princeps prepared by Giovanni Sulpicio da Veroli in the 1480s.

4. Mechanisms of textual change and their stemmatic value

The following examples illustrate how textual changes can arise. They are
methodological examples, not reported readings assigned to named
Vitruvian witnesses. A change acquires stemmatic significance only when
its distribution, probability, and relation to contamination have been
established from the apparatus or the manuscripts.

I. Omission by homoeoteleuton. A scribe’s eye may pass between similar
endings and omit the intervening text. A shared, unlikely omission may

                           986

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER

indicate common ancestry, provided independent recurrence and later
correction have been considered.

II. Dittography. A word or phrase may be copied twice. The same
repetition in several witnesses can be significant, but a common copying
error may also arise independently.

III. Corruption of Greek terminology. An unfamiliar Greek expression
may be altered, transliterated inconsistently, or replaced. Its evidential
value depends on the  precise reading and  its distribution among
identified witnesses.

IV. Explanatory substitution. A technical expression may be replaced by
a more familiar one. Such a substitution must be documented before it is
attributed to a particular witness or branch.

V. Transposition. Words, clauses, or larger units may change position.
Shared unusual dislocations can be valuable evidence, particularly where
they reveal the arrangement of an earlier exemplar.

VI. Grammatical normalization. A copyist or editor may regularize an
unfamiliar construction or  spelling. An assimilated spelling  is not
inherently  preferable  to  an  unassimilated  one,  and  common
normalizations alone rarely establish a unique genealogy.

VII. Numbers and proportions. Numerals, fractions, and dimensional
signs are especially vulnerable in technical texts. Agreement must be
assessed at a specific locus; a plausible reconstructed dimension does not
independently establish the transmitted figure.

VIII. Suppression of repetition. A passage judged redundant may be
shortened. The editor must distinguish deliberate abbreviation from
accidental omission and from an author’s own repetition.

IX. Explanatory additions. A marginal or interlinear gloss may enter the
running text. Its origin and date cannot be inferred from brackets alone;
the relevant edition’s editorial signs must be read in context.

X. Contamination. Consultation of more than one exemplar can
produce a witness that shares readings with different groups. A stemma
therefore requires an account of corrections and mixed readings as well as
a diagram of descent.

5. The primacy of H and the constitution of the text
Harley MS 2767 (H), copied in the first quarter of the ninth century, is the
oldest known surviving witness. Krohn distinguishes its side of the tradition,
with S, from the Gudianus witnesses E and G. The precise genealogy remains an
editorial reconstruction; neither the age of H nor a simplified stemma proves
that all later manuscripts descend directly from it.
The constitution of the text requires comparison of readings, not a presumption
that all witnesses descend directly from H. Krohn’s printed text supplies the
principal control for the running Latin in this edition. The explanatory notes
below discuss the adopted wording and its interpretation; an attribution to an
individual manuscript  requires an  identifiable apparatus entry or  direct
examination of that witness.

Vitruvius frequently uses Greek technical vocabulary, sometimes in Greek

corruption, and a dictionary lemma need not be the inflected form printed in

I. Aesthetic and modular concepts (Book I, chapter 2)

1. τάξις (taxis)
    Textual form: τάξις in Krohn, I.2.1.
Restitution: τάξις (nominative singular, from τάσσω, ‘to set in order’, ‘to arrange
in a row’).

   Vitruvian equivalent: ordinatio.
Note: not to be confused with the mere placing of objects. In Aristotle and
Hellenistic usage τάξις implies a mathematical and quantitative ordering.
Vitruvius defines it as the measure of the members of a work in relation to the
whole through the module (modulus): the establishment of the basic metric
pattern.

2. διάθεσις (diathesis)
    Textual form: διάθεσιν, accusative singular, in Krohn, I.2.1.
Restitution: διάθεσις (Vitruvius uses the accusative διάθεσιν; from διατίθημι, ‘to
dispose’, ‘to arrange effectively’).

   Vitruvian equivalent: dispositio.
Note: the expression of the τάξις in design. It is made visible through three modes
of graphic representation (ideae): ichnographia (plan), orthographia (elevation)
and scaenographia (perspective).

3. οἰκονομία (oikonomia)
    Textual form: οἰκονομία in Krohn,  I.2.1; oeconomia  is a Latin
    transliteration.
    Restitution:  οἰκονομία  (from  οἶκος,  ‘house’,  and  νόμος,  ‘law,
   management’).

   Vitruvian equivalent: distributio.
Note: under Augustus the term carries a double, technical and financial nuance.
It implies the prudent management of materials and budget (sumptus), but also

4. εὐρυθμία (eurythmia)
   Corrupt reading: eurithmia, euritmia (direct Latinisation).
Lexical form: εὐρυθμία, with the prefix εὖ and the noun ῥυθμός, ‘rhythm’ or

Note: a qualitative concept of visual perception. Whereas τάξις  is purely

5. συμμετρία (symmetria)
Latinised form: symmetria. The Greek lemma explains the technical vocabulary;

    Restitution: συμμετρία (from σύν, ‘with’, and μέτρον, ‘measure’).

VITRUVIUS TODAY: SURVIVAL OF A

CANON

De architectura is not a museum piece. Its categories continue to operate,
sometimes  explicitly,  in  contemporary  architectural  culture, and   it  is

                           997

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

appropriate to conclude this study by pointing out three lines of enduring
influence.
The Triad and the Modulor. The celebrated triad firmitas, utilitas, venustas—
solidity, utility, beauty—continues to be the implicit framework by which built
works are judged.  Its most direct descendant in the 20th century  is Le
Corbusier's Modulor  (1948),  a  system  of  proportions  based on  the
measurements of the human body and the golden section, which reinterprets,
in modern language, the ancient Vitruvian doctrine of the body as measure
(homo bene  figuratus, De  architectura  3.1). Le  Corbusier  consciously
acknowledged himself as the heir to this tradition: the Modulor is, in essence, a
reinterpretation of Vitruvius's anthropometric canon in light of industrial
standardization.
Proportion, Parametrization, and BIM. The Vitruvian idea of symmetria—the
commensurability  of  the  parts with  the whole based on  a module—
conceptually prefigures current parametric design, where the geometry of the
building is governed by relationships and rules rather than fixed dimensions.
Building Information Modeling (BIM) methodologies, which integrate design,
construction, and maintenance information into a single model, also revive
Vitruvius's ambition of an architecture understood as a holistic knowledge that
articulates materials, technique, function, and understanding.
Firmitas and Sustainability. Finally, Vitruvius's concern for site selection,
orientation, air quality, and the use of local resources (Books I, VI, and VIII)
resonates  strongly with  the contemporary agenda  of  sustainability and
bioclimatic architecture. Firmitas, as understood today, is not only structural
solidity but also durability and environmental responsibility: the building that
endures and is wisely integrated into its surroundings. In this sense, Vitruvius
remains a relevant voice twenty centuries later.

Appendix Q · Status quaestionis: a survey of modern
Vitruvian scholarship

The study of De architectura has been transformed over the past century by new
critical editions, philological commentary, and—most recently—archaeology.
The following survey outlines the principal questions that continue to occupy
specialists, so that the reader may situate the present edition within the living
debate.

On the text and its transmission. The editions of Valentin Rose (1867;
1899) and Fritz Krohn (1912) remain central to the constitution of the
Latin text. Harley MS 2767 is the oldest known surviving copy and a
witness of substantial authority. Krohn distinguishes H and S from E and
G; the later witnesses cannot all be dismissed as a single contaminated
group. The weight of each reading must be considered at its locus.
On the date and unity of the work. The treatise is generally dated between 27
and 23 BCE and dedicated to Augustus. While some scholars have detected
signs of stratified composition or later interpolation in particular passages, the
substantial unity of the ten books is now broadly accepted.
On the author’s identity. Almost nothing is known of Vitruvius’s life beyond
what the prefaces disclose: military service under Caesar and a pension obtained
through the mediation of Octavia. The cognomen Pollio rests on slender and
late evidence, and the older identification of the author with Mamurra
(proposed by Thielscher) is now generally rejected.
On the foundational categories. The interpretation of ordinatio, dispositio,
eurythmia, symmetria, decor, and distributio is a central crux. Following the
commentary of Pierre Gros in the Budé edition and the philological studies of
Louis Callebat, symmetria is now understood as commensurability—modular
proportion—rather than modern  bilateral symmetry. In the Anglophone
sphere, the translation and commentary of Ingrid D. Rowland and Thomas
Noble Howe (1999) and the work of Indra Kagis McEwen on the Vitruvian
body have reframed much of the discussion.
On the Greek sources and reception. Vitruvius drew on lost Greek treatises,
including those of Hermogenes and Pytheos and the authors cataloged in Book

VII. The extent of his Hellenistic debt remains a subject of scholarship.
Leonardo’s drawing of about 1490 belongs to an early phase of Renaissance

excavation, it would permit his theoretical prescriptions to be tested against

EDITORIAL RATIONALE

Ratio editionis

This edition presents the Latin text of the ten books of De architectura with an
accompanying English translation, technical commentary, and a selective
apparatus. It is a reading edition grounded in the named printed editions; the
identification of each quoted reading remains essential to  its philological
argument.
The stated reference text of this reading edition is Fritz Krohn’s Vitruvii de
architectura libri decem (Leipzig: B. G. Teubner, 1912). Rose (1899) remains a
comparative edition, and the Budé volumes provide further textual and
architectural reference where cited. The English derives from the author’s
Spanish translation and is checked against the Latin at doubtful terms and
passages. References to these editions do not constitute a new collation of the
manuscripts or certify that every Budé apparatus has been checked afresh.
Substantive departures from the stated base require explicit explanation at the
relevant locus.

The manuscript tradition. De architectura survives through a complex
medieval transmission. Harley MS 2767 is an important Carolingian
witness, while Gudianus 69 preserves a collateral line of value for textual
criticism. The documented provenance of Harley must be distinguished
from accounts of Renaissance discoveries at St Gall. The original

Apparatus fontium (selective). Vitruvius acknowledges his debts —above
all in the preface to Book VII—, though all his sources are lost. The principal
authorities he names are, by field: in architecture and proportions, Pythius and
Hermogenes of Priene, Silenus, Theodorus, Arcesius, and Philo (and the less
celebrated  Nexaris,  Theocydes,  Demophilos,  Pollis,  Leonides,  Silanion,
Melampus, Sarnacus, and Euphranor); in mechanics (7 pr. 14), Diades,
Archytas,  Archimedes,  Ctesibius, Nymphodorus,  Philo  of  Byzantium,
Diphilus, Democles, Charidas, Polyidus, Pyrrus, and Agesistratus; in music,
Aristoxenus of Tarentum; in scene-painting and perspective, Agatharchus of
Samos, with Democritus and Anaxagoras; in astronomy and gnomonics,
Berosus the Chaldean, Aristarchus of Samos, Eudoxus, Apollonius, Scopinas,
Thales, and Anaximander; in philosophy and science, Plato (the doubling of the
square, 9 pr.) and Pythagoras. Among the Latins he cites Fuficius (the first to
write on architecture in Latin), Terentius Varro (who included architecture
among his Disciplinae), and Publius Septimius. Modern scholarship (Granger,
Gros) accepts that Vitruvius selected what was useful from these works, partly
through Varro, partly at first hand.

Glossary of philological principles (for the non-specialist reader)
Archetype (Ω) — the  lost common ancestor from which  all surviving
manuscripts descend; because it is lost, the editor must reconstruct its readings
from the descendants.



                           1007

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

Stemma codicum — the genealogical tree of the manuscripts, showing which
copies depend on which and so which readings are likeliest to go back to Ω.
Apparatus criticus — the band of notes printed beneath the Latin text
recording the variant readings of the witnesses and the reasons for the editor’s
choice; what may look like “mere grammar” is in fact the recovery of the original
sense.
Lectio difficilior potior — “the more difficult reading  is the stronger”:
between two readings the harder is the likelier original, since copyists tend to
simplify an unfamiliar text — and Vitruvius’s technical Latin was often
unfamiliar.
Lectio facilior — the “easier” reading, frequently a later simplification or a
fifteenth-century humanist “correction” that smoothed the grammar at the cost
of authenticity.
Contaminatio — the mixing of readings from two or more manuscript
families in a single copy (as in the Selestadiensis), producing a hybrid text that
the editor must disentangle.
Crux desperationis (†) — the “cross of despair”, placed in the text where a
passage is so corrupt that it cannot be restored with certainty — a mark of
editorial honesty rather than of failure.

The oldest codices and their history

The transmission of De architectura rests almost entirely on the work of
Carolingian copyists. When, around the year 800, the cultural renaissance
fostered by Charlemagne and his teachers — Alcuin of York, Theodulf of
Orléans — promoted the systematic copying of ancient authors, Vitruvius's
treatise was one of the technical texts that escaped oblivion. The essential
testimony of the entire tradition dates from that period.

H · Codex Harleianus 2767

Harley MS 2767, copied in Caroline minuscule in the first quarter of the ninth
century, is the oldest known surviving copy of De architectura. The British
Library gives Cologne or Aachen as possible places of origin and treats the
palace-scriptorium  association  as  uncertain.  Its  documented  medieval
provenance includes St Pantaleon in Cologne. Two leaves are now in Oxford,
