Bodleian Library, Rawlinson MS D. 893,  ff. 135–136. The later history
recorded by the catalog leads through the collections of Graevius, the Elector
Palatine, Zamboni and the Harleys; it does not establish a discovery by Poggio
at St Gall. Its authority is therefore assessed through its text and documented
history, without making it the sole source of every surviving witness.

G · Codex Gudianus 69

Preserved in the Herzog August Bibliothek in Wolfenbüttel, it is the principal
witness to the second lineage of the tradition. Although somewhat later than the
Harleian, it occasionally transmits its own readings and valuable corrections not
found in H, which is why modern editors systematically compare  it. The
famous divergence in De arch. 6.6.4 — the granaries with " solid " (according to
H) or " raised " (according to G) floors — illustrates the usefulness of comparing
both families.

Other ancient witnesses

Other early witnesses. The relations of the Leiden, Pithoeanus and Selestadiensis
witnesses must be established within the sigla and argument of a particular
edition. Krohn groups the Selestadiensis (S) with H, while placing the Gudianus
witnesses E and G on the other side of the tradition. Contamination, correction
and collateral descent require textual evidence. A hypothetical chain through lost
manuscripts at Fulda or Reichenau should not be presented as a documented
provenance of Harley MS 2767.

It is worth remembering, contrary to the common notion of Vitruvius being "
rediscovered " during the Renaissance, that the treatise never completely fell out of
use: it was known and cited by medieval scholars such as Alcuin, Einhard, Hugh
of Saint Victor, Vincent of Beauvais, and Hildegard of Bingen. Poggio's discovery
in 1416 did not rescue the text from oblivion, but rather returned its finest
testimony to scholarly circulation.

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

Theses on Vitruvius

This chapter gathers, in concise form, the principal scholarly positions that
underlie the present edition. They are offered as theses for discussion: where a
statement rests on textual, archaeological, or philological evidence it is presented
as such; where it belongs to the editor’s interpretive proposal, it is expressly
marked as the author’s hypothesis and not as established consensus. The chapter
is deliberately brief and may be expanded in subsequent editions.

1. A single complete witness, not the “first architect.”
De architectura  is not the earliest architecture ever written but the only
complete treatise on the subject to survive from classical antiquity. Vitruvius’s
historical importance lies in this completeness and in the systematic ambition of
his ten books, not in any claim to have founded the discipline. The Greek
treatises of Hermogenes, Pytheos and others that Vitruvius cites as his sources
are lost; what survives of the ancient theory of building survives largely through
him, so the claim this edition defends is one of transmission and completeness,
not of priority.

2. The triad is a system, not a checklist.
firmitas, utilitas, and venustas (De architectura 1.3.2) are neither optional nor
separable. In Vitruvius’s conception, beauty arises from, and is inseparable
from, sound construction and fitness for use; the same proportional reasoning
that makes a building stand also makes it pleasing. Read in this way the three
terms are not a checklist to be satisfied in turn but a single requirement seen
from three sides, and the later reception that treated them as separable departs
from Vitruvius’s own emphasis on their interdependence.

3. symmetria is modular commensurability, not modern
symmetry.
Vitruvian symmetria (συμμετρία) denotes the proportional correspondence of
the parts to one another and to the whole through a common module; it must
not be read as the modern, post-eighteenth-century notion of bilateral or mirror
symmetry. The confusion  is  consequential,  for rendering symmetria  as
“symmetry” imports a modern visual idea of balance that the Latin does not
carry and obscures the modular reasoning — the use of a common module
(modulus) — on which the whole proportional system rests.

                           1012

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER

4. The homo bene figuratus is not the “Vitruvian Man.”
Vitruvius (3.1) describes a well-proportioned human figure inscribed within
circle and square as a canon of proportion; he does not give the celebrated phrase
or image later associated with Leonardo. The Renaissance “Vitruvian Man” is
an interpretive elaboration, not a quotation of the text. His concern is to derive
the proportions of the temple from those of the well-formed body; the image of
a single figure simultaneously inscribed in circle and square, with its famous
shifting of centers, is Leonardo’s graphic solution to a problem the text poses
but does not itself resolve.

5. Pythagorean number-symbolism is the author’s hypothesis.
Vitruvius names Pythagoras and the practice of composing precepts in “cubes”
of 216 verses (6³) in the preface to Book V; his use of number is technical. Any
further reading of 216 or of the cube as a carrier of cosmic or sacred meaning is
advanced here explicitly as the author’s interpretive proposal, not as Vitruvius’s
stated intention. The distinction  is methodological: the technical use of
proportion is documented and defended philologically, whereas the symbolic
resonance of particular numbers is offered as a separate and clearly labeled
interpretive layer.

6. The transmission preserves collateral witnesses.
The text descends through a complex medieval manuscript tradition in which
the Carolingian Harleianus 2767 (H) is a major witness and Gudianus 69 (G)
preserves an important collateral line. The Latin in this edition follows Krohn
(1912), checked against Rose (1899) and the Budé volumes. Greek technical
terminology,  sometimes  corrupted  or  transliterated  in  transmission,  is
normalized in the present text according to the critical editions and discussed in
Appendix N and the Conspectus of Greek Terms.

7. The Basilica at Fano is the one work Vitruvius claims — and a current
test case.
The basilica at Fanum Fortunae is the building Vitruvius explicitly says he
designed and supervised (5.1.6–10). On 19 January 2026 the Italian Ministry of
Culture announced the identification of the remains in Piazza Andrea Costa as
that basilica, and further archaeological investigation continued. Institutional
identification, excavated evidence, the ancient measurements and modern

8. The survival of a canon.
The afterlife of De architectura — from its Carolingian copying and humanist
rediscovery to the editio princeps of 1486 and the treatises of the Renaissance
— is itself part of its meaning: Vitruvius matters not only for what he records of
Roman practice but for the canon of proportion and decorum that later ages
built upon his text. The present edition is itself a moment in that reception: a
bilingual critical text addressed to the architect-reader as much as to the
philologist.

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

Excursus · The Querelle of Proportion: Vitruvius,
Palladio, and Perrault

No question runs deeper through the reception of the De architectura than this
one: are the proportions that Vitruvius records grounded in nature, and
therefore binding upon every architect in every age, or are they conventions —
beautiful because they are familiar, authoritative because they are old? On the
answer hangs the whole status of Vitruvius’ canon. If proportion is a law of
nature, the treatise is a body of science; if it is custom, the treatise is a record of
taste. The debate came to a head in seventeenth-century France, but its terms
are already latent in Vitruvius himself.
Vitruvius grounds beauty in symmetria — the commensurability of every part
with a fixed module — and derives that commensurability from the proportions
of the well-formed human body (3.1) and, by analogy, from the consonances of
music (5.4). For him the orders are not arbitrary: the Doric carries the
proportions of a man, the Ionic those of a matron, the Corinthian those of a
maiden  (4.1). Proportion  is thus a natural and quasi-mathematical  fact,
discovered rather than invented.
Andrea Palladio (1508–1580) inherited this conviction and gave it its most
influential modern form. In the I quattro libri dell’architettura (Venice, 1570)
he prescribes seven “most beautiful” room-shapes whose ratios — the square,
the diagonal of the square, and the simple musical proportions 2:3, 3:4, 3:5 —
echo the harmonic intervals. For Palladio, as for Alberti before him (De re
aedificatoria, 1452), the architect who follows these ratios does not impose a
private preference but obeys a harmony written into the cosmos. This is the
doctrine that Rudolf Wittkower named the “harmonic” or “musical” theory of
proportion.
Claude Perrault (1613–1688), physician, anatomist and member of the
Académie des Sciences, also participated in the Louvre colonnade project. His
French translation, Les dix livres d’architecture de Vitruve (Paris, 1673; revised
1684), brought together commentary and engraved illustrations. His criticism
of proportional authority must be read in the context of that close engagement
with the treatise.

In the preface to that translation, and at length in the Ordonnance des cinq
espèces de  colonnes  selon  la méthode  des  anciens  (Paris, 1683),  Perrault
distinguished two kinds of architectural beauty. Positive beauty (beauté positive)
rests on causes that convince everyone — richness of material, precision and
cleanness of execution, bilateral regularity, and magnitude. Arbitrary beauty
(beauté arbitraire), by contrast, comprises the proportions of the orders; these
please us, Perrault argued, not because reason or nature compels them but
because custom and association have accustomed the eye to them. There is no
single ratio that nature dictates: the proof, he observed, is that the proportions
admired by the ancients themselves vary from building to building and from
author to author.
From this premise Perrault drew a practical method as radical as his theory.
Rather than seek the one true proportion, he proposed a mean or averaged
system, derived by reconciling the divergent measures of the most admired
ancient buildings into a simple, memorable rule. Proportion, for Perrault, was
to be regulated by reasonable convention — by the architect’s judgment and the
consensus of taste — not deduced from a law of nature.
The challenge did not go unanswered. François Blondel (1618–1686), first
director of the Académie Royale d’Architecture, defended the older view in his
Cours  d’architecture (1675–1683),  insisting that proportion  possesses an
objective foundation in number, in music, and in nature, exactly as Vitruvius
had  taught. The exchange between  Perrault and  Blondel became  the
architectural front of the wider querelle des anciens et des modernes: Blondel for
the ancients and the absolute, Perrault for the moderns and the conventional.
The quarrel was never settled, and that is its importance. It exposed, once and
for all, that the Vitruvian canon can be read in two incompatible ways, and that
a reader must choose. Later theory has oscillated between the poles. The
harmonic tradition revived in the proportional systems of the nineteenth
century and in Le Corbusier’s Modulor (1948), which sought once more to
anchor design in the measures of the body; the conventionalist tradition fed the
historicism and, ultimately, the proportional skepticism of much modern
practice.
For the present edition the controversy carries a precise consequence. When
Vitruvius states that a column shall be of such-and-such a diameter, or that the

eustyle intercolumniation shall measure two and a quarter diameters, the
modern reader is entitled to ask whether such figures record a discovered law or
a codified habit. This edition takes no side in the metaphysical question. It
renders the proportions faithfully, as Vitruvius gives them, and leaves to the
architect — as Perrault would have wished, and as Palladio would have resisted
— the freedom to regard them either as nature’s rule or as the accumulated
wisdom of a tradition. The text is law for those who read it as law, and counsel
for those who read it as counsel.

The Fano basilica: the case of direct verification
The basilica of Fanum Fortunae is the only building Vitruvius claims to have
designed and supervised himself (conlocavi curavique faciendam, 5.1.6), and so
it offers an exceptional test of the text against material remains. In January 2026
the Italian authorities (the Marche Region, the Municipality of Fano and the
Soprintendenza) announced the identification, in Piazza Andrea Costa at Fano,
of the remains of a monumental basilica attributed to this work. The features
made public correspond strikingly to the Vitruvian description: a rectangular

Augustan age. It should be stressed, however, that the excavation is still in

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY

EPILOGUE

The figure of Vitruvius presents a paradox characteristic of many foundational
authors: while we know remarkably little about his life, his De architectura has
shaped  architectural thought  for more than two thousand  years. This
disproportion between the obscurity of the author and the enduring legacy of
his work is not accidental: it is the very nature of foundational texts, which
survive precisely because they cease to belong to their author and become the
heritage of their readers.
Vitruvius’s treatise has come down to us mutilated, deprived of its original
figures. The illustrations that accompanied the text — the diagrams of the
orders, the plans of the temples, the layouts of the machines — were lost
somewhere in the chain of copies, and the Renaissance had to reconstruct them
with ruler and compass from the words alone. This loss, far from impoverishing
the work, made it fruitful: it forced Alberti, Cesariano, Palladio, and Barbaro to
read Vitruvius with pencil in hand, transforming philology into a project and
commentary into architecture.
If this journey through the Ten Books teaches us anything, it is that the triad
Vitruvius enunciated — firmitas, utilitas, venustas — does not describe three
separable qualities, but rather three facets of the same measure. Solidity without
utility is premature ruin; utility without beauty, mere construction; beauty
without solidity, ephemeral scenery. For Vitruvius, architecture begins where
the three converge, and this conviction — that number, matter, and form obey
a single reason — remains the core of any architectural theory worthy of the
name.
This edition has sought to uphold a twofold commitment: historical and
philological rigor, on the one hand, and openness to the symbolic dimension of
the treatise, on the other, always maintaining the distinction between what the
sources allow us to affirm and what belongs to the author's interpretation.
Perhaps this is the most faithful way to honor Vitruvius, who wrote convinced
that the architect should master both the square and astronomy, construction
and reasoning, the hand and number.
A debt and a hope remain. Every edition of a classical work is provisional:
further collation, closer translation and a more precise apparatus can always

surviving voice. As he observes, the gifts of fortune are quickly lost, whereas
